text:
COURS: Duration_Models (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Chapitre 2 : Hazards Model
SECTION: Time Dependent Covariates
SLIDE: Variables that linearly increase with time
CONTENU:
- A common source of confusion is whether the age variable is time dependent

- Indeed, the age increases with time itself

- $\Rightarrow$ the age is definitely a time dependent variable

- But it has no effect on the model if one includes it as time varying covariate

- To see why this happens defined the current age of a subject by

$$ x(t) = x(0) + t $$

where $x(0)$ denotes the age at entry into the study

- $\Rightarrow$ Then, the hazard function is given by

$$ h(t) = h_{0}(t)e^{\beta x(t)} = \big( h_{0}(t)e^{\beta t} \big) e^{\beta x(0)} $$

such that once we insert $h(t)$ in the partial likelihood,

$$ e^{\beta t} $$

appears in both the numerator and the denominator of each factor

- $\Rightarrow$ Hence, it cancels out as does the baseline hazard
slide_title: Variables that linearly increase with time

text:
COURS: Duration_Models (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model
SECTION: Competing Risks
SLIDE: Clustered survival times
CONTENU:
- Until now, we have considered data with a single cause of failure

- Also, we have assumed that survival times were independent

- $\Rightarrow$ How to deal with events that are dependent across individuals ?

- Covid-19 propagation is an example of what we call clustered data

- $\Rightarrow$ contamination are more likely to occur for people in a same unit

- e.g. children in the same school, employees in the same office, etc.

- In such a case, survival times within a cluster are more similar to each other than to those from other clusters

- $\Rightarrow$ the independence assumption no longer holds

- $\Rightarrow$ How to deal with an event that can occur repeatedly ?

- The seizure (crise d'épilespsie) is another example of clustered data

- $\Rightarrow$ the event may repeat indefinitely per person
chapter: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model

text:
COURS: Duration_Models (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model
SECTION: Competing Risks
SLIDE: Washington Ashkenazi study : dependent data
CONTENU:

text:
COURS: Duration_Models (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model
SECTION: Competing Risks
SLIDE: Marginal Survival Models (MSM)
CONTENU:
- This approach ignores clustered data when estimating the model

- $\Rightarrow$ Clusters are accounted for when computing standard errors of $\widehat\beta$

- MSM relies on standard Cox model estimation

- Assume there is one covariate with parameter estimate $\widehat\beta$ and $\sigma^{2}_{\widehat\beta} = \mathbb{V}(\widehat\beta)$

- $\sigma^{2}_{\widehat\beta}$ can be misleading as it assumes that all subjects are independent

- $\Rightarrow$ It has to be corrected for the clustering impact

- The correction requires to first define the following score residuals

$$ s_{ij} = \delta_{ij}\big(x_{ij} - \bar{x}(t_{ij})\big) - \sum_{t_{u}\leq t_{ij}}\big(x_{i} - \bar{x}(t_{ij})\big) e^{x_{i}\beta}\Big(\widehat{H}_{0}(t_{u}) - \widehat{H}_{0}(t_{u-1}) \Big) $$

where we can notice that the first part is the Schoenfeld residuals

- The variance correction is then given by

$$ C = \sum_{i=1}^{G}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{i}}\sum_{m=1}^{n_{i}}s_{ij}s_{im}, \;\; G \text{ and } n_{i} \text{ are defined in the next slide} $$

where the cluster-adjusted standard error for $\widehat\beta$ is $\sigma_{\widehat\beta}^{*} = (\mathbb{V}(\widehat\beta)\times C)^{1/2}$
chapter: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model

text:
COURS: Duration_Models (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model
SECTION: Competing Risks
SLIDE: Cluster-adjusted standard errors
CONTENU:
- When there are $q$ covariates in the Cox model, $\beta$ is a vector

- We hence have to apply the correction to the whole estimated covariance matrix of $\beta$

- The score residuals are now $1\times q$ matrices and C is a $q \times q$ matrix as

$$ C = \sum_{i=1}^{G}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{i}}\sum_{m=1}^{n_{i}}s_{ij}'s_{im} $$

where $G$ is the number of clusters (assumed to be known here) and $n_{i}$ is the number of failure in the $i$th cluster

- Then, the cluster-adjusted covariance matrix is given by

$$ V^{*} = \mathbb{V}(\widehat\beta) C \mathbb{V}(\widehat\beta) $$

the traditional sandwich estimator

- $\Rightarrow$ Adjusted standard errors are then derived as follows

$$ se(\widehat\beta) = \operatorname{diag}(V^{*})^{1/2} $$
chapter: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model

text:
COURS: Duration_Models (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model
SECTION: Competing Risks
SLIDE: Frailty survival models : recall
CONTENU:
- Another approach is to generalize to clustered data the likelihood

- Recall Under the independence assumption, we may write (see Chapter 1)

$$ \mathcal{L}(\beta; x_{i}) = \prod_{i = 1}^{n} f(t_{i},\beta)^{\delta_{i}}S(t_{i},\beta)^{1-\delta_{i}} = \prod_{i = 1}^{n} h(t_{i},\beta)^{\delta_{i}}S(t_{i},\beta) $$

- Recall Under proportional hazards assumption (Cox) it becomes

$$ \mathcal{L}(\beta; x_{i}) = \prod_{i = 1}^{n}\Big( h_{0}(t_{i})e^{x_{i}\beta} \Big)^{\delta_{i}}e^{-H_{0}(t_{i})\exp(x_{i}\beta)} $$

where

$$ H_{0}(t_{i}) = - \int_{0}^{t_{i}} h_{0}(v)dv $$

is the baseline cumulative hazard
chapter: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model

text:
COURS: Duration_Models (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model
SECTION: Competing Risks
SLIDE: Frailty survival models : principle
CONTENU:
- The idea is to assign each individual in a cluster a common factor

- $\Rightarrow$ this common factor is known as frailty or random effect and denoted

$$ \omega_{i} $$

for the $i$th cluster

- Then, for the $j$th subject in the $i$th cluster, the hazard function is

$$ h_{ij}(t_{ij}) = h_{0}(t_{ij})\omega_{i}e^{x_{ij}\beta} $$
- We allow for $\omega_{i}$ to vary from one cluster to another

- $\Rightarrow$ a common model that governs this variability is a gamma distribution

$$ g(\omega,\theta) = \frac{\omega^{1/\theta - 1}e^{-\omega/\theta}}{\Gamma(1/\theta)\theta^{1/\theta}} $$
- An alternative is to use a standard normal distribution

$$ h_{ij}(t_{ij}) = h_{0}(t_{ij})\omega_{i}e^{x_{ij}\beta} = h_{0}(t_{ij})e^{x_{ij}\btxt{\beta}+\ntxt{u_{i}\sigma}}, \text{ as } \omega_{i} = e^{u_{i}\sigma} $$

such that the random and fixed effects are put on the same level
chapter: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model

text:
COURS: Duration_Models (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model
SECTION: Competing Risks
SLIDE: Frailty survival models : unfeasible estimation
CONTENU:
- Assuming that the frailties $\omega_{i}$ are observed, the joint likelihood is

$$ \mathcal{L}_{ij}(\beta,\theta;\omega_{i},t_{ij},\delta_{ij},x_{ij}) = g(\omega_{i},\theta)\Big(h_{0}(t_{ij})\omega_{i}e^{x_{ij}\beta}\Big)^{\delta_{ij}}e^{-H_{0}(t_{ij})\omega_{i}\exp(x_{ij}\beta)} $$

and the full likelihood is

$$ \mathcal{L}_{ij}(\beta,\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^{G}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{i}}\mathcal{L}_{ij}(\beta,\theta;\omega_{i},t_{ij},\delta_{ij},x_{ij}) $$

- MLE of $\beta$ and $\theta$ is feasible under assumption that

$$ \omega_{i}, \;\; t_{ij}, \;\;\delta_{ij}, \;\; x_{ij} $$

are observed

- Although we can have an idea of the number of clusters, the frailties

$$ \omega_{i} $$

are in general not observed directly
chapter: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model

text:
COURS: Duration_Models (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model
SECTION: Competing Risks
SLIDE: Frailty survival models : EM algorithm
CONTENU:
- In the more realistic case where $\omega_{i}$ are unknown

- ... one can use the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm

- $\Rightarrow$ It alternates between finding expected values for $\omega_{i}$ based on current estimates of

$$ \beta \text{ and } \theta $$

and using these expected values to find updated estimates for

$$ \beta \text{ and } \theta $$

until convergence

- If we use a parametric distribution for

$$ f(t,\beta) $$

setting up the EM algorithm is fairly direct

- Generalizing this to the semi-parametric Cox model is more complex

text:
COURS: Duration_Models (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model
SECTION: Competing Risks
SLIDE: Cause-specific hazards
CONTENU:
- Until now we have considered a single, well-defined outcome

- In some study we may face multiple causes of failure

- e.g. an employee can quit the job for different reasons: fired, retirement, ...

- A naive solution is to focus on a particular type of failure

- ... and treat the others as a type of censoring

- This is questionable as censoring relies on an independence assumption

- $\Rightarrow$ What we face here are competing risks, and we have to examine them

- Note 1 Interpretation of survival analyses in the presence of competing risks will always be subject to at least some ambiguity due to uncertainty about the degree of dependence among the competing outcomes

- Note 2 For a particular subject, we observe only one cause of failure

text:
COURS: Duration_Models (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model
SECTION: Competing Risks
SLIDE: The cumulative incidence functions
CONTENU:
- How to formally address this issue in a non-parametric framework ?

- To develop a formal model to accommodate competing risks,

- ... assume that there are $K<\infty$ distinct causes of failure

- Also assume that the subject can experience at most one of the $K$ causes

- Then, for each cause of interest, we defined as sub-distribution function

$$ F_{j}(t) = \mathbb{P}(T\leq t, C = j) = \int_{0}^{t}h_{j}(u)S(u)du $$

also known as cumulative risk (or incidence) function for the $j$th cause

- It is increasing as any cumulative distribution function

- ... but goes, in the limit, to the probability of failure from the $j$th cause rather than to 1

$$ F_{j}(\infty) = \mathbb{P}(C=j) $$
chapter: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model

text:
COURS: Duration_Models (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model
SECTION: Competing Risks
SLIDE: The cause-specific hazard
CONTENU:
- The cause-specific hazard is hence defined conditionally to $C=j$

$$ h_{j} = \lim\limits_{\delta \to 0}\Big(\frac{\mathbb{P}(t<T< t+\delta, C = j|T>t)}{\delta}\Big) $$
- One can obtain the whole hazards function as follows

$$ h(t) = \sum_{j=1}^{K}h_{j}(t) $$
- $\Rightarrow$ The risk of failure at a particular time is simply the sum of the risks of all specific causes at that time

- Now assume that we have $D$ distinct ordered failure times $t_{1},t_{2},\ldots,t_{D}$

- We may estimate the hazard at the $i$th time $t_{i}$ using

$$ \widehat{h}(t_{i}) = d_{i}/n_{i} $$

and the cause-specific hazard for the $k$th type cause as

$$ \widehat{h}_{k}(t_{i}) = d_{ik}/n_{i} $$

i.e. the # of events of type $k$ at $t_{i}$ divided by the # of subjects at risk
chapter: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model

text:
COURS: Duration_Models (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model
SECTION: Competing Risks
SLIDE: Estimating cause-specific hazards
CONTENU:
- The sum over all cause-specific hazards is estimated as

$$ \widehat{h}(t_{i}) = n_{i}^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{K}d_{ik} $$
- The probability of failure from any cause at $t_{i}$ is

$$ \widehat{S}(t_{i-1}) \times \widehat{h}(t_{i}) $$

and hence, for a particular cause $k$ we have

$$ \widehat{S}(t_{i-1}) \times \widehat{h}_{k}(t_{i}) $$

from which we obtain an estimate of the cumulative incidence function

$$ \widehat{F}_{k}(t) = \sum_{t_{i}\leq t}\widehat{S}(t_{i-1}) \times \widehat{h}_{k}(t_{i}) $$

text:
COURS: Duration_Models (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model
SECTION: Competing Risks
SLIDE: The Fine-Gray method for cause-specific hazards
CONTENU:
- A solution that can overcome this issue is to set

$$ h_{k}(t) = \lim\limits_{\delta \to 0}\Big(\frac{\mathbb{P}(t<T_{k}< t+\delta|E)}{\delta}\Big) $$

i.e. to define the effects of covariates on the cause specific hazards where

$$ E = \Big((T_{k}>t \text{ or } (\ntxt{T_{k'}\leq t} \text{ and } k' \neq k) \Big) $$

denotes the conditional event

- The effects of the covariates enter the sub-distribution hazard as follows

- $\Rightarrow$ the conditioning set specifies not only $T_{k}>t$ but also allows other events

- ... in which case we must have $\ntxt{T_{k'}\leq t}$

- $\Rightarrow$ the risk set includes not only those currently alive and at risk for the $k$th event type but also those who failed earlier of causes of type $k'$

text:
COURS: Duration_Models (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model
SECTION: Competing Risks
SLIDE: The Fine-Gray method and the model of Cox
CONTENU:
- The Fine-Gray framework meets the proportional hazard models by setting

$$ h_{k}(t) = -\frac{\delta \log(1-F_{k}(t))}{\delta t} $$
- A proportional Cox-type equation is then apply to sub-distribution hazard

$$ h_{k}(t,x,\beta) = h_{0,k}(t)e^{x\beta} $$
- $\Rightarrow$ the sub-distribution hazard for a subject with covariate $x$ is proportional to a baseline sub-distribution function $h_{0,k}(t)$

SLIDE: The parametric approach
CONTENU:
- In what follows, we develop further the MLE section of Chapter 1

- Non-parametric (e.g. KME) and semi-parametric (e.g. Cox model) approaches are powerful

- but they accommodate complex censoring and truncation less directly

- $\Rightarrow$ In the parametric framework, the standard likelihood theory applies

- but its validity depends on the appropriateness of the selected model

- Here we essentially review

- the exponential distribution

- the Weibull distribution

- the log-normal distribution

- the log-logistic distribution
chapter: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model

text:
COURS: Duration_Models (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model
SECTION: Parametric Models
SLIDE: The exponential distribution
CONTENU:
- In Ch. 1, we saw that the simple distribution to work with is the exponential one

- It has constant hazard function $h(t) = \lambda$ ($\Rightarrow$ memory-less property)

- $\Rightarrow$ The risk of facing the event of interest is the same at any point in time

- i.e. neither declines nor increases in time

- Recall The p.d.f and survival functions are

$$ f(t;\lambda) = \lambda e^{\lambda t} \text{ and } S(t;\lambda) = e^{-\lambda t} $$

- In general, it is not flexible enough but it can help in some specific applications

- $\Rightarrow$ power and size calculations

- $\Rightarrow$ The Weibull distribution, of which the exponential distribution is a special case, offers more flexibility
chapter: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model

text:
COURS: Duration_Models (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model
SECTION: Parametric Models
SLIDE: The Weibull distribution
CONTENU:
- Recall The hazard and survival functions are

$$ h(t) = \alpha\lambda t^{\alpha - 1} \text{ and } S(t) = e^{-(\lambda t)^{\alpha}} $$
- In view of introducing covariates in the parametric model, let define

$$ \mu = -log \lambda \text{ and } \sigma = 1/\alpha $$

a location and scale parameter for the distribution

- $\Rightarrow$ One can hence rewrite the hazard and survival functions as

$$ h(t) = \frac{1}{\sigma}e^{-\mu/\sigma} t^{1/\sigma - 1} \text{ and } S(t) = e^{-e^{-\mu/\sigma} t^{1/\sigma}} $$
- Note Obviously, when $\sigma = 1$, this reduces to the exponential distribution
chapter: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model

text:
COURS: Duration_Models (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model
SECTION: Parametric Models
SLIDE: Diagnostic tool for the Weibull distribution
CONTENU:
- Consider now the $g(u) = \log(-\log(u))$ transformation function for $S(t)$

$$ g(S(t_{i})) = \alpha \log(\lambda) + \alpha\log(t_{i}) = -\frac{\mu}{\sigma} + \frac{1}{\sigma}\log(t_{i}) $$
- This will allow for assessing how well a set of survival data follow a Weibull distribution

- 1 First compute the KME $\widehat{S}(t_{i})$ and define

$$ y_{i} = g(\widehat{S}(t_{i})) $$
- 2 Then, plot $y_{i}$ versus $\log(t_{i})$ and fit the linear equation

$$ y = b + m \log t $$

where $m = 1/\sigma$ and $b = -\mu/\sigma$

- $\Rightarrow$ If the plotted points fall along this fitted line, a Weibull distribution should approximate well the distribution of the data

text:
COURS: Duration_Models (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model
SECTION: Parametric Models
SLIDE: MLE of Weibull parameters for a single group of survival data
CONTENU:
- The linear approach is limited but provides good entries for the MLE

- The log-likelihood function is (see Ch. 1)

$$ \ell(\lambda,\alpha) = \sum_{i = 1}^{n}\Big( \delta_{i}\log h(t_{i}) + \log S(t_{i}) \Big) $$
- Substituting the expressions for $h(t_{i})$ and $S(t_{i})$ we get

$$ \ell(\lambda,\alpha) = d\log\alpha + d\alpha\log\lambda + (\alpha -1)\sum_{i = 1}^{n}\delta_{i}\log t_{i} - \lambda^{\alpha}\sum_{i = 1}^{n}t_{i}^{\alpha} $$

with $d = \sum_{i = 1}^{n} \delta_{i}$

- The expression can of course be expressed in terms of $\mu$ and $\sigma$

- Once implemented and applied to the smokers data, we obtain

$$ \widehat\mu_{MLE} = 4.656329 \text{ and } \widehat\sigma_{MLE} = 2.041061 $$
- $\Rightarrow$ The results are not so far from the linear approach

- Note In general, the standard errors are computed for $\widehat\mu_{MLE}$ and $\log\widehat\sigma_{MLE}$

$$ \widehat\sigma_{\mu} = 0.2170 \text{ and } \widehat\sigma_{\log\sigma} = 0.0919 $$
chapter: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model
slide_title: MLE of Weibull parameters for a single group of survival data

text:
COURS: Duration_Models (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model
SECTION: Parametric Models
SLIDE: Profile Weibull likelihood
CONTENU:
- Suppose that a survival random variable $T$, follows a Weibull distribution

$$ T \sim \operatorname{Weib}(\alpha) $$
- For a given value of $\alpha$ one can define a new random variable

$$ T^{*} = T^{\alpha} \sim \exp(\lambda^{\alpha}) $$
- In such a case (see Ch. 1), the analytic solution of the MLE is known

$$ \widehat{\lambda}(\alpha) = (d/V)^{1/\alpha} $$

with $V = \sum t_{i}^{\alpha}$ and $d$ the total number of deaths

- Since the MLE $\widehat{\lambda}(\alpha)$ can easily be obtained, we can define as

$$ \ell^{*}(\alpha) = \ell(\widehat{\lambda}(\alpha),\alpha) $$

the Weibull profile likelihood

- Maximizing $\ell^{*}(\alpha)$ yield the MLE of $\alpha$ and the MLE for $\lambda(\alpha)$ is

$$ \widehat{\lambda}(\widehat\alpha) = (d/V)^{1/\widehat\alpha} $$

$$ \widehat\sigma = 1 / \widehat\alpha = 2.041063 $$

which is almost identical to $\widehat\sigma_{MLE}$

- Then, $\widehat\alpha$ is used to obtain $\widehat{\lambda}$ and finally

$$ \widehat\mu = 4.656329 $$

which is indistinguishable from $\widehat\mu_{MLE}$

- $\Rightarrow$ As the MLE only relies on 1 parameter we can plot the profile likelihood

text:
COURS: Duration_Models (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model
SECTION: Parametric Models
SLIDE: The Accelerated Failure Time model
CONTENU:
- When comparing patients of two groups (e.g. treatment and control)

$$ e^{\beta}, $$

i.e. the hazard ratio, was the quantity we used

- It was assumed to be time-invariant (proportional hazards hypothesis)

- $\Rightarrow$ If the treatment group is effective in increasing survival

$$ \beta < 0, $$

i.e. the log-hazard ratio, such that the hazard ratio is less than 1

- An alternative way of comparing two groups is called AFT

- We assume here that the survival time of the first group is a multiple

$$ \theta = e^{\gamma} $$

of what the survival time would have been had if the patient was in the second group
chapter: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model

text:
COURS: Duration_Models (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model
SECTION: Parametric Models
SLIDE: More intuition on AFT models
CONTENU:
- The AFT approach assumes that the effect of a covariate is to accelerate or decelerate the life course of a disease by some constant

- e.g. If $\theta = 2$ everything in the life history of patient happens twice as fast

- $\Rightarrow$ If the model concerns the development of a tumor, this implies that

- 1 all of the stages progress twice as fast as for the unexposed individual

- 2 the expected time until the failure event is 0.5 of the baseline time

- $\Rightarrow$ Formally, the survival distributions for the AFT models are given by

$$ S_{1} = S_{0}(e^{-\gamma}t) $$

and the hazards are given by

$$ h_{1}(t) = e^{-\gamma}h_{0}(e^{-\gamma}t) $$
chapter: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model

text:
COURS: Duration_Models (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model
SECTION: Parametric Models
SLIDE: The AFT model with Weibull distribution
CONTENU:
- In the case of the Weibull distribution we have (see S)

$$ h_{1}(t) = e^{-\gamma}h_{0}(e^{-\gamma}t) = e^{-\gamma}\frac{1}{\sigma}e^{-\mu/\sigma}(e^{-\gamma}t)^{1/\sigma-1} $$
- Rearranging, we have

$$ h_{1}(t) = e^{-\gamma/\sigma}\frac{1}{\sigma}e^{-\mu/\sigma}t^{1/\sigma-1} = e^{-\gamma/\sigma}h_{0}(t)= e^{\beta}h_{0}(t) $$

that is, the AFT model is equivalent to the Cox model with $\beta = -\gamma/\sigma$

- Note This equivalence only exists for the Weibull distribution

text:
COURS: Duration_Models (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model
SECTION: Parametric Models
SLIDE: Interpreting the intercept in the AFT model
CONTENU:
- The Cox-model fit provides only 1 estimate, $\widehat\beta$

- The AFT Weibull model provides 3 estimates, 2 of them being linked to the baseline Weibull distribution

- In particular, the intercept $\mu$, cannot be estimated in the Cox approach

- $\Rightarrow$ it would cancel out of the partial likelihood (as the baseline hazard does)

- The AFT model allows for direct estimation of the baseline hazard as

$$ \widehat\mu = 5.286 \text{ and } \widehat\sigma = 1.992 $$

lead to $\widehat\alpha = 1/1.992 = 0.502$ and $\widehat\lambda = \exp(-5.286) = 0.00506$ and finally

$$ \widehat{S}_{0}(t) = e^{-(\widehat\lambda t)^{\widehat\alpha}} $$

text:
COURS: Duration_Models (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model
SECTION: Parametric Models
SLIDE: AFT-Weibull-based regression
CONTENU:
- An alternative way of looking at Weibull AFT model is to define

$$ \log(T) = \mu + \gamma x + \sigma \varepsilon^{*} $$

i.e. to model the $\log$-survival time as a location-scale model where

$$ \varepsilon^{*} = \log \varepsilon $$

with $\varepsilon$, a unit exponential distribution and $x$ a vector of covariates

- Then, the survival function is given by

$$\begin{aligned}
S(t) & = \mathbb{P}(T>t) = \mathbb{P}(\varepsilon^{*}>\frac{\log(t) - \mu - \gamma x}{\sigma}) \\
& = S_{0} (t e^{- \gamma x})
\end{aligned}$$
- This formulation is quite general as different choices for

$$ \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{L}(\theta) $$

can lead to other parametric survival models

text:
COURS: Duration_Models (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model
SECTION: Lasso Methods for Selection
SLIDE: Large set of covariates
CONTENU:
- One of the purpose analysis is to understand how covariates contributes to survival times

- Sometimes we focus on specific covariates such as age, employment, etc.

- By contrast, we can focus on the predictive ability of a set of covariates

- $\Rightarrow$ In many cases, dozens or thousands or predictors may be available

- In such a study, many of them are unrelated with survival

- and those that are relevant may be strongly correlated amongst themselves

- $\Rightarrow$ this multicollinearity is likely to complicate estimation and inference

- $\Rightarrow$ Penalized methods such as the Lasso method are useful in such situation
chapter: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model

text:
COURS: Duration_Models (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model
SECTION: Lasso Methods for Selection
SLIDE: The Lasso method for survival models
CONTENU:
- This approach maximizes the partial likelihood function but now with

- ... the additional stipulation that the $L_{1}$ norm of $\beta_{j}$ satisfies

$$ \sum^{p}_{j=1}|\beta_{j}|\leq t $$

for a constant $t$ and with $p$ the number of parameters

- $\Rightarrow$ This may be shown to be equivalent to maximizing the penalized likelihood

$$ \ell_{p}(\beta) = \ell(\beta) - \lambda \sum_{j = 1}^{p}|\beta_{j}| $$

for $\lambda$ a pre-specified value of $\lambda$

- Note 1 Adding this constraint on coefficients shrinks them toward zero (as compared to non-penalized MLE)

- Note 2 A too large $\lambda$ will result in no covariates at all in the model

- Note 3 A too small $\lambda$ will result in a large number of covariates in the model
chapter: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model
slide_title: The Lasso method for survival models

text:
COURS: Duration_Models (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model
SECTION: Lasso Methods for Selection
SLIDE: Optimization issues with the Lasso method
CONTENU:
- A complication is that $\ell_{p}(\beta)$ may not be strictly concave (weakly concave or flat)

- $\Rightarrow$ this causes convergence problems

- A crucial issue is hence to select $\lambda$

- $\Rightarrow$ As in other econometric fields, cross validation procedures are helpful

- 1 we randomly divide the data set into 5 subsets of equal size

- 2 we select 1 subset to be the so-called « validation » set

- 3 we combine the remaining subsets in the so-called « training » set

- 4 we use the training set ($\approx 80\%$ of the data) to build the Lasso model

- 5 we use this model to predict the survival times in the validation set

- 6 we use a partial-likelihood-based measure of goodness-of-fit to this set

- 7 we repeat steps 1-6 with each of the remaining 4 subsets in turn playing the role of the validation set

- 8 we derive an average partial-likelihood goodness-of-fit

- 9 we repeat the whole process for a wide range of values of $\lambda$

- 10 we select the value of $\lambda$ that produces the optimum goodness-of-fit: $\lambda^{*}$
chapter: Chapter 3 — Chapitre 3 : Beyond the Cox Model
slide_title: Optimization issues with the Lasso method

- Standard time series analysis rests on important concepts such as stationarity, spherical errors, and on a central family of models, the autoregressive moving average (ARMA) models.

- But these concepts are insufficient for the analysis of financial time series

- 1 First recall standard time series properties

- 2 Then discuss the main stylized facts of financial series

CONTENU:
- Modeling financial time series is a complex problem (see Mandelbrot 1963)

- There is a variety of the series in use (stocks, exchange rates, interest rates, etc.)

- The availability of very large data sets at different frequencies

- Mainly because of statistical regularities ( stylized facts) which are common to a large
number of financial series and are difficult to reproduce artificially using stochastic models

**Définition** : A **stochastic process**, $\{Y_{t}(\omega),\omega \in \Omega,t \in \mathbb{R}\}$, is an ordered sequence or random variables defined on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$ with

- $\Omega$ the set of events

- $\mathcal{F}$ a $\sigma$-field representing the events

- $\mathbb{P}$ a probability mesure such that $\mathbb{P}(A)$ is the probability of event $A$

- $\Rightarrow$ In the following $\{Y_{t}(\omega),\omega \in \Omega,t \in \mathbb{R}\}$ is denoted $\{Y_{t}\}_{t \in \mathbb{R}}$ or $Y_{t}$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Introduction — Reminders and Stylized Facts
SECTION: Reminders
SLIDE: Definitions
CONTENU:
**Définition** : The **unconditional central moments** of $Y_{t}$ may be written as the expected value of $h(Y_{t})$, which is a continuous function of $Y_{t}$

$$ \mathbb{E}(h(Y_{t})) = \int h(Y_{t}) f(Y_{t}) d Y_{t} $$

with $f(Y_{t})$ the unconditional density function of $Y_{t}$

- To compute the expected value of $Y_{t}$ we choose $h(Y_{t}) = Y_{t}$

$$ \mathbb{E}(Y_{t}) = \mu_{t} $$
- To compute the variance of $Y_{t}$ we choose $h(Y_{t}) = (Y_{t} - \mathbb{E}(Y_{t}))^2$

$$ \mathbb{V}(Y_{t}) = \sigma^{2}_{t} $$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Introduction — Reminders and Stylized Facts
SECTION: Reminders
SLIDE: Definitions
CONTENU:
**Définition** : The **unconditional central moments** of $Y_{t}$ may be written as the expected value of $h(Y_{t})$, which is a continuous function of $Y_{t}$

$$ \mathbb{E}(h(Y_{t})) = \int h(Y_{t}) f(Y_{t}) d Y_{t} $$

with $f(Y_{t})$ the unconditional density function of $Y_{t}$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Introduction — Reminders and Stylized Facts
SECTION: Reminders
SLIDE: Definitions
CONTENU:
**Définition** : The **autocovariance** function of $Y_{t}$ is obtained from the joint density of $(Y_{t},Yy_{t-1},\ldots,Y_{t-h})$ and is denoted by

$$\begin{aligned}
\gamma(h) & = Cov(Y_{t},Y_{t-h}) \\
& = \mathbb{E}\Big((Y_{t}-\mu_{t})(Y_{t-h} - \mu_{t-h})\Big) \\
& = \int \ldots \int (Y_{t} - \mu_{t})(Y_{t-h} - \mu_{t-h}) f(Y_{t},\ldots,Y_{t-h})dY_{t}\ldots dy_{t-h}
\end{aligned}$$

with $f(Y{t},\ldots,Y{t-h})$ the unconditional density function of $Y_{t}$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Introduction — Reminders and Stylized Facts
SECTION: Reminders
SLIDE: White noises
CONTENU:
**Définition** : A Gaussian White Noise ${\varepsilon}_{t}$ is a sequence of $\operatorname{~i.i.d.~}$ random variable with ${\varepsilon}_{t} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^{2}_{{\varepsilon}})$

**Définition** : A Strong White Noise ${\varepsilon}_{t}$ is a sequence of $\operatorname{~i.i.d.~}$ random variable with $\mathbb{E}({\varepsilon}_{t}) = 0$ and $\mathbb{E}({\varepsilon}_{t}^{2}) = \sigma^{2}_{{\varepsilon}}$

**Définition** : A Weak White Noise $\tilde{\varepsilon}_{t}$ is a sequence of uncorrelated random variable with $\mathbb{E}(\tilde{\varepsilon}_{t}) = 0$ and $\mathbb{E}(\tilde{\varepsilon}_{t}^{2}) = \sigma^{2}_{\tilde{\varepsilon}}$. For instance $\tilde{\varepsilon}_{t} = u_{t} u_{t+1} \cdots u_{t+k}$ is a Weak White Noise.

CONTENU:

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Introduction — Reminders and Stylized Facts
SECTION: Reminders
SLIDE: Second order stationarity
CONTENU:
- Let $\{Y_{t}\}_{t \in \mathbb{Z}}$, denoted $Y_{t}$, be a sequence of random variables

**Définition** : $Y_{t}$ is **second order stationary** if

- $\forall t \in \mathbb{Z}, \;\; \mathbb{E}(Y_{t}) = \mu < \infty$

- $\forall t,h \in \mathbb{Z}, \;\; Cov(Y_{t},Y_{t+h}) = \gamma(h) < \infty$

- $\Rightarrow$ $\forall t \in \mathbb{Z}, \;\; \mathbb{V}(Y_{t}) = \sigma^{2} < \infty$ as $Cov(Y_{t},Y_{t+h}) =\mathbb{V}(Y_{t})$ for $h = 0$

- We summarize here the stability in distribution of the process $Y_{t}$ only through its first two moments

- Relevant in the Gaussian case but restrictive in general

- This **weak** form of stationarity is simple to test

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Introduction — Reminders and Stylized Facts
SECTION: Reminders
SLIDE: Second order stationarity
CONTENU:
**Définition** : $Y_{t}$ is **second order stationary** if

- $\forall t \in \mathbb{Z}, \;\; \mathbb{E}(Y_{t}) = \mu < \infty$

- $\forall t,h \in \mathbb{Z}, \;\; Cov(Y_{t},Y_{t+h}) = \gamma(h) < \infty$

- $\Rightarrow$ $\forall t \in \mathbb{Z}, \;\; \mathbb{V}(Y_{t}) = \sigma^{2} < \infty$ as $Cov(Y_{t},Y_{t+h}) =\mathbb{V}(Y_{t})$ for $h = 0$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Introduction — Reminders and Stylized Facts
SECTION: Reminders
SLIDE: Strict Stationarity
CONTENU:
- Let $Y_{t}$ be a sequence of random variables

**Définition** : $Y_{t}$ is **strictly stationary** if the joint distribution of $Y_{t}$ and $Y_{t+h}$, $\forall t,h$ does not depend on $t$ but only on $h$

$$ (Y_{t},\ldots,Y_{t-h}) \,{\buildrel d \over =}\, (Y_{\tau},\ldots,Y_{\tau-h}) $$

with $t \neq \tau$

- The joint distribution of the process $Y_{t}$ should hence be **shift-invariant in time**

- Relevant in non-Gaussian and Gaussian cases

- This **strong** form of stationarity is difficult to test

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Introduction — Reminders and Stylized Facts
SECTION: Reminders
SLIDE: Strict Stationarity
CONTENU:
**Définition** : $Y_{t}$ is **strictly stationary** if the joint distribution of $Y_{t}$ and $Y_{t+h}$, $\forall t,h$ does not depend on $t$ but only on $h$

$$ (Y_{t},\ldots,Y_{t-h}) \,{\buildrel d \over =}\, (Y_{\tau},\ldots,Y_{\tau-h}) $$

with $t \neq \tau$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Introduction — Reminders and Stylized Facts
SECTION: Reminders
SLIDE: Theorem : Wold decomposition
CONTENU:
**Théorème** : Let $\{Y_{t}\}_{t = 0}^{n}$ be a second order stationary process. We can show that $Y_{t}$ can always be written as a weighted sum of innovations of $Y_{t}$ and a deterministic component $\mu_{t}$

$$ Y_{t} = \mu_{t} + \sum_{j = 0}^{\infty}a_{j}\varepsilon_{t-j} $$

with $\sum_{j = 0}^{\infty}a_{j}^{2}<\infty$ and $\varepsilon_{t} \sim i.i.d.(0,\sigma^{2}_{\varepsilon}<\infty)$

- The mean-square convergence of $a_{j}$ is important as

$$ \mathbb{E}(Y_{t}^{2}) = \sum_{j = 0}^{\infty}a_{j}^{2}\sigma^{2}_{\varepsilon}<\infty $$

if for $m>n$, $\mathbb{E}(\sum_{j = 0}^{m}a_{j} - \sum_{j = 0}^{n}a_{j})^{2} < c \Rightarrow \sum_{j = 0}^{\infty}a_{j}^{2}<\infty$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Introduction — Reminders and Stylized Facts
SECTION: Reminders
SLIDE: Theorem : Wold decomposition
CONTENU:
**Théorème** : Let $\{Y_{t}\}_{t = 0}^{n}$ be a second order stationary process. We can show that $Y_{t}$ can always be written as a weighted sum of innovations of $Y_{t}$ and a deterministic component $\mu_{t}$

$$ Y_{t} = \mu_{t} + \sum_{j = 0}^{\infty}a_{j}\varepsilon_{t-j} $$

with $\sum_{j = 0}^{\infty}a_{j}^{2}<\infty$ and $\varepsilon_{t} \sim i.i.d.(0,\sigma^{2}_{\varepsilon}<\infty)$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Introduction — Reminders and Stylized Facts
SECTION: Reminders
SLIDE: Wold Theorem and autocovariance
CONTENU:
- The rate of decrease of the coefficients $a_{j}$ determines also the shape of the autocovariance of $y_{t}$ as

$$\begin{aligned}
\gamma(h) & = \mathbb{E}\Big((Y_{t} - \mu_{t})(Y_{t - h} - \mu_{t})\Big) \\
& = \mathbb{E}\Big(\sum_{m = 0}^{\infty}a_{m}\varepsilon_{t-m}\sum_{s = 0}^{\infty}a_{s+h}\varepsilon_{t-s+h}\Big) \\
& = \sum_{m,s = 0}^{\infty}a_{m}a_{s+h}\gamma_{\varepsilon}(m-s+h) \\
& = \sigma^{2}_{\varepsilon}\sum_{m,s = 0}^{\infty}a_{m}a_{s+h}
\end{aligned}$$

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
$\varepsilon_{t}$ étant un bruit blanc, $\gamma_{\varepsilon}$ est nul en tout point excepté en 0 où $\gamma_{\varepsilon}(0) = \sigma^{2}_{\varepsilon}$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Introduction — Reminders and Stylized Facts
SECTION: Reminders
SLIDE: Stochastic trend and unit root
CONTENU:
- Suppose an AR(1): $Y_{t} = \rho Y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_{t}, \;\;\;\;\varepsilon_{t} \sim i.i.d.\; (0,\sigma^{2}_{\varepsilon}<\infty)$

- If $\rho = 1$ we have $Y_{t} = Y_{0} + \sum_{j = 0}^{t - 1} \varepsilon_{t - j}$ and hence

$$ Cov(Y_{t},Y_{t-j}) = (t-j)\sigma^{2}_{\varepsilon} \text{ et } \mathbb{V}(Y_{t}) = \mathbb{V}\Bigg(\sum_{j = 0}^{t - 1}\varepsilon_{t - j}\Bigg) = t \sigma^{2}_{\varepsilon} $$
- $\Rightarrow$ The variance of $Y_{t}$ depends of $t$ $\Rightarrow$ $Y_{t}$ is **non-stationary**

- $\Rightarrow$ $\rho = 1$ places a solution of the lag polynomial on the unit circle, so $Y_{t}$ is a **unit root** process

- $\Rightarrow$ $Y_{t}$ is a **random walk** of conditional expectation
$$ \mathbb{E}(Y_{t}|Y_{t-1}, Y_{t-2},\cdots,Y_{0}) = Y_{t-1} = \sum_{j = 1}^{t - 1} \varepsilon_{t - j} = \text{stochastic trend} $$
- $\Rightarrow$ $Y_{t}$ is a **discrete martingale** of **stochastic trend** $\sum_{j} \varepsilon_{t - j}$

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
Solution du polynôme charactéristique $1- \rho z = 0$

$$ z = 1/\rho \Rightarrow \text{ si } \rho = 1 \text{ on a } z = 1 $$

Si $|\rho|<1 \Rightarrow z=|1/\rho|>1$ la racine est en dehors du cercle unité et le processus est stationnaire. Si $|\rho|>1$ la racine est dans le cercle unitaire et le processus admet une solution stationnaire mais non-causale (en temps inversé).

Une martingale est un processus stochastique $Y_{t}$ dont l'espérance en $t$, sachant l'information passée $I_{s}$ au temps $s$, est égale à $Y_{s}$

$$ \mathbb{E}(Y_{t}|I_{s}) = Y_{s} $$

On parle de sous-martingale si

$$ \mathbb{E}(Y_{t}|I_{s}) \geq Y_{s} $$

On parle de sur-martingale si

$$ \mathbb{E}(Y_{t}|I_{s}) \leq Y_{s} $$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Introduction — Reminders and Stylized Facts
SECTION: Reminders
SLIDE: Stochastic trend and differenciation
CONTENU:
- Suppose an AR(1): $Y_{t} = \mu + \rho Y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_{t}, \;\;\;\;\varepsilon_{t} \sim i.i.d.\; (0,\sigma^{2}_{\varepsilon}<\infty)$

- If $\rho = 1$ and $Y_{0} = 0$, the $MA(\infty)$ representation gives

$$ Y_{t} = \rho^{t}Y_{0} + \mu \sum_{j = 0}^{t}\rho^{j} + \sum_{j = 0}^{t - 1} \rho^{j}\varepsilon_{t - j} = \mu t + \sum_{j = 0}^{t}\varepsilon_{t - j} $$
- We see that

$$ \mathbb{E}(Y_{t}) = \mu t $$
- The **variance** and **expected value** are not independent of $t$

- $\Rightarrow$ $Y_{t}$ is an **explosive** processus of **random walk** type and **derivative** $\mu$

- $Y_{t}$ is first difference **stationary** as

$$ \Delta Y_{t} = (1 - L) Y_{t} = Y_{t} - Y_{t - 1} = \mu + \varepsilon_{t} $$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Introduction — Reminders and Stylized Facts
SECTION: Stylized Facts
SLIDE: Financial Series
CONTENU:
Notations

$S_t$ : asset (or portfolio) price at time $t$

$p_t$ : asset (or portfolio) log-price at time $t$

$r_t$ : the continuously compounded or log-return of a financial asset (or portfolio) at time $t$

$r_t=p_t-p_{t-1}$

$r_t=log(1+R_t)$ with $R_t=\frac{S_t-S_{t-1}}{S_{t-1}}$

- Their properties have been amply commented upon in the financial literature
- These stylized facts are mainly concerned with daily stock prices

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Introduction — Reminders and Stylized Facts
SECTION: Stylized Facts
CONTENU:
- Nonstationarity of price series

- The stochastic process $S_t$ is generally non-stationary in the sense of
second-order stationarity

- Stationarity of return series

- The stochastic process $r_t$ is compatible with the second-order
stationarity property

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
Samples paths of prices are generally close to a random walk without intercept

CAC 40 returns (March 2, 1990 to October 15, 2008). August 19, 1991, Soviet Putsch
attempt; September 11, 2001, fall of the Twin Towers; January 21, 2008, effect of the subprime
mortgage crisis; October 6, 2008, effect of the financial crisis.

The oscillations of returns vary a great deal in magnitude, but are almost constant
in average over long subperiods.

The recent extreme volatility of prices, induced by the financial crisis of 2008, is worth noting.

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Introduction — Reminders and Stylized Facts
SECTION: Stylized Facts
SLIDE: Autocorrelation
CONTENU:
- Absence of autocorrelation for the price variations : (a)

- The series of price variations generally
displays small autocorrelations, making it close to a white noise

- Autocorrelations of the squared price returns : (b)

- Squared returns ($r_t^2$ ) or absolute returns ($|r_t |$)
are generally strongly autocorrelated

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Introduction — Reminders and Stylized Facts
SECTION: Stylized Facts
SLIDE: Volatility clustering
CONTENU:
- Large absolute returns |$r_t$| tend to appear in clusters

- Turbulent (high-volatility) sub-periods

are followed by quiet (low-volatility) periods. These sub-periods are recurrent but do not
appear in a periodic way (which might contradict the stationarity assumption)

- In other
words, volatility clustering is not incompatible with a homoscedastic (i.e. with a constant
variance) marginal distribution for the returns

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Introduction — Reminders and Stylized Facts
SECTION: Stylized Facts
SLIDE: Fat-tailed distributions
CONTENU:
- The empirical distribution of daily returns does not resemble a Gaussian one

- The densities have fat tails and are sharply peaked at zero: they are called leptokurtic

- When the time interval over which the returns are computed
increases, leptokurticity tends to vanish and the empirical distributions get closer to a
Gaussian (Aggregational Gaussianity property)

- Note : Below is represented the Kernel estimator of the CAC 40 returns density (solid line) and density of a Gaussian
with mean and variance equal to the sample mean and variance of the returns (dotted line).

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Introduction — Reminders and Stylized Facts
SECTION: Stylized Facts
SLIDE: Conditional fat tails
CONTENU:
- Even after accounting for volatility clustering, (by using for example ARCH / GARCH models as we will see in the next section), the distribution of the residuals is leptokurtic

- Its kurtosis is however smaller than in the case of a residuals of a simple ARMA model

SLIDE: Leverage effects
CONTENU:

- A diminishing price generates an increase in volatility larger than a price increase of the same amount

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Introduction — Reminders and Stylized Facts
SECTION: Stylized Facts
SLIDE: Summary
CONTENU:
- Any satisfactory statistical
model for daily returns must be able to capture these main stylized facts, mainly leptokurticity, the unpredictability of returns, and
the existence of positive autocorrelations in the squared and absolute returns

- Classical models (such as ARMA models) centered on the second-order structure are inappropriate

- There is evidence of conditional heterokedasticity (time-varying volatility):

$$ \mathbb{V}(r_t| r_{t-1}, r_{t-2},...) \not\equiv const $$
- Conditional heteroscedasticity is perfectly compatible with stationarity, just as the existence of a non-constant conditional mean is compatible with stationarity

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: Modelling Approaches
CONTENU:
- Objective: account for the very specific nature of financial series

- Example: Stationary AR$(1)$ provides a model specification for the conditional mean

$$ r_t = \theta r_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t $$

with $\varepsilon_t \operatorname{~i.i.d.~} N(0, \sigma^2_\varepsilon)$

- We hence have

$$ \mathbb{E}(r_{t+1})=0 $$

and
$$ \mathbb{E}(r_{t+1}|r_t, r_{t-1},...) = \theta r_{t} $$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: Modelling Approaches
CONTENU:
- Engle (1982)'s idea : account for other conditional moments of the return processus

- But, for an AR(1) process

$$ \mathbb{E}(r_{t+1}^2 )=\sigma^2_\varepsilon / (1-\theta^2) $$

$$ \mathbb{E}(r_{t+1}^2|r_t, r_{t-1},...) = \sigma^2_\varepsilon $$

are constants

- Such models are unable to measure changes in forecast error variance although we want them to be impacted by their past evolution

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: Modelling Approaches
CONTENU:
Solution

- Models that capture time-varying volatility are written in the multiplicative form

$$ r_t=\sigma_t z_t $$
- where ($z_t$) and ($\sigma_t$) are real processes such that:

- $\sigma_t$ is measurable with respect to a $\sigma$-field, denoted $\mathcal{I}_{t-1}$;

- $z_t$ is a strong white noise process with unit variance, $z_t$ being independent of $\mathcal{I}_{t-1}$ and $\sigma(r_u; u < t)$;

- $\sigma_t >0$

- This formulation implies that the sign of the current price variation (that is, the sign of $r_t$) is that
of $z_t$, and is independent of past price variations

- Most importantly, if the first two conditional moments of $r_t$ exist, they are given by

$$ \mathbb{E}(r_t|\mathcal{I}_{t-1})=0, \ \ \mathbb{E}(r^2_t|\mathcal{I}_{t-1})=\sigma^2_t $$
- The random variable $\sigma_t$ is called the volatility of $r_t$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: Modelling Approaches
CONTENU:
- As $Cov(r_t,r_{t-h})=\mathbb{E}(z_t)\mathbb{E}(\sigma_tr_{t-h})=0$, $r_t^2$, generally have nonzero autocovariances

- $\Rightarrow$ $r_t$ is a weak white noise

- The kurtosis coefficient of $r_t$, if it exists, is related to that of $z_t$

$$ \frac{\mathbb{E}(r_t^4)}{\mathbb{E}(r_t^2)^2}=k_z [1+\frac{Var(\sigma^2)}{\mathbb{E}(\sigma^2)^2}] $$
- Hence, the leptokurticity of financial time series can be taken into account in two
different ways:

- either by using a leptokurtic distribution for the weak white noise sequence ($z_t$ ),

- or by specifying a process ($\sigma^2_t$) with a great variability

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: Modelling Approaches
CONTENU:
Different classes of models can be distinguished depending on the specification adopted for $\sigma_t$

- Conditionally heteroscedastic (or GARCH-type) processes

- Here $\mathcal{I}_{t-1} = \sigma(r_s ;s < t)$ is the $\sigma$-field generated by the past of $r_t$
- The volatility is here a deterministic function of the past of $r_t$

- Processes of this class differ by the choice of a specification for this function

- The GARCH model is characterized by a volatility specified as a linear function
of the past values of $r^2_t$
- Stochastic volatility processes

- Here $\mathcal{I}_{t-1}$ is a $\sigma$-field generated by ${v_t, v_{t-1},\cdots}$,
where ($v_t$ ) is a strong white noise and is independent of ($z_t$ )
- volatility is a latent process
- a popular specification is the one where the process $\log\sigma_t$ follows an AR(1)

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: Conditionally heteroscedastic processes
CONTENU:
- In these models, the key concept is the conditional variance: the variance conditional on the past

- We can reproduce the autocorrelation empirically seen in conditional volatility by
using the information in the previous value(s) of $r^2_t$

- $\Rightarrow$ in an ARCH$(q)$ specification, perturbations follow an AR process of order $q$

- $\Rightarrow$ ARCH$(q)$ are autoregressive conditionally heteroskedastic models

$$ \mathbb{V}(r_t)=const $$

$$ \mathbb{V}(r_t|\mathcal{I}_{t-1})=f(r_{t-1}, r_{t-2}, \cdots;\theta) $$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: ARCH test
CONTENU:
Usual (Ljung-Box) autocorrelation test on squared returns

- H0: $\rho_1=\rho_2=\ldots=\rho_K=0$

$$ Q_{LB}(K) =T(T+2)\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{\hat\rho_k^2}{T-k}\underset{T\rightarrow \infty}{\,{\buildrel d \over \longrightarrow}\,} \chi^2(p), $$

where $\hat\rho_k$ is the empirical autocorrelation

ARCH-LM test

- Auxiliary regression

$$ \hat\varepsilon_t^2=\phi_0 + \phi_1 \hat\varepsilon^2_{t-1}+\cdots + \phi_p \hat\varepsilon_{t-p}^2+\eta_t $$
- H0': $\phi_1=\cdots=\phi_p=0$
- Test-statistic: $LM(p) = T\times R^2 \underset{T\rightarrow \infty}{\,{\buildrel d \over \longrightarrow}\,} \chi^2(p)$

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
- test basé sur l'écriture AR d'un ARCH

- H0 : aucune persistance dans la variance conditionnelle

- $\varepsilon_t$ est la série d'innovations d'un modèle de moyenne conditionnelle

- si ACF et PACF des carrées de résidus indiquent la présence de la dépendance (pérsistance dans les 2 graphiques), ce n'est pas le cas des innovations standardisées $\hat z_t=\hat\varepsilon_t^2/ \hat \sigma^2_t$, hyp de bruit blanc semble tenir

(Sheppard chapter 7)

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: Family of ARCH-type models
CONTENU:
- Linear models

- $\Rightarrow$ ARCH(q), GARCH(p, q), IGARCH(p, q), etc.

- Non-linear models (i.e. asymmetric models)

- $\Rightarrow$ EGARCH(p, q), GJRGARCH(p,q), TGARCH(p, q), etc.

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: ARCH models Engle (1982)
CONTENU:
**Modèle** : $r_t$ follows an ARCH(1) if

$$ r_t=z_t\sqrt{(\sigma^2_t)}, \;\;\; \sigma^2_t=\alpha_0+\alpha_1 r_{t-1}^2 $$

and $z_t$ is a strong white noise with $\sigma^2_t$ deterministic and positive process conditionally on the $\sigma$-field

- For the ARCH we have :

$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{V}(r_t| \mathcal{I}_{t-1}) & =\mathbb{V}(z_t\sqrt{(\sigma^2_t)} | \mathcal{I}_{t-1}) \\
& = \sigma^2_t \mathbb{V}(z_t| \mathcal{I}_{t-1}) \\
& = \sigma^2_t
\end{aligned}$$
- If $\mathbb{V}(z_t| \mathcal{I}_{t-1})$ is normalized to 1 we can see that $\sigma^2_t$ is the conditional variance of $r_t$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: ARCH models Engle (1982)
CONTENU:
**Modèle** : $r_t$ follows an ARCH(1) if

$$ r_t=z_t\sqrt{(\sigma^2_t)}, \;\;\; \sigma^2_t=\alpha_0+\alpha_1 r_{t-1}^2 $$

and $z_t$ is a strong white noise with $\sigma^2_t$ deterministic and positive process conditionally on the $\sigma$-field

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: Moments of ARCH(1) process
CONTENU:
- Regarding the conditional mean :

$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}(r_t| \mathcal{I}_{t-1}) &= \mathbb{E}(z_t\sigma_t| \mathcal{I}_{t-1})\\
&=\sigma_t\mathbb{E}(z_t| \mathcal{I}_{t-1})=0\ \text{if}\ z_t\ \text{is weak white noise}
\end{aligned}$$
- Regarding the unconditional mean :
$$ \mathbb{E}(r_t)=\mathbb{E}(\mathbb{E}(r_t)| \mathcal{I}_{t-1})=0 $$
- Regarding the conditional variance :

$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{V}(r_t| \mathcal{I}_{t-1}) &=\sigma^2_t \mathbb{V}(z_t| \mathcal{I}_{t-1}) =\sigma^2_t \mathbb{V}(z_t)\\
&=\sigma^2_t=\alpha_0 +\alpha_1 r_{t-1}^2.
\end{aligned}$$
- Regarding the unconditional variance :

$$ \mathbb{V}(r_t)=\mathbb{E}\big((r_t- \mathbb{E}(r_t))^2\big)=\mathbb{E}(r_t^2) $$
- Under stationarity assumption, we hence have $\mathbb{E}(r_t^2)=\alpha_0 +\alpha_1\mathbb{E}(r_t^2)$ and

$$ \mathbb{E}(r_t^2)=\mathbb{V}(r_t)=\frac{\alpha_0}{1-\alpha_1} $$

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
= $r_t^2$ suit un AR(1)

- si l'ensemble d'info est plus éloigné (t-h; t-h-1, ...)

- par la loi des espérances itérées: $\mathbb{E}(X| F1)=E[(X|F2)|F1]$ où $F1 \subseteq F2$, Le processus ARCH $r_t$ est orthogonal à tout passé $\mathbb{E}(r_t|r_{t-h}) = \mathbb{E}(\mathbb{E}(r_t|r_{t-1}) |r_{t-h}) = \mathbb{E}(0 |r_{t-h}) =0$

- $\mathbb{V}(r_t|r_{t-h})=\mathbb{E}(r_t^2| r_{t-h})= \alpha_0(\frac{1-\alpha_1^h}{1-\alpha_1})+\alpha_1^h r_{t-h}^2 \ \forall t$

Par itération successive, on a :

$r_t^2 = \alpha_0(1+\alpha_1 +\alpha_1^2 +..+\alpha_1^{h})+\varepsilon_t +\alpha_1\varepsilon_{t-1} +\alpha_1^2\varepsilon_{t-2} +.. +\alpha_1^{h-1}\varepsilon_{t-h+1} + \alpha_1^h r_{t-h}^2$

Sachant que
$\mathbb{E}(\varepsilon_{t-j}|r_{t-h}) = 0, \ \forall j = 0,..,h-1$

et $\mathbb{E}(r_{t-h}^2|r_{t-h}) = r_{t-h}^2$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathbb{V}( r_t|r_{t-h})=\alpha_0(\frac{1-\alpha_1^h}{1-\alpha_1})+\alpha_1^h r_{t-h}^2 \ \forall t$

Lorsque $h$ va à l'infini, ces variances conditionnelles convergent vers la variance non conditionnelle, et on retrouve alors la formule de la propriété 1:

$$ \mathbb{V}(X)=\lim_{h \to \infty} \mathbb{V}(r_t|r_{t-h})=\lim_{h \to \infty} \alpha_0(\frac{1-\alpha_1^h}{1-\alpha_1})+\alpha_1^h r_{t-h}^2=\frac{\alpha_0}{1-\alpha_1} $$

- sous hyp de stationnarité on peut calculer cette limite
- note: processus intégré, $alpha_1=1$; impact persistent sur la variance!!! on n-a plus cette convergence
- 2eme facon de calculer : $\mathbb{V}(x)=\mathbb{E}(x^2)$ où $x^2=a0+a1 x^2_{t-1}$ $-> \mathbb{V}(x)=\mathbb{E}(x^2)=a0/(1-a1).$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: ARCH$(q)$ Models
CONTENU:
**Modèle** : $r_t$ follows an ARCH(q) process if $r_t = z_t\sigma_t$ with

$$ \sigma^2_t=\alpha_0+ \sum_{i=1}^{q} \alpha_i r_{t-i}^2 $$

and where $z_t$ is a strong white noise such that $\mathbb{E}(z_t) = 0$ et $\mathbb{E} (z_t^2) = \sigma^2_z$.

This model fulfills the martingale difference and time-varying conditional variance properties

$$ \mathbb{E} (r_t|r_{t-1}) = 0 \text{ and }\mathbb{V}(r_t| r_{t-1})=\alpha_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{q} \alpha_i r_{t-i}^2 $$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: ARCH$(q)$ Models
CONTENU:
**Modèle** : $r_t$ follows an ARCH(q) process if $r_t = z_t\sigma_t$ with

$$ \sigma^2_t=\alpha_0+ \sum_{i=1}^{q} \alpha_i r_{t-i}^2 $$

and where $z_t$ is a strong white noise such that $\mathbb{E}(z_t) = 0$ et $\mathbb{E} (z_t^2) = \sigma^2_z$.

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: ARCH-errors model
CONTENU:
**Modèle** : Consider $r_t = \mathbb{E}(r_t|r_{t-1}) + \varepsilon_t$ with $\varepsilon_t$ a weak white noise satisfying the martingale difference hypothesis :
$$ \mathbb{E}(\varepsilon)=0 \text{ and }\mathbb{E}(\varepsilon_t \varepsilon_s )=0. $$

Then, $r_t$ follows an ARCH-errors model if $\varepsilon_t = z_t\sigma_t$ with

$$ \sigma^2_t=\alpha_0+ \sum_{i=1}^{q} \alpha_i r_{t-i}^2 $$

and where $z_t$ is a strong white noise

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: Example of ARCH-errors model
CONTENU:
$\bullet$ AR(1) - ARCH(1)

$Y_t=\mu+\rho Y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t$, $\varepsilon_t = z_t \sigma_t$

with $\sigma^2_t = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2$ and $|\rho|<1$

The model describes the evolution of both the conditional mean and the conditional variance of $Y_t$ through time

$\bullet$ $\varepsilon_t$ : residuals

$\bullet$ $z_t$ : standardized residuals

Residuals $\varepsilon_t$ satisfy the properties of an ARCH process:

martingale difference; time-varying conditional variance; zero conditional auto-covariances; leptokurtic distribution

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: Non-negativity constraints and Limits of ARCH
CONTENU:
- Non negativity constraints

- For a ARCH$(1)$ model , $\alpha_0 \geq 0$; $\alpha_1\geq 0$

- For an ARCH$(q)$ model, $\alpha_i\geq 0, \ \forall i=0,1,\ldots,q$

- Limitations of ARCH$(q)$ models

- $q$, number of lags of the squared residuals, is potentially very large

- Non negativity constraints might be violated

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
=T.G. For the ARCH family, the decay rate of the unconditional autocorrelation function is too rapid when compared to what is observed in financial time series, unless the maximum lag q is long.

=T.G. The conditional variance of a GARCH has the property that the unconditional autocorrelation function can decay slowly, although the decay rate is still exponential. It is a more parsimonious model of the conditional
variance than a high-order ARCH model, the users prefer it to the simpler ARCH alternative.

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: Generalised ARCH(1,1) or GARCH(1,1) Models
CONTENU:
- Bollerslev (1986): the conditional variance depends on its own past values and on past values of $\varepsilon_{t}^{2}$

- GARCH(1,1) model containing 3 parameters is a very parsimonious infinite ARCH model

$$ \sigma^2_t= \alpha_0+\alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 +\beta \sigma_{t-1}^2 $$

with $\alpha_0>0, \alpha_1>0$ and $\beta>0$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: The GARCH$(p,q)$ model
CONTENU:
**Modèle** : A process $\varepsilon_t$ satisfies a GARCH(p, q) representation if $\varepsilon_t = z_t\sigma_t$ and

$$ \sigma^2_t= \alpha_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{q} \alpha_i \varepsilon_{t-i}^2 + \sum_{i=1}^{p}\beta_i \sigma^2_{t-i} $$

where $z_t$ is a weak white noise and where $\alpha_0 > 0$, $\alpha_i \geq 0$ , $i = 1,...,q$ and $\beta_i \geq 0$, $i = 1,...,p$

- The conditional variance of the error term depends on own $p$ past
values and on $q$ past values of the squared residuals

- But in general a GARCH(1,1) model will be sufficient to capture the
volatility clustering in the data

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: The GARCH$(p,q)$ model
CONTENU:
**Modèle** : A process $\varepsilon_t$ satisfies a GARCH(p, q) representation if $\varepsilon_t = z_t\sigma_t$ and

$$ \sigma^2_t= \alpha_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{q} \alpha_i \varepsilon_{t-i}^2 + \sum_{i=1}^{p}\beta_i \sigma^2_{t-i} $$

where $z_t$ is a weak white noise and where $\alpha_0 > 0$, $\alpha_i \geq 0$ , $i = 1,...,q$ and $\beta_i \geq 0$, $i = 1,...,p$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: Moments of GARCH
CONTENU:
- $\mathbb{E}(\varepsilon_t|\varepsilon_{t-1}) = 0$

- $\mathbb{V}(\varepsilon_t|\varepsilon_{t-1})= \sigma^2_t = \alpha_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{q} \alpha_i \varepsilon_{t-i}^2 + \sum_{i=1}^{p}\beta_i \sigma^2_{t-i}$

Unconditional Variance

- $\mathbb{V}(r_t)=\mathbb{E}(r_t-\mathbb{E}(r_t)^2) =\mathbb{E}(r_t^2)$
- $\mathbb{V}(r_t)=\mathbb{E}(r_t^2)= \alpha_0 \times \Big(1-\sum_{i=1}^{max(p,q)} (\alpha_i+\beta_i \Big)^{-1}$

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
- mêmes demos qu'avant

- Innovation - introduite dans l'eq $\sigma^2_t$

-Attention, le degré p ici apparaît comme le degré moyenne mobile de la représentation ARMA dans $\varepsilon^2_t$ .

- ARCH -> AR(q)

- GARCH -> ARMA( max(p,q), p)

- a+b = la persistance du processus de variance conditionnelle

= généralement a - [0.02 - 0.25] et b - [0.75 - 0.98]

ecriture var non-cond est basee sur l'écriture ARMA de $\varepsilon_t^2$ du modèle GARCH stationnaire ($\varepsilon_t^2 =\alpha_0+\sum_{i=1}^{max(p,q)} (\alpha_i+\beta_i) \varepsilon_{t-i}^2 +\mu_t- \sum_{i=1}^p \beta_i \mu_{t-i}$, avec innovations $\mu_t = \varepsilon_t^2 - \sigma^2_t$)

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: The GARCH model meets financial stylized facts
CONTENU:
- Under additional assumptions (second-order stationarity of $\varepsilon_t^2$), we can state that if $\varepsilon_t$ is GARCH$(p, q)$, then $\varepsilon_t^2$ is an ARMA(p, q) process

$$ \varepsilon_t^2 =\alpha_0+\sum_{i=1}^{max(p,q)} (\alpha_i+\beta_i) \varepsilon_{t-i}^2 +v_t- \sum_{i=1}^p \beta_i v_{t-i} $$

where $v_t = \varepsilon_t^2 - \sigma_t^2$ are the innovations of the process

- GARCH processes are hence able to capture one important characteristic of financial series: squared returns are autocorrelated

- The sum $\alpha+\beta$ is referred to as the persistence of the conditional
variance process
slide_title: The GARCH model meets financial stylized facts

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
CONTENU:
The GARCH model meets financial stylized facts

- Contrary to standard time series models (ARMA), the GARCH structure allows the magnitude of
the noise $\varepsilon_t^{2}$ to be a function of its past values.

- Thus, periods with high volatility level (corresponding
to large values of $\varepsilon_{t-i}^2$) will be followed by periods where the fluctuations have a smaller amplitude.

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: GARCH Stationarity
CONTENU:
**Théorème** : A process $\varepsilon_t$ satisfies a GARCH(p, q) representation if $\varepsilon_t = z_t\sigma_t$,

$$ \sigma^2_t= \alpha_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{q} \alpha_i \varepsilon_{t-i}^2 + \sum_{i=1}^{p}\beta_i \sigma^2_{t-i} $$

where $z_t$ is a weak white noise and where $\alpha_0 > 0$, $\alpha_i \geq 0$ ,$i = 1,...,q$ and $\beta_i \geq 0$, $i = 1,...,p$.

Also, $\varepsilon_t$ is asymptotically second-order stationary if and only if

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{q} \alpha_i+ \sum_{j=1}^{p} \beta_j\leq 1 $$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: GARCH
CONTENU:
Drost & Nijman, 1993 define 3 types of GARCH

- The strong GARCH where $z_t$ is a Strong White Noise
- The semi-strong GARCH where $z_t$ is a Weak White Noise
- The weak GARCH where only projections of the conditional variance are considered

- $\Rightarrow$ We focus on the simplest case : the strong GARCH

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
we consider strong GARCH models generally

SECTION: GARCH models

CONTENU:
