COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: IGARCH(p,q)
CONTENU:
- When
$$ \sum_{i=1}^{q} \alpha_i+ \sum_{j=1}^{p} \beta_j= 1 $$

the model is called an integrated GARCH(p, q) or IGARCH(p, q) model (see Engle and Bollerslev,
1986)

- There is a unit root in the autoregressive part of the ARMA representation of $\varepsilon_t^2$
representation

- Returns are strictly stationary with an infinite variance

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: Maximum Likelihood (ML)
CONTENU:
- Easy to implement once the density function of $z_t$ is specified

- Let us call $\theta$ the vector of the parameters to be estimated

- If $z_t$ are assumed to be normally distributed, then the log likelihood function for a sample of $T$ observations is:

$$\begin{aligned}
\ell(\varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2, ..., \varepsilon_T; \theta) &=\sum\limits_{t=1}^{T}\log f\big(\varepsilon_t| \mathcal{I}_{t-1} \big)\\
&=-\frac{T}{2}\log(2\pi) -\frac{1}{2}\sum\limits_{t=1}^{T}\log\big(\sigma^2_t(\theta) \big)-\frac{1}{2} \sum\limits_{t=1}^{T}\frac{\varepsilon_t^2(\theta)}{\sigma^2_t(\theta)},
\end{aligned}$$

where $\frac{\varepsilon_t^2(\theta)}{\sigma^2_t(\theta)}=z_t^2$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: Maximum Likelihood (ML)
CONTENU:
$$ z_t^2=z_t^2(\theta)=\frac{r_t-\mathbb{E}(r_t|\mathcal{I}_{t-1})}{\sigma^2_t} $$

and

$$ \sigma^2_t= \alpha_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{q} \alpha_i \varepsilon_{t-i}^2 + \sum_{i=1}^{p}\beta_i \sigma^2_{t-i} $$

- Note that $\sigma^2_t$ is not observed for $t = 0,-1, \ldots ,-p + 1$

- To initialize the process, the unobserved squared residuals are

1. set to their sample mean

2. set to the unconditional variance

3. obtained using a pre-sample

4. or considered as additional parameters to be estimated

- Under the regularity assumptions, this estimator

$$ \sqrt{T}(\hat{\theta}-\theta_{0}) \,{\buildrel d \over \longrightarrow}\, \mathcal{N}(0,V_{T}^{-1}(\theta_{0})) $$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: Maximum Likelihood (ML)
CONTENU:
- $\widehat\theta$ does not have a closed-form formula and numerical optimization methods are used

- We need

1. Initial condition

2. Moving rule

3. Stopping rule

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: Maximum Likelihood (ML) Example 2
CONTENU:
- Annualized GARCH(1,1) volatility fitted to daily US market returns

$$ \sigma^2_t= \underset{(4.46)}{0.0} + \underset{(8.59)}{0.09}\varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \underset{(80.19)}{0.9} \sigma^2_{t-1} $$
- Volatility is : time varying, persistent, mean-reverting

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: GARCH Extensions
CONTENU:
- GARCH models are doing better than ARCH models (e.g., persistence in volatility) but there are still some issues (e.g., tails are
not enough fat, etc)

- Improvements in various directions:

- Non-normality of the conditional distribution: e.g. GARCH-t model

- Asymmetric GARCH models : e.g. Exponential GARCH model (EGARCH), Threshold GARCH model (TGARCH), GJR model

- Trade-off mean vs variance : e.g. GARCH-in-mean model

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: GARCH Extensions
CONTENU:
In case of non-normality:

- Student distribution
- Skewed Student distribution
- Generalized error distribution (GED)

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: GARCH Extensions
CONTENU:
The GJR-GARCH(1,1) Model

- Due to Glosten, Jaganathan and Runkle

$$ \sigma^2_t= \alpha_0 +\alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 +\beta \sigma^2_{t-1} + \gamma \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 I_{t-1} $$

where $I_{t-1}= \begin{cases} 1 \ \text{if}\ \varepsilon_{t-1}<0 \\ 0 \ \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$

- For a leverage effect, we would see $\gamma>0$

- We require $\alpha_1 +\gamma\geq0$ and $\alpha_1\geq0$ for non-negativity

- We require $\alpha_1 +0.5\gamma+\beta<1$ for stationarity

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: GARCH Extensions
CONTENU:
The GJR-GARCH(1,1) Model

- Using monthly S&P 500 returns, December 1979- June 1998

- Estimating a GJR model, we obtain the following results

$$ r_t=\underset{(3.198)}{0.172} $$

$$ \sigma^2_t= \underset{(16.372)}{1.243} +\underset{(0.437)}{0.015} \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 +\underset{(14.999)}{0.498} \sigma^2_{t-1} + \underset{(5.772)}{0.604} \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 I_{t-1} $$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: News Impact Curves
CONTENU:
- The news impact curve plots the next period volatility ($\sigma_t$) that would arise from various positive and negative values of $\varepsilon_{t-1}$, given an estimated model

- News Impact Curves for S&P 500 Returns using Coefficients from GARCH and GJR Model Estimates

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: EGARCH
CONTENU:
- Suggested by Nelson (1991)

- The variance equation is given by

$$ \log(\sigma^2_t)=\alpha_0+\sum\limits_{i=1}^{q} a_i z_{t-i}+\sum\limits_{i=1}^{q} b_i (|z_{t-i}|-\mathrm{E}[|z_{t-i}|])
+\sum\limits_{i=1}^{p} \beta_i log(\sigma^2_{t-i}) $$
- Advantages of the model

- Since we model the $\log\sigma^2_t$, then even if the parameters are negative, $\sigma^2_t$ will be positive

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH models
SLIDE: GARCH-in-mean or GARCH-M
CONTENU:
- Asset pricing models suppose that higher risks should be rewarded by higher returns

- The GARCH-in-mean model lets the mean of an asset’s returns to be determined by its lagged conditional volatility

$$ r_t=\mu+\delta G(\sigma^2_t)+\varepsilon_t, \ \varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2_t) $$

with $G(\sigma^2_t)$ a linear or square-root function and

$$ \sigma^2_t=\alpha_0+\alpha_1\varepsilon_{t}^2+\beta \sigma^2_{t-1}, $$
- The parameter $\delta$ can be interpreted as the price of risk and can thus be assumed to be positive

- Hence, if $\delta > 0$, increases in risk (given by increases in conditional volatility) lead to higher mean returns

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH-based Portfolio Optimization
SLIDE: Portfolio: optimization problem
CONTENU:
- Consider two assets and their log-returns $r_{t} = (r_{1,t}, r_{2,t})'$, denoted $\bm{r}$ when stacked over time.

- If the market is efficient, returns are unpredictable with mean $\mu$

- The conditional covariance matrix
$$ H_{t} = \begin{pmatrix} h_{11t} & h_{12t} \\ h_{21t} & h_{22t} \end{pmatrix} $$
is however predictable if one can fit a stationary GARCH-type model for $r_{1,t}$ and $r_{2,t}$

- Let define $\Sigma_\tau$, the forecast of $H_{t}$ at date $\tau$ and the expected (targeted) return for the portfolio, $\tilde\mu$

- What is of interest for the portfolio manager is to find a minimum risk portfolio (efficient) subjected to provide the targeted return :

$$\begin{aligned}
& \min_{\omega} \sigma_{p}^{2}(\omega) = \omega' \Sigma_\tau \omega \\
& \text{s.c.} \quad \omega' \mu = \tilde\mu \quad \text{ and } \quad \omega' \iota = 1
\end{aligned}$$

with $\iota$ a unit vector and $\omega$ the allocation weights

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH-based Portfolio Optimization
SLIDE: Portfolio: resolution
CONTENU:
- You should be able to derive the following results (based here on the Lagrangien).

$$ \mathcal{L}(\omega, \lambda_1, \lambda_2) = \omega' \Sigma_\tau \omega + \lambda_1 (\omega' \mu - \tilde\mu) + \lambda_2 (\omega' \iota - 1) $$
- The partial derivatives lead to the following system

$$\begin{aligned}
2 \Sigma_\tau \omega + \lambda_1 \mu + \lambda_2 \iota &= 0 \Rightarrow \omega = \frac{1}{2} \Sigma_\tau^{-1} (-\lambda_1 \mu - \lambda_2 u) \\
\omega' \mu - \tilde\mu & = 0 \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2}\lambda_1 \mu' \Sigma_\tau^{-1} \mu + \frac{1}{2} \lambda_2 \iota' \Sigma_\tau = \tilde\mu \\
\omega'\iota - 1 & = 0 \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2}\lambda_1 \mu' \Sigma_\tau^{-1} \iota + \frac{1}{2} \lambda_2 \iota' \Sigma_\tau = 1
\end{aligned}$$
- Denoting $A = \iota'\Sigma_\tau^{-1}\mu = \mu'\Sigma_\tau^{-1}\iota$, $B = \mu'\Sigma_\tau^{-1}\mu$ and $C = \iota'\Sigma^{-1}\iota$ we have

$$\begin{aligned}
A\lambda_{1} + B\lambda_{2} & = 2\tilde\mu \\
A\lambda_{1} + C\lambda_{2} & = 2
\end{aligned}$$
- Solving this system we obtain

$$ \lambda_{1} = 2(C\tilde\mu - A)(BC - A^{2})^{-1} \text{ et } \lambda_{2} = 2(B -A\tilde\mu)(BC - A^{2})^{-1} $$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH-based Portfolio Optimization
SLIDE: Portfolio: resolution
CONTENU:
- Substituting in the weight equation we finally get

$$\begin{aligned}
\omega^{*}(\tilde\mu) &= \frac{1}{2} \Sigma_\tau^{-1} \left[ \lambda_1 \mu + \lambda_2 \iota \right] \\
& = \frac{1}{2} \Sigma_\tau^{-1} \left[ 2 \left( \frac{C \tilde\mu - A}{D} \right) \mu + 2 \left( \frac{B - A \tilde\mu}{D} \right) \iota \right] = \frac{1}{D} \Sigma_\tau^{-1} \Big[ (C \tilde\mu - A) \mu + (B - A \tilde\mu) \iota \Big] \\
& = \frac{1}{D} \Sigma_\tau^{-1} \Big[ (B\iota - A \mu) + (C\mu - A \iota) \tilde\mu \Big] = \frac{1}{D} \Sigma_\tau^{-1} (B\iota - A \mu) + \frac{1}{D} \Sigma_\tau^{-1} (C\mu - A \iota) \tilde\mu \\
& =E\tilde\mu + F
\end{aligned}$$
- The minimal risk (efficient) portfolio is hence given by

$$ \sigma_{p}^{2}(\tilde\mu) = \omega^{*}(\tilde\mu)'\Sigma_\tau^{-1}\omega^{*}(\tilde\mu) $$
- If we omit the investor preferences ($\tilde\mu$) in the minimization problem the solution simplifies to

$$ \omega^{*} = \frac{\Sigma_\tau^{-1}\iota}{\iota' \Sigma_\tau^{-1} \iota} $$

and we get the so-called minimum-variance portfolio

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: GARCH-based Portfolio Optimization
SLIDE: Portfolio: implementation
CONTENU:
- After estimating individual GARCH models, collect conditional variance $h_{t,ii}$, $i = 1, 2$

- Forecast $\widehat{h}_{ii,t}$ at horizon $k$, $k$ being the investment date or next portfolio rebalancing

- As here we assume $r_{t}$ unpredictable, we just use the unconditionnal mean as a predictor

- In a univariate framework, we need a constant correlation assumption to go further because :

$$ \rho_{ij,t} = \frac{h_{ij,t}}{\sqrt{h_{ii,t}h_{jj,t}}} $$
- $\Rightarrow$ If $\rho_{ij,t} = \rho_{ij}$ we can use the Pearson correlation and $h_{ij,t} = \sqrt{h_{ii,t}h_{jj,t}}\rho_{ij}$ to reconstruct $\widehat{\Sigma}_\tau$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: Multivariate GARCH models
CONTENU:
- While the volatility of univariate series has been the focus of the previous chapters, modeling the comovements of several series is of great practical importance
- The standard linear modeling of real time series has a natural multivariate extension through the framework of the vector ARMA (VARMA) models
- Similarly, here we introduce the concept of multivariate GARCH model
- Essential for asset pricing and risk management crucially depend on the conditional covariance structure of the assets of a portfolio

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: Multivariate GARCH models
CONTENU:
Let denote by $r_t$ a column vector of $k$ asset returns and the vector of their conditional expectations by $\mu_t$

- Returns' equation implies a conditional covariance matrix $H_{t}$:

$$ r_t-\mu_t=\varepsilon_{t} = H_{t}^{1/2}z_{t},\;\;\;\; H_{t}^{1/2}(H_{t}^{1/2})' = H_{t} $$

- $\varepsilon_{t}$ is a vector, not a scalar as previously

- where $H_{t}$ is a matrix $k \times k$ with elements $h_{ijt}$

- and $z_{t}$ is i.i.d Gaussian such that $\mathbb{E}(z_{t}) = 0$ and $\mathbb{E}(z_{t}z_{t}') = I$ with $I$ a $k \times k$ identity matrix

- The conditional covariance matrix $H_{t}$ takes the form

$$ H_{t} = f(H_{t-1},H_{t-2},\cdots, \varepsilon_{t-1}, \varepsilon_{t-2},\cdots) $$
- If $H_{t}^{1/2}$ exists, $H_{t}$ is positive definite

- $\Rightarrow$ the transformation $f(.)$ ought to insure that $H_{t}$ is symmetric and positive definite (strictly positive eigen-values)

- But $f(H_{t-1},H_{t-2},\cdots, \varepsilon_{t-1}, \varepsilon_{t-2},\cdots)$ is complex...

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
$\varepsilon_t=r_t-\mu_t$ with $\mu_t$ its conditional mean vector

The elements of $\mu_t$ and $H_t$ must be measurable with respect to the $\sigma$-field $F_{t-1}$ generated by $y_{t-j}$ for $j \geq 1$ and possibly by other variables available at time $t-1$.

The matrix $H^{1/2}$ can be chosen to be symmetric and positive definite but it can also be chosen to be triangular, with positive diagonal elements (FZ)

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: Multivariate GARCH models
CONTENU:
Choosing a specification for $H_t$ is obviously more delicate than in the univariate framework
because:

- (i) $H_t$ should be (almost surely) symmetric, and positive definite for all $t$
- (ii) the specification should be simple enough to be amenable to probabilistic study (existence of solutions, stationarity, ... ), while being of sufficient generality
- (iii) the specification should be parsimonious enough to enable feasible estimation
- (iv) but, the model should not be too simple to be able to capture the - possibly sophisticated - dynamics in the covariance structure

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: Multivariate GARCH models
CONTENU:
- Moreover, it may be useful to have the so-called stability by aggregation property
- If $\varepsilon_t= H_{t}^{1/2}z_{t}$ is satisfied, the process $\tilde\varepsilon_t = P\varepsilon_t$, where $P$ is an invertible square matrix, is such that

$$ \mathbb{E}(\tilde\varepsilon_t|\tilde\varepsilon_u, u<t)=0,\ \ \mathbb{V}(\tilde\varepsilon_t| \tilde\varepsilon_u,u<t)=\tilde H_t =P H_t P $$
- The stability by aggregation of a class of specifications for $H_t$ requires that the conditional variance matrices $\tilde H_t$ belong to the same class for any choice of $P$
- Relevance: if the components of the vector $\varepsilon_t$ are asset returns, $\tilde \varepsilon_t$ is a vector of portfolios of the same assets, each of its components consisting of amounts (coefficients of the corresponding row of $P$) of the initial assets

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: Distribution of multivariate GARCH models
CONTENU:
- Generally $z_t$ is assumed to follow the multivariate Gaussian distribution, $z_t \sim N(0,I)$, since it provides the basis of QML estimation as in the univariate case
- Another choice of density for $z_t$ is the multivariate $t$
- Multivariate skewed distributions can also be used (e.g. the skewed-t of Bauwens and Laurent, 2005)
- As in the univariate case, distributions with fat-tails and skewness are usually better fitting data than the Gaussian

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: Representation of multivariate GARCH models
CONTENU:
- Unlike the ARMA models, however, the GARCH model specification does not suggest a natural extension to the multivariate framework
- Indeed, the (conditional) expectation of a vector of size $k$ is a vector of size $k$, but the (conditional) variance is a $k \times k$ matrix
- Important milestones are

- the BEKK model of Engle and Kroner (1995)

- the constant conditional correlation (CCC) model of Bollerslev (1990)

- the dynamic correlation model (DCC) of Engle (2002a)

- the time-varying correlation (TVC) model of Tse and Tsui (2002)

- Earlier models had too many parameters to be useful for
modeling more than two asset returns jointly (e.g. VEC model)

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: VEC models
CONTENU:
- Take the case of a bivariate ($k=2$) GARCH$(p,q)$:

$$ H_{t} = \begin{pmatrix} h_{11t} & h_{12t} \\ h_{21t} & h_{22t} \end{pmatrix} \Rightarrow h_{t} = vec(H_{t}) = \begin{pmatrix} h_{11t} \\ h_{12t} \\ h_{21t} \\ h_{22t} \end{pmatrix} $$
- Note : the operator $vec(.)$ consists in vectorizing a matrix by stacking the columns of the matrix on top of one another
- Using this operator, Engle et Kroner (1995) propose the VEC model:

$$ h_{t} = \omega + \sum_{i=1}^{q}\alpha_{i}vec(\varepsilon_{t-i}\varepsilon_{t-i}') + \sum_{i=1}^{p}\beta_{i}h_{t-i} $$

with $\omega$ a $k\times 1$ vector, and $\alpha_{i}$ and $\beta_{i}$ $k \times k$ matrices

- Problem:

- the model is big and some equations are redundant: $h_{12t} = h_{21t}$ as $H_{t}$ is a covariance matrix

- it will not in general produce positive definite covariance matrices $H_t$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: VECH models
CONTENU:
- Apply a $vech(.)$ operator now to the previous $GARCH(p,q)$:

$$ H_{t} = \begin{pmatrix} h_{11t} & h_{12t} \\ h_{21t} & h_{22t} \end{pmatrix} \Rightarrow h_{t} = vech(H_{t}) = \begin{pmatrix} h_{11t} \\ h_{21t} \\ h_{22t} \end{pmatrix} $$
- Note : The operator $vech(.)$ consists in vectorizing a matrix by stacking the columns of the lower triangular part of its argument square matrix

- One obtains the VECH model where $h_{t} = vech(H_{t})$

**Modèle** : The process $\varepsilon_t$ is said to admit a VEC-GARCH(p,q) representation (relative to the i.i.d sequence $z_t$) if it satisfies

$$\begin{aligned}
\varepsilon_t &=H^{1/2}_t z_t, \ \text{where $H_t$ is positive definite such that}\\
vech(H_{t}) &= \omega+\sum\limits_{i=1}^{q}A^{(i)}vech(\varepsilon_{t-1}\varepsilon_{t-1}') +\sum\limits_{j=1}^{p}B^{(j)}vech(H_{t-j}),
\end{aligned}$$

where $\omega$ is a vector of size $\{k(k + 1)/2\} \times 1$, and the $A^{(i)}$ and $B^{(j)}$ are matrices of dimension $k(k+1)/2\times k(k+1)/2$.

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: VECH models
CONTENU:
**Modèle** : The process $\varepsilon_t$ is said to admit a VEC-GARCH(p,q) representation (relative to the i.i.d sequence $z_t$) if it satisfies

$$\begin{aligned}
\varepsilon_t &=H^{1/2}_t z_t, \ \text{where $H_t$ is positive definite such that}\\
vech(H_{t}) &= \omega+\sum\limits_{i=1}^{q}A^{(i)}vech(\varepsilon_{t-1}\varepsilon_{t-1}') +\sum\limits_{j=1}^{p}B^{(j)}vech(H_{t-j}),
\end{aligned}$$

where $\omega$ is a vector of size $\{k(k + 1)/2\} \times 1$, and the $A^{(i)}$ and $B^{(j)}$ are matrices of dimension $k(k+1)/2\times k(k+1)/2$.

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: VEC models
CONTENU:
- In particular, for a bivariate VECH-GARCH(1,1)

$$ h_{t} = \begin{pmatrix} h_{11t} \\ h_{21t} \\ h_{22t} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} c_{1} \\ c_{2} \\ c_{2} \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} \alpha_{11} & \alpha_{12} & \alpha_{13} \\ \alpha_{21} & \alpha_{22} & \alpha_{23} \\ \alpha_{31} & \alpha_{32} & \alpha_{33} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \varepsilon_{1,t-1}^{2} \\ \varepsilon_{1,t-1}\varepsilon_{2,t-1} \\ \varepsilon_{2,t-1}^{2} \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} \beta_{11} & \beta_{12} & \beta_{13} \\ \beta_{21} & \beta_{22} & \beta_{23} \\ \beta_{31} & \beta_{32} & \beta_{33} \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} h_{11,t-1} \\ h_{21,t-1} \\ h_{22,t-1} \end{pmatrix} $$

- Every conditional covariance is a function of lagged conditional variances as well as lagged cross-products of all components

- More parsimonious model than the VEC-GARCH

- But the VECH-GARCH still implies a big number of coefficients

- Problem: VEC and VECH are not able to generally insure that $H_{t}$ is positive definite

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
the most direct generalization of univariate GARCH

In some sense, everything is explained by everything, which makes this model very general but also not very parsimonious.

This model is very general, flexible and we can also directly interpret the coefficients, however, it brings two major disadvantages in applications.

- The first at that the number of parameters in the model equals to $(p + q)(k(k + 1)/2)2 + k(k + 1)/2$, which makes this model practicable in practice only in the bivariate case.

- Second is that there exist only sufficient conditions on the parameters to ensure that conditional variance matrices $H_t$ are positive definite almost surely for all $t$.

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: Diagonal VECH-GARCH models
CONTENU:
- To further simplify the model and its estimation, one may assume that volatilities and covariances depend only on their past values (Bollerslev, Engle, and Wooldridge, 1988)

- $\Rightarrow$ Non-diagonal coefficients of $A_{i}$ and $B_{i}$ are null

- For instance, the diagonal VECH-GARCH(1,1) gives

$$ h_{t} = \begin{pmatrix} h_{11t} \\ h_{21t} \\ h_{22t} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} c_{1} \\ c_{2} \\ c_{2} \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} \alpha_{11} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \alpha_{22} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \alpha_{33} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \varepsilon_{1,t-1}^{2} \\ \varepsilon_{1,t-1}\varepsilon_{2,t-1} \\ \varepsilon_{2,t-1}^{2} \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} \beta_{11} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \beta_{22} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \beta_{33} \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} h_{11,t-1} \\ h_{21,t-1} \\ h_{22,t-1} \end{pmatrix} $$

- More parsimonious than the VEC-GARCH

- The diagonal VEC-GARCH is stable by aggregation

- In this case it is possible to obtain conditions for positive definiteness of $H_t$ for all $t$

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
DVECH reduces the number of parameters to $(p + q + 1)n(n + 1)/2$ and
in this case it is also possible to obtain conditions for positive definiteness of $H_t$
for all $t$.

However, DVECH representation seems to be too restrictive since no
interaction is allowed between the different conditional variances and covariances.

By writing the parameter matrices in the form of $\tilde C\tilde C'$, $\tilde A\tilde A'$ and $\tilde G\tilde G$ instead of just $\tilde C$, $\tilde A$ and $\tilde G$ the positive semi-definiteness is guaranteed in estimation without imposing any further restrictions.

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: BEKK model
CONTENU:
- Developed by Baba, Engle, Kraft and Kroner, in a preliminary version of Engle and Kroner (1995)

**Modèle** : Let ($z_t$) denote an i.i.d. sequence with common distribution. The process ($\varepsilon_t$) is called a BEKK-GARCH(p, q), with respect to the sequence ($z_t$), if it satisfies

$$\begin{aligned}
\varepsilon_t & = H_t^{1/2} z_t \\
H_{t} & = C'C + \sum_{n=1}^{N}\sum_{i=1}^{q} A_{in}\varepsilon_{t-i}\varepsilon'_{t-i} A'_{in} + \sum_{n=1}^{N}\sum_{i=1}^{p} B'_{in}H_{t-i} B'_{in}
\end{aligned}$$

with $A_{in}$, $B_{in}$, $n\in \{1,\ldots,N\}$, and $C$ matrices of dimension $k \times k$

- Each BEKK model implies a unique VECH model, while the converse implication is not true
- The BEKK class contains the diagonal models by choosing diagonal matrices $A_{ik}$ and $B_{jk}$
- Note: The sum over $N$ introduces a complex generalization so we consider only the case $N = 1$ hereafter

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
L'introduction de la somme sur l'entier k est motivee par un problème de généralité du modèle

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: BEKK model
CONTENU:
**Modèle** : Let ($z_t$) denote an i.i.d. sequence with common distribution. The process ($\varepsilon_t$) is called a BEKK-GARCH(p, q), with respect to the sequence ($z_t$), if it satisfies

$$\begin{aligned}
\varepsilon_t & = H_t^{1/2} z_t \\
H_{t} & = C'C + \sum_{n=1}^{N}\sum_{i=1}^{q} A_{in}\varepsilon_{t-i}\varepsilon'_{t-i} A'_{in} + \sum_{n=1}^{N}\sum_{i=1}^{p} B'_{in}H_{t-i} B'_{in}
\end{aligned}$$

with $A_{in}$, $B_{in}$, $n\in \{1,\ldots,N\}$, and $C$ matrices of dimension $k \times k$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: BEKK model
CONTENU:
**Théorème** : $H_t$ is positive definite if matrices $H_{t-i},\ i = 1,\ldots, p$, are almost surely positive definite and
$$ ker\{C\}\overset{p}{\underset{j=1}{\cap}}\overset{N}{\underset{n=1}{\cap}}ker\{B_{jn}\} = \{0\} $$

- This is a weak condition, requiring only that $C$ and $B_{jn}$ are full rank (e.g. triangular C with positive diagonal elements)

- an identifiability restriction is needed, $H_{jj,t}$ being invariant to a change of sign of the $j$-th row of any matrix $A_i$

- BEKK-GARCH$(1,1)$ in the bivariate case ($k=2$) with $N=1$

$$\begin{aligned}
H_{t} & = C'C + \begin{pmatrix} \alpha_{11} & \alpha_{12} \\ \alpha_{21} & \alpha_{22} \end{pmatrix}' \begin{pmatrix} \varepsilon_{1,t-1}^{2} & \varepsilon_{1,t-1}\varepsilon_{2,t-1} \\ \varepsilon_{1,t-1}\varepsilon_{2,t-1} & \varepsilon_{2,t-1}^{2} \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} \alpha_{11} & \alpha_{12} \\ \alpha_{21} & \alpha_{22} \end{pmatrix} \\
& + \begin{pmatrix} \beta_{11} & \beta_{12} \\ \beta_{21} & \beta_{22} \end{pmatrix}' \begin{pmatrix} h_{11,t-1}^{2} & h_{12,t-1}\\ h_{21,t-1} & h_{22,t-1}^{2} \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} \beta_{11} & \beta_{12} \\ \beta_{21} & \beta_{22} \end{pmatrix}
\end{aligned}$$

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
- On voit que les conditions pour obtenir une matrice Ht définie positive
quelque soit $t \in N$ sont faibles : la condition portant sur les noyaux des matrices $C$ et $B_{jn},\ j \in {1,\ldots ,n}$ est vérifiée si la matrice $C$ ou l'une des matrices
$B_{jn}$ est de plein rang

The kernel of a linear map (e.g. matrix A with coefficients in a field R) is the set of solutions $\hat x$ to the equation $Ax = 0$ where 0 is the 0 vector.

- la partie ARCH est semidefinie positive car $\varepsilon_{t-i}\varepsilon_{t-i}'$ est psd, donc que la constante et le terme GARCH sont constraints

- positive diagonal elements of triangular C insures that the matrix of constants has a unique representation C'C

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: BEKK model
CONTENU:
**Théorème** : $H_t$ is positive definite if matrices $H_{t-i},\ i = 1,\ldots, p$, are almost surely positive definite and
$$ ker\{C\}\overset{p}{\underset{j=1}{\cap}}\overset{N}{\underset{n=1}{\cap}}ker\{B_{jn}\} = \{0\} $$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: Stationarity of the BEKK model
CONTENU:
**Définition** : Let $C$ be an upper triangular $n\times n$ matrix and $A_{in}$, $B_{in}$ be $n\times n$ parameter matrices. Let $z_t$ be an i.i.d. process with mean zero and unit variance. Hence $z_t$ is independent of $\mathcal{I}_{t-1}$, and $cov(z_t| \mathcal{I}_{t-1}) = cov(z_t) = I$.

There exists a covariance stationary BEKK process $\varepsilon_t$, such that $\varepsilon_t = H_t^{1/2}z_t$, where $H_t = cov(\varepsilon_t| \mathcal{I}_{t-1})$ and $\mathcal{I}_{t} = \sigma(\varepsilon_t, \varepsilon_{t-1},\ldots)$ if and only if all the eigenvalues of
$$ \sum_{i=1}^{q} A_{in}\otimes A_{in} + \sum_{n=1}^{N}\sum_{i=1}^{p} B_{in}\otimes B_{in} $$
are less than one in modulus.

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: Estimation of the BEKK model
CONTENU:
- Under the assumption
that $z_t$ are i.i.d. conditionally on initial values, the quasi log-likelihood function of the BEKK model is given by

$$ L_n(\theta) = L_n(\theta; \varepsilon_1, \ldots, \varepsilon_{n})=\sum\limits_{t=1}^{n} -\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi) - \frac{1}{2}\log |H_t| -\frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_{t}'H_t^{-1} \varepsilon_{t}, $$

where

$$\begin{aligned}
\varepsilon_t & = H_t^{1/2} z_t \\
H_{t} & = C'C + \sum_{n=1}^{N}\sum_{i=1}^{q} A_{in}\varepsilon_{t-i}\varepsilon'_{t-i} A'_{in} + \sum_{n=1}^{N}\sum_{i=1}^{p} B'_{in}H_{t-i} B'_{in}
\end{aligned}$$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: Estimation of the BEKK model
CONTENU:
- Comte and Lieberman (2003) provide conditions for strong consistency and
asymptotic normality of the quasi maximum likelihood estimator

- Strong consistency
$$ \hat\theta_n \to \theta_0 \ almost \ surely \ when \ n\to\infty $$

- Asymptotic normality

$$ \sqrt{n}(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0) \,{\buildrel d \over \longrightarrow}\, \mathcal{N}(0,J^{-1}I J^{-1}), $$

where $J$ is a positive definite matrix and $I$ is a positive semi-definite matrix, defined by

$$ I = \mathbb{E}\big(\frac{\partial l_t(\theta_0)}{\partial\theta}\frac{\partial l_t(\theta_0)}{\partial\theta'}\big), \ \ J = \mathbb{E}\big(\frac{\partial^2 l_t(\theta_0)}{\partial\theta\partial\theta'} \big) $$

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
for $\theta_n$ mle and $\theta_0\in\Theta$ the true parameters, assume that

- $\Theta$ compact, $C; A_i; B_i$ are continuous functions of $\theta$ and there exists
a $c > 0$ such that $inf_{\theta\in \Theta}det(C(\theta))\geq c > 0$,

- model is identifiable in the sense of Engle and Kroner

- rescaled errors $z_t$ admit a density absolutely continuous with respect to the
Lebesgue measure and positive in a neighborhood of the origin,

- the process is stationary (the largest module of the eigenvalues is <1)

- for normality add:
$C, A_i G_i,$ admit continuous derivatives up to order 3 on $\Theta$ ; components of $z_t$ are independent; $\varepsilon_t$ admits bounded moments of order 8; the initial states of the process $H_t$ are fixed stationary.

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: Conditional correlations
CONTENU:
- Multivariate GARCH models allow one to compute conditional variances and covariances

- Conditional correlations can hence be reconstructed

$$ \rho_{ij,t} = \frac{h_{ij,t}}{\sqrt{h_{ii,t}h_{jj,t}}} $$

with $\{i,j\} = 1,\cdots,k$ and $i \neq j$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: Constant Conditional Correlations models
CONTENU:
- Suppose that for a multivariate GARCH process of the form
$$ \varepsilon_t= H_{t}^{1/2} \tilde z_{t} $$
all the past information on $\varepsilon_{it}$, involving all the variables $\varepsilon_{j,t-i}$, is summarized in the conditional variance

- The standardized innovations $z_{it} =h^{-1/2}_{ii,t}\varepsilon_{it}$ are sequences of i.i.d (0,1) variables generally correlated

- Denote the covariance matrix $R=\mathbb{V}(z_t)=(\rho_{i,j}),$ with $z_t=(z_{1t}, \ldots, z_{kt})$

- In CCC models the conditional covariances $h_{ij,t}$ are obtained as $h_{ij,t}=\rho_{i,j}\sqrt{(h_{ii,t}h_{jj,t})}$ for $i \neq j$ and they are time varying although the correlations are constant

- In matrix notations,

$$ H_{t} = D_{t} R D_{t} = \rho_{i,j}\sqrt{(h_{ii,t}h_{jj,t})} $$

with $D_{t}$ a $k \times k$ diagonal matrix with $\sqrt{h_{11,t}},\cdots,\sqrt{h_{kk,t}}$ on its main diagonal

- $\Rightarrow$ $H_t$ is positive-definite if $h_{ii,t}$ is positive for all $i$ and $R_t$ is positive-definite

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
The cov matrix of (univariate)-standardized residuals $z_t$, i.e. $R_t$, is a correlation matrix as all variances=1 ;

Since $z_t=e_t / h_t = D^{-1} e_t$, $cov(z_t z_t ') =R$ and $cov(e_t e_t ')=H_t$, then $E(z_t z_t ') = E(D^{-1} e_t e_t' D^{-1})$ so that $H=DRD$.

R matrix with elements $\rho_{ij}$ off diagonal in lower triangular part, same whatever $t$ (symmetric matrix)

If the elements of $\omega$ on next slide and the
diagonal elements of $A_s$ and $B_v$ are positive, and the conditional correlation matrix
$R$ is positive definite, then the conditional covariance matrix $H_t$ is positive
definite. However, positivity of the diagonal elements of $A_s$ and $B_v$ is not necessary
for $R$ to be positive definite unless $p = q = 1$. This CCC model contains
$k(k + 5)=2$ parameters.

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: Constant Conditional Correlations models
CONTENU:
**Définition** : Let $\tilde z_t$ be a sequence of i.i.d. variables. A process $\varepsilon_t$ is called CCC-GARCH(p, q) if it satisfies

$$\begin{aligned}
\varepsilon_t &=H_t^{1/2} \tilde z_t \\
H_t &=D_t R D_t \\
\boldsymbol{h}_t &= \boldsymbol{\omega}+\sum\limits_{s=1}^{q}\boldsymbol{A}_{s}\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{t-s}+\sum\limits_{v=1}^{p}\boldsymbol{B}_{v}\boldsymbol{h}_{t-v},
\end{aligned}$$

where $R=cov(z_t z'_t)$ is a correlation matrix, $D_t=diag(\sqrt{\boldsymbol{h}_{t}})$, $\boldsymbol{h}_t$ is the vector of $k$ conditional variances with elements $(h_{ii,t}),$ $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_t$ is the vector of $k$ squared innovations (non-standardized), $\omega$ is a $m\times 1$ vector with positive coefficients, $\boldsymbol{A}_{s}$ and $\boldsymbol{B}_{v}$ are $k \times k$ matrices with nonnegative coefficients

- Note that $\varepsilon_t=D_t z_t$, where $z_t = R^{1/2} \tilde z_t$ is a centered vector with covariance matrix $R$ such that

$$ \varepsilon_{i,t}=h_{ii,t}^{1/2} z_{i,t} $$
- Note that $h_{ii,t}$ may depend on the past of all the components of $\varepsilon_t$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: Constant Conditional Correlations models
CONTENU:
**Définition** : Let $\tilde z_t$ be a sequence of i.i.d. variables. A process $\varepsilon_t$ is called CCC-GARCH(p, q) if it satisfies

$$\begin{aligned}
\varepsilon_t &=H_t^{1/2} \tilde z_t \\
H_t &=D_t R D_t \\
\boldsymbol{h}_t &= \boldsymbol{\omega}+\sum\limits_{s=1}^{q}\boldsymbol{A}_{s}\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{t-s}+\sum\limits_{v=1}^{p}\boldsymbol{B}_{v}\boldsymbol{h}_{t-v},
\end{aligned}$$

where $R=cov(z_t z'_t)$ is a correlation matrix, $D_t=diag(\sqrt{\boldsymbol{h}_{t}})$, $\boldsymbol{h}_t$ is the vector of $k$ conditional variances with elements $(h_{ii,t}),$ $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_t$ is the vector of $k$ squared innovations (non-standardized), $\omega$ is a $m\times 1$ vector with positive coefficients, $\boldsymbol{A}_{s}$ and $\boldsymbol{B}_{v}$ are $k \times k$ matrices with nonnegative coefficients

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: Strict stationarity of the CCC model
CONTENU:
**Définition** : The CCC-GARCH(p,q) model admits a second-order stationary solution if the vector of parameters is such that the roots of the polynomial $\det(I-\sum_{i=1}^{s}(A_i + B_i)\lambda)$ with $s=sup(p,q)$, are outside the unit cercle. This solution is unique and ergodic.

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: Estimation of CCC models
CONTENU:
- By the quasi-maximum likelihood method

- Overall there are $k+k^2(p+q)+k(k-1)/2$ parameters to estimate $\theta=(\boldsymbol{\omega}',\alpha',\beta',\rho')'$

- Let $(\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_n)$ be a sample of length $n$ of the unique nonanticipative and strictly stationary variable $\varepsilon_t$ of the CCC model

- Conditionally on nonnegative initial values $\varepsilon_0,\ldots,\varepsilon_{1-q}, h_0,\ldots, h_{1-p}$, the Gaussian quasi-likelihood is written as

$$ L_n(\theta)=L_n(\theta; \varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_n) = \prod_{t=1}^{n}\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{k/2}| H_t|^{1/2}} \exp\big(-\frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_t' H_t^{-1} \varepsilon_t\big), $$

where $H_t$ are recursively defined, for $t\geq 1$, by

$$\begin{aligned}
H_t &= D_t R D_t, \ \ D_t = \{\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{ h_t})\}^{1/2}\\
\boldsymbol{ h_t} &= \boldsymbol{h_t}(\theta) = \boldsymbol{\omega}+ \sum\limits_{s=1}^{q}\boldsymbol{A}_{s}\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{t-s}+\sum\limits_{v=1}^{p}\boldsymbol{B}_{v}\boldsymbol{ h}_{t-v}
\end{aligned}$$

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
$k$ constants+$k^2(p+q)$ ARCH and GARCH (bold a and B matrices) +$k(k-1)/2$ correlations

initial values have no influence on the asymptotic properties of the estimator as in univariate case

$z_t$ known also as degarched returns

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: Estimation of CCC models
CONTENU:
- Under the assumption that each conditional variance is specified as a function of its own lags and the $i^{th}$ element of $\varepsilon_t$ (denoted by $\varepsilon_{it}$), for example, by a GARCH(1,1) equation, an important simplification is obtained in QML estimation

- This assumption splits the log-likelihood function into two parts

$$\begin{aligned}
l_n(\theta)=\log L_n(\theta) =&-\frac{1}{2}\sum\limits_{t=1}^n (2\log |D_t| +\log |R| + z_t' R z_t)\\
=&-\frac{1}{2}\sum\limits_{t=1}^n (2\log |D_t| + z'_t z_t)\\
& -\frac{1}{2}\sum\limits_{t=1}^n (\log |R| + z_t' R z_t- z'_t z_t)
\end{aligned}$$
- The parameters of the conditional variances appear only in $D_t$ (first term), while
the parameters of the conditional correlation matrix $R_t$ appear only in the second term

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: Estimation of CCC models
CONTENU:
- So the estimation can be performed in two steps

- Estimate univariate GARCH models for each asset $i=1,\ldots, k$ and construct standardized residuals

$$ z_{t} = D_{t}^{-1} \varepsilon_{t} $$

- In a second step, estimate the correlation model (i.e. the constant conditional correlations) based on
$$ \mathbb{E}(z_t z_t') = D_t^{-1} H_t D_t^{-1} = R, $$

where R is symmetric and positive definite

- Remark: The separate estimation of each conditional variance model and of the correlation model is the key to enable estimation of MGARCH models of conditional correlations when $k$ is large, where large means more than, say, 5

- Remark: The price to pay for this is the impossibility of including spillover terms in the conditional variance equations, i.e. terms involving $\varepsilon_{t-1,j}$ or $h_{t-1,j}$ for $j\neq i$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: Estimation of CCC models
CONTENU:
- A QMLE of $\theta$ is defined as a measurable solution $\hat \theta_n = \underset{\theta \in \Theta}{\arg \max} \; L_n (\theta)$

- Under several assumption the following asymptotic properties of the QMLE estimator can be established (Francq and Zakoïan, 2010)

- Strong consistency
$$ \hat\theta_n \to \theta_0 \ almost \ surely \ when \ n\to\infty $$

- Asymptotic normality

$$ \sqrt{n}(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0) \,{\buildrel d \over \longrightarrow}\, \mathcal{N}(0,J^{-1}I J^{-1}), $$

where $J$ is a positive definite matrix and $I$ is a positive semi-definite matrix, defined by

$$ I = \mathbb{E}\Big(\frac{\partial l_t(\theta_0)}{\partial\theta}\frac{\partial l_t(\theta_0)}{\partial\theta'}\Big), \ \ J = \mathbb{E}\Big(\frac{\partial^2 l_t(\theta_0)}{\partial\theta\partial\theta'} \Big) $$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: CCC models
CONTENU:
- The hypothesis of CCCs is not tenable except for specific cases and short periods

- Several tests of the null hypothesis of constant correlations exist: see e.g. Silvennoinen and Terasvirta (2005)

- Indeed, many empirical work show that the matrix $R$ is time-varying

$$ H_{t} = D_{t} R_{t} D_{t}, $$

with $R_t$ measurable with respect to the past variables $\{ \varepsilon_u, u < t\}$

- Dynamic conditional correlations GARCH (DCC-GARCH) of Engle et Sheppard (2001) is the most well known multivariate approach introducing dynamics for the conditional correlation

- For reasons of parsimony, it seems reasonable to choose diagonal matrices $\boldsymbol{A}_s$ and $\boldsymbol{B}_v$ as discussed on slide regarding the definition of CCC models (on slide ), corresponding to univariate GARCH models for each component

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: DCC models
CONTENU:
- Dynamic conditional correlations GARCH models are an extension of CCC-GARCH,
obtained by introducing a dynamic for the conditional correlation (Engle 2002)

**Définition** : The DCC process is a martingale difference sequence $\varepsilon_t$ relative to a given filtration $\mathcal{I}_t$, whose conditional covariance matrix $H_t = cov(\varepsilon_t | \mathcal{I}_{t-1})$ satisfies

$$ H_{t} = D_{t} R_{t} D_{t} $$

where $D_t=diag(h_{11,t}^{1/2} \ldots h_{kk,t}^{1/2})$ and $R_t$ is a $k \times k$ time varying correlation matrix of $z_t$.

Besides, $h_{ii,t}$ is defined as univariate GARCH(p, q) model where the usual restrictions for non-negativity and stationarity are imposed.

- The univariate GARCH models can have different orders

- The number of parameters to be estimated is quite large when $k$ is large (e.g. equal to $(k + 1)(k + 4)/2$ in bivariate case for a DCC(1,1))

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: DCC models
CONTENU:
**Définition** : The DCC process is a martingale difference sequence $\varepsilon_t$ relative to a given filtration $\mathcal{I}_t$, whose conditional covariance matrix $H_t = cov(\varepsilon_t | \mathcal{I}_{t-1})$ satisfies

$$ H_{t} = D_{t} R_{t} D_{t} $$

where $D_t=diag(h_{11,t}^{1/2} \ldots h_{kk,t}^{1/2})$ and $R_t$ is a $k \times k$ time varying correlation matrix of $z_t$.

Besides, $h_{ii,t}$ is defined as univariate GARCH(p, q) model where the usual restrictions for non-negativity and stationarity are imposed.

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: DCC models
CONTENU:
Different DCC(1,1) models are obtained depending on the specification of $R_t$

- Simple GARCH-like formulation
$$ R_t = \theta_0 R + \theta_1 \Psi_{t-1} + \theta_2 R_{t-1}, $$
with
$R$ a constant correlation matrix, and $\Psi_{t-1}$ the empirical correlation matrix of $z_{t-1},\ldots, z_{t-M}$ and
$$ R_{t} = \operatorname{diag}(Q_{t})^{-1/2}Q_{t}\operatorname{diag}(Q_{t})^{-1/2}, $$

where
$$ Q_{t} =\theta_0 \bar Q + \theta_1 z_{t-1}z'_{t-1} + \theta_2 Q_{t-1} $$

with $\theta_1>0$, $\theta_2>0,$ $\theta_1 + \theta_2<1$, $\theta_0=1-\theta_1-\theta_2$, and $\bar Q=cov(z_{t}z_{t}' )$

- One can test the assumption of constant conditional covariance matrix through the restriction $\theta_2 = \theta_3 = 0$

- Both ensure that $H_t$ is positive definite if $R_t$ is positive definite with elements in the unit cercle. For this, $Q_t$ and its initial value have to be positive definite.

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
($D_t$ is positive definite since all the diagonal elements are positive); $R$ correl matrix

two extra parameters with respect to CCC

$Q_t$ covariance matrix dynamics similar to that of a GARCH

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: Estimation of the DCC model
CONTENU:
Suppose that the process $z_t$ is multivariate Gaussian distributed such that $\mathbb{E}(z_t) = 0$ and $\mathbb{E}(z_t z_t') = I$.

- The DCC model can be estimated by a two-step procedure as the conditional variance
$H_t = D_t R_t D_t$ can be divided into volatility part and correlation part (Engle 2002)

- The method is thought to produce consistent but not efficient estimators

- The log-likelihood takes the form of

$$\begin{aligned}
l_n (\theta) & =-\frac{1}{2} \sum_{t=1}^{n} \big( \log (|H_t|) + \varepsilon^{'}_t H_{t}^{-1} \varepsilon_t \big) \\
& = -\frac{1}{2} \sum_{t=1}^{n} \big( 2\log (|D_t|)+ \log (|R_t|) + \varepsilon^{'}_t D_{t}^{-1} R_{t}^{-1}D_{t}^{-1} \varepsilon_t\big)
\end{aligned}$$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: Estimation of the DCC model
CONTENU:
- In the first step the likelihood involves replacing $R_t$ with the identity matrix $I$

$$\begin{aligned}
l_{1,n} (\theta_a) & = -\frac{1}{2} \sum_{t=1}^{n} \big( 2\log (|D_t|)+ \log (|I|) + \varepsilon^{'}_t D_{t}^{-1} I^{-1}D_{t}^{-1} \varepsilon_t\big)\\
& = -\frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{t=1}^{n}\Big( \log (h_{ii,t})+ \frac{\varepsilon^{2}_{ii,t}}{h_{ii,t}}\Big),
\end{aligned}$$

where $\theta_a$ corresponds to the vector of parameters of the univariate GARCH model for all series

- Once $\theta_a$ is estimated, $h_{ii,t}$ is estimated such that $z_t$ and $\bar Q$ can be estimated as well

- In the second step, $\theta_b = (\theta_1, \theta_2)$ is estimated, given the estimated parameters from step one

$$\begin{aligned}
l_{2,n} (\theta_b | \hat\theta_a) & = -\frac{1}{2} \sum_{t=1}^{n} \big( 2\log (|D_t|)+ \log (|R_t|) + \varepsilon^{'}_t D_{t}^{-1} R_{t}^{-1}D_{t}^{-1} \varepsilon_t\big)\\
& = -\frac{1}{2} \sum_{t=1}^{n}\big( 2\log (|D_t|)+ \log (|R_t|) +z'_t R_{t}^{-1}z_t\big)
\end{aligned}$$

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
- L1 is the sum of the log-likelihoods of the univariate GARCH processes of $k$ return series

- L2QML is conditional on first step

- Since we are conditioning on $\theta_a$, the $D_t$ terms are constant and we can exclude those terms

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 1 — GARCH Type Models
SECTION: Multivariate GARCH models
SLIDE: Estimation of the DCC model
CONTENU:
- Asymptotic properties of the two-step estimation procedure have been studied
in Engle and Sheppard (2001)

- However, Aielli (2009) showed that the estimation of $Q$ by $\hat R$ is inconsistent since

$$ \mathbb{E}(z_t z_t)=\mathbb{E}(\mathbb{E}(z_t z'_t |\mathcal{I}_{t-1}))= \mathbb{E}(R_t)\neq \mathbb{E}(Q_t) $$

- The consistent DCC (cDCC) relies on a consistent specification of $Q_t$

$$ Q_t = (1-\theta_1-\theta_2)\bar Q+ \theta_1 \operatorname{diag}(Q_{t-1}^{1/2}) z_{t-1} z'_{t-1}\operatorname{diag}(Q_{t-1}^{1/2}) + \theta_2 Q_{t-1}, $$

such that $\bar Q$ is the unconditional covariance matrix of $\operatorname{diag}(Q_{t-1}^{1/2}) z_t$

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
i.e. assumptions for consistency and asymptotic normality

Since the conditional covariance matrix of $z_t$ is $R_t$ (not $Q_t$), the process $Q_t$ is not linear MGARCH.

$R_t =cov(z_t z_t^{'})$ while
$H_t =cov(\varepsilon_t \varepsilon'_t)$

In fact, treating $Q_t$ as a linear MGARCH process can lead to misleading conclusions. For example, for $\theta_1 + \theta_2 = 1$, the process $q_{ij,t}$ which is thought of as an integrated GARCH process (Engle 2002, eq. (17)), is weakly stationary.

See here $\operatorname{diag}(Q_{t-1}^{1/2}) z_t$ as a sort of epsilon whose covariance we model

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Market Efficiency
SLIDE: Efficiant Market Hypothesis (EMH)
CONTENU:
- The EMH applies rational expectations to asset pricing

- Let $S_{t}$ be an asset price and $\mathcal{I}_{t}$ the information available up to $t$

- EMH : if investors use all available information in forming expectations

$$ \mathbb{E}(S_{t+1} | \mathcal{I}_{t}) = S_{t} $$
- $\Rightarrow$ future prices are impossible to forecast

- As we also assume that

$$ \mathbb{E}(|S_{t}|) < \infty \text{ and } \mathbb{E}(S_{t+1} - S_{t}| \mathcal{I}_{t}) = 0, $$

$S_{t}$ is defined as a martingale

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Market Efficiency
SLIDE: Brownian motion (or Wiener process)
CONTENU:
- The martingale property is crucial in finance

- $\Rightarrow$ it is the cornerstone of most of asset pricing theories

- A particular type of martingale is the Wiener process $W_{t} \in \mathcal{M}$

- $W_{0} = 0$

- $W_{t+u} - W_{t}$, $\forall u\geq0$ is independent of $W_{s}$, $s \leq t$

- $W_{t+u} - W_{t} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,u)$

- $W_{t}$ is continuous in $t$

- $\Rightarrow$ Asset prices are often defined as Brownian martingales

$$ S_{t} = \mu t + \sigma W_{t} \text{, with } \mu \text{ a drift and } \sigma \text{ a finite constant volatility } $$

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Market Efficiency
SLIDE: Semimartingale
CONTENU:
- A stochastic process $M_{t}$ can satisfy locally the martingale property

- $\Rightarrow$ $M_{t}$ is a local martingale ($\mathcal{LM}$) : $M_{t} \in \mathcal{LM}$

- $M_{t}$ enters a more general class of processes : the semimartingale ($\mathcal{SM}$)

- If a stochastic process $S_{t} \in \mathcal{SM}$, then it can be decomposed as

$$ S_{t} = A_{t} + M_{t} $$

where $A_{t}$ is a càdlàg adapted process with locally bounded variation

- $\Rightarrow$ « càdlàg » means « continue à droit et limite à gauche »

- $\Rightarrow$ « adapted » means « that cannot see into the future »

- $\Rightarrow$ « bounded variation » means « a function whose total variation is finite »

- $M_{t}$ often describes the continuous part of the asset price dynamics

- $A_{t}$ often describes a drift term or predictable path

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Market Efficiency
SLIDE: $\sigma$-martingale
CONTENU:
- Many asset prices are represented by semimartingales

- $\Rightarrow$ e.g. Brownian martingales are semimartingales

- $\Rightarrow$ e.g. stochastic volatility models can be semimartingales

- $\Rightarrow$ e.g. stochastic processes with jumps can be semimartingales

- $\Rightarrow$ if $S_{t}$ has an integral representation it is a $\sigma$-martingale (more general)

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Market Efficiency
SLIDE: Fundamental Theorem of Asset Pricing (FTAP)
CONTENU:
- Asset pricing requires market equilibrium to exist

- Under the EMH the market exists but risk free profit is impossible

- $\Rightarrow$ FTAP ensures that for an $\mathbb{R}^{d}$-valued semimartingale $S = (S_{t})_{0\leq t \leq T}$ :

- $\Rightarrow$ if there exists a risk-neutral probability measure $\mathbb{Q}$ equivalent to the

- ... original probability measure $\mathbb{P}$ under which $S$ is a $\sigma$-martingale, then

- ... $S$ does not permit free lunch with vanishing risk

- $\Rightarrow$ any arbitrage is mathematically prohibited
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Market Efficiency
SLIDE: A trivial model
CONTENU:
- Let's define $\mathbb{P}$, $\mathbb{Q}$ and explain that theorem with a trivial model

- a. $(B_{t})_{t = 0,1} = 1 \ \forall \ t$, the price of a risk free bond with null interest rate

- b. $(S_{t})_{t = 0,1}$, the price of a risky asset with $S_{0} = 1$

- $S_{1}$ being uncertain, it is a random variable defined on a probability space

$$ (\Omega,(\mathcal{F}_{t})_{t = 0,1},\mathbb{P}) $$

- $\Rightarrow$ $\Omega$ is the set of all possible outcomes

- $\Rightarrow$ $\mathcal{F}_{t}$ is the set of events

- $\Rightarrow$ $\mathbb{P}$ is a probability function assigning a probability to each event

- To simplify, let $\Omega$ consist of only two elements $g$ and $b$

- $\Rightarrow$ any random element $\omega \in \Omega$ has outcomes $g$ or $b$

- $\Rightarrow$ $g$ and $b$ stand for « good » and « bad »' and occur with probability

$$ \mathbb{P}(g) = \mathbb{P}(b) = 1/2 $$
- $\Rightarrow$ At time $t = 1$, we finally define that

$$ S_{1}(\omega) = \Bigg\{ \begin{array}{c} 2 \;\; \text{for} \;\; \omega = g \\ 1/2 \;\; \text{for} \;\; \omega = b \end{array} \Bigg. $$
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Market Efficiency
SLIDE: Option pricing
CONTENU:
- An interesting strategy to prevent $b$ or $g$ is to buy an Option

- $\Rightarrow$ the investor buys the right but not the obligation to buy $S_{t}$

- ... at time $t = 1$ at the pre-defined strike price $K = 1$

- At Option expiration (i.e. at time $t = 1$), the payoff is simply

$$ C_{1}(\omega) = (S_{1}(\omega) - K)_{+} = \Bigg\{ \begin{array}{c} 1 \;\; \text{for} \;\; \omega = g \\ 0 \;\; \text{for} \;\; \omega = b \end{array} \Bigg. $$
- Knowing $C_{1}(\omega)$, the Option pricing puzzle is to determine $C_{0}$

- $\Rightarrow$ What is the price at which the investor will buy the Option today ?

- In M1 we have studied: for risky assets, « expectation » is a bad criterion

$$ C_{0} := \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}(C_{1}) = 1/2 < \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}(B_{1}) = 1 < \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}(S_{1}) = 1.25 $$

Reminder : expectation operator is valid only for risk neutral investors

- $\Rightarrow$ The binomial model (Cox, Ross et Rubinstein) provides a solution
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Market Efficiency
SLIDE: Reminder : binomial model
CONTENU:
- The investor going long in the Option can try to cover its position

- $\Rightarrow$ invests in a portfolio that replicates the Option profit $(S_{1}(\omega) - K)_{+}$

$$ P_{1} = \alpha S_{1} + \beta B_{1} = C_{1} $$

where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the quantities invested in the stock and the bond

- Solving that system (composed by each state of the nature) gives

$$ \alpha^{*} = 2/3 \text{ and } \beta^{*} = -1/3 $$
- Indeed, the system is

$$\begin{aligned}
C_{1} = 1 & = 2\alpha + \beta \text{ for } \omega = g \\
C_{1} = 0 & = \alpha/2 + \beta \text{ for } \omega = b
\end{aligned}$$
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Market Efficiency
SLIDE: Reminder : binomial model
CONTENU:
- $P_{0}$ equals the Option price $C_{0}$ by « no arbitrage argument »

$$ \btxt{P_{0}} = 2/3S_{0} - 1/3B_{0} = \btxt{1/3 = C_{0}} $$

- Proof by contradiction : suppose that $\ntxt{C_{0} = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}(C_{1}) = 1/2} \neq P_{0}$

- $\Rightarrow$ As the portfolio replicates the Option

- ... free lunch would be possible by going long in $P_{0}$ and going short in $C_{0}$

- ... and getting back arbitrage profit $C_{0} - P_{0} = 1/6$

- $\Rightarrow$ Arbitrage opportunities vanish only for $C_{0} \to P_{0}$
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Market Efficiency
SLIDE: Risk-neutral measure (or equivalent martingale measure)
CONTENU:
- Suppose that the world is governed by a new probability measure $\mathbb{Q}$

- $\Rightarrow$ $\mathbb{Q}$ assigns new weights to $g$ and $b$ such that $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}(S_{1}) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}(B_{1})$

- As the bond is free of risk, $\mathbb{Q}$ is called risk-neutral probability measure

- $\Rightarrow$ recall that $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}(B_{1}) = 1$ and the unique solution ensuring $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}(S_{1}) = 1$ is

$$ \mathbb{Q}(g) = 1/3 \text{ and } \mathbb{Q}(b) = 2/3 $$

as $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}(S_{1}) = 2 \times 1/3 + 1/2 \times 2/3 = 1$

- Strictly speaking, $\mathbb{Q}$ is a martingale measure for $S$

- ... or equivalently, $S$ is a martingale under $\mathbb{Q}$

- The now valid expectation criterion can be applied to determine $C_{0}$

$$ C_{0} = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}(C_{1}) = 1 \times 1/3 + 0 \times 2/3 = 1/3 $$
- $\Rightarrow$ $C_{0}$ is compatible with the « arbitrage-free » value obtained under $\mathbb{P}$
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Market Efficiency
SLIDE: Risk-neutral measure in continuous time models
CONTENU:
- This trivial example can be extended to more general processes

- $\Rightarrow$ let $(S_{t})_{0\leq t \leq T}$ be a continuous-time Brownian martingale

$$ S_{t} = \sigma W_{t} $$

modeled on a filtered probability space $(\Omega,(\mathcal{F}_{t})_{0\leq t \leq T},\mathbb{P})$

- For $C_{T}$ any contingent claim, i.e. a $\mathcal{F}_{T}$-measurable random variable

- $\Rightarrow$ $C_{0} := \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}(C_{T})$ yields the arbitrage-free prices for $C_{T}$ when $\mathbb{Q}$ runs

- ... through the probability measures on $\mathcal{F}_{T}$ which are equivalent to $\mathbb{P}$

- ... under which the stochastic process $S$ is a martingale

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Market Efficiency
SLIDE: No free lunch with vanishing risk
CONTENU:
- When the risk-neutral measure is unique, one may replicate $C_{T}$ as

$$ C_{T} = C_{0} + \int_{0}^{T} P_{t}dS_{t} $$

where $P_{t}$ is a predictable trading strategy (e.g. replication portfolio)

- $\Rightarrow$ $P_{t}$ models the holding in $S$ during the infinitesimal interval $[t,t+dt]$

- Many models like the one of Black & Scholes use that result to find $C_{0}$

- We now get more intuition on the importance of the FTAP

- $\Rightarrow$ roughly speaking, the absence of arbitrage possibilities for a stochastic process $S$ is equivalent to the existence of an equivalent martingale measure for $S$
