text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Spot and Integrated Volatility
SLIDE: Stochastic differential equation (SDE)
CONTENU:
- Financial observations are often sampled at high frequency

- $\Rightarrow$ to the limit, infinitesimal differences can be considered :
$$ dt = (t + h) - t, \;\;\; h \to 0 $$
- Applied to $S_{t}$, infinitesimal calculus comes down to the differential $dS_{t}$

- Assume the following Itô drift-diffusion for the returns of $S_{t}$

$$ \frac{dS_{t}}{S_{t}} = \mu dt + \sigma dW_{t} \Rightarrow \ntxt{dS_{t} = S_{t}(\mu dt + \sigma dW_{t})} $$
- As $S_{t}$ is stochastic, solving the SDE $dS_{t}$ is not immediate

- $\Rightarrow$ Itô's lemma is a powerful alternative to chain rule derivatives and states

$$ d\big(f(S_{t},t)\big) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(S_{t},t)dt + \frac{\partial f}{\partial S_{t}}(S_{t},t)dS_{t} + \frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial^{2} f}{\partial S_{t}^{2}}(S_{t},t)\sigma^{2}dt $$
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Spot and Integrated Volatility
SLIDE: Solution of Itô drift-diffusion
CONTENU:
- Define $f(S_{t},t) = \log(S_{t})$ and apply Itô's lemma

$$\begin{aligned}
d\big(\log(S_{t})\big) &= 0dt + \frac{1}{S_{t}}\ntxt{dS_{t}} + \frac{1}{2}\Bigg(-\frac{1}{\btxt{S_{t}^{2}}} \Bigg)\sigma^{2}\btxt{S_{t}^{2}}dt \\
& = \frac{1}{S_{t}} \ntxt{(\mu S_{t} dt + \sigma S_{t} dW_{t})} - \frac{1}{2}\sigma^{2}dt \\
& = \Big( \mu - \frac{1}{2}\sigma^{2}\Big)dt + \sigma dW_{t}
\end{aligned}$$
- Now, we can integrate and obtain the solution of the SDE

$$\begin{aligned}
\log(S_{t}) & = \log(S_{0}) + \int_{0}^{t}\mu ds - \frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{t}\sigma^{2} ds + \int_{0}^{t}\sigma dW_{s} \\
& = \log(S_{0}) + \mu t - \frac{\sigma^{2}}{2}t + \sigma W_{t} \\
S_{t} & = S_{0} \exp\Big(\mu t - \frac{\sigma^{2}}{2}t + \sigma W_{t}\Big)
\end{aligned}$$

- $\Rightarrow$ Modeling log-price ensures the stochastic path to be positive
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Spot and Integrated Volatility
SLIDE: Martingale property of the Wiener integral under $\mathbb{P}$
CONTENU:
- Any integrable process $X_{t}$

- whose increments are independent

- and centered under probability measure $\mathbb{P}$ : $\mtxt{\mathbb{E}(X_{t} - X_{s})} = 0$

- ... is a martingale with respect to the filtration $\mathcal{F}_{t}$ as for $0 \leq s \leq t$ we have

$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}(X_{t}|\mathcal{F}_{s}) & = \mathbb{E}(X_{t} - X_{s} + X_{s}|\mathcal{F}_{s}) \\
& = \mathbb{E}(X_{t} - \btxt{X_{s}|\mathcal{F}_{s}}) + \mathbb{E}(\btxt{X_{s}|\mathcal{F}_{s}}) \\
& = \mtxt{\mathbb{E}(X_{t} - X_{s})} + X_{s} \\
& = X_{s}
\end{aligned}$$
- The Wiener process $W_{t}$, whose stochastic integral representation is

$$ W_{t} = \int_{0}^{t} dW_{s}, $$

has centered and independent increments and hence $W_{t} \in \mathcal{M}$
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
slide_title: Martingale property of the Wiener integral under $\mathbb{P}$

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Spot and Integrated Volatility
SLIDE: Martingale property of the Itô integral under $\mathbb{P}$
CONTENU:
- The Wiener integral is a particular type of Itô integral

- ... which is a stochastic generalization of the Riemann–Stieltjes integral (limit of Riemann sums) where the integrands and the integrators are stochastic

$$ \int_{0}^{t} u_{\tau}dX_{\tau} = \lim\limits_{M \to \infty} \sum_{i = 1}^{M} u_{t_{i}}(X_{t_{i}} - X_{t_{i-1}}) $$

with $t-1 = t_{0} < t_{1} < \ldots < t_{M} = t$ and $X_{\tau}$ a semi-martingale

- This more general representation, where $X_{\tau}$ is not necessarily a Wiener process, can help to generate more realistic price dynamics

- If $X_{t} = W_{t}$, the Itô integral of any square integrable adapted process $u_{t}$ is a martingale as

$$ \mathbb{E}\bigg( \int_{0}^{t} u_{\tau}dW_{\tau} | \mathcal{F}_{s} \bigg) = \int_{0}^{s} u_{\tau}dW_{\tau} $$
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
slide_title: Martingale property of the Itô integral under $\mathbb{P}$

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Spot and Integrated Volatility
SLIDE: No arbitrage in continuous time
CONTENU:
- Under a risk-neutral probability measure $\mathbb{Q}$, the return of the risky asset
- ... equals the return of the risk-less asset if it is discounted by $r$

$$ \tilde{S}_{t} = e^{-r t} S_{t} = \frac{S_{t}}{B_{t}/B_{0}} $$

with $r$ the risk-free rate of a zero-coupon bond $B_{t}$

- $\Rightarrow$ The discounted process $\tilde{S}_{t}$ satisfies

$$\begin{aligned}
d\tilde{S}_{t} & = d(e^{-r t} S_{t}) \\
& = S_{t}d(e^{-r t}) + e^{-r t}dS_{t} + (de^{-r t})dS_{t}\\
& = -re^{-r t}S_{t}dt + e^{-r t}\ntxt{dS_{t}} + (-re^{-r t}dt)\bullet\ntxt{dS_{t}} \\
\text{Itô rules : } & \btxt{dt \bullet dt = 0 \text{ | } dt \bullet dW_{t} = 0 \text{ | } dW_{t} \bullet dW_{t} = dt} \\
& = -re^{-r t}S_{t}dt + \mu e^{-r t}S_{t}dt + \sigma e^{-r t}S_{t}dW_{t} \\
& = (\mu - r)\tilde{S}_{t}dt + \sigma \tilde{S}_{t} dW_{t}
\end{aligned}$$

and $\tilde{S}_{t} \in \mathcal{M}$ under $\mathbb{Q}$ when $\mu = r \Rightarrow$ no arbitrage by FTAP theorem

- When $\mu \neq r$, one can define a martingale under $\mathbb{Q}$ but Girsanov Theorem is necessary
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Spot and Integrated Volatility
SLIDE: Time-varying instantaneous variance
CONTENU:
- In previous model, $S_{t}$ as well as $\tilde{S}_{t}$ have constant volatility $\sigma$ but

- ... Itô's lemma remains valid if volatility changes in time

- At this stage assume $\sigma_{t}$ is càdlàg, a.s. positive and consider $p_{t} = \log(S_{t})$

$$ dp_{t} = m_{t}dt + \sigma_{t}dW_{t}, \;\;\;m_{t} = \mu_{t} - \sigma_{t}^{2}/2, \;\;\; t \geq 0 $$
- It turns out that log returns are

$$ r_{t} = p_{t} - p_{t-1} = \int_{t-1}^{t}m_{s}ds + \int_{t-1}^{t}\sigma_{s}dW_{s} $$
- ... and distributed as follows

$$ r_{t} \sim \mathcal{N}\Bigg(\int_{t-1}^{t}m_{s}ds, \int_{t-1}^{t}\sigma_{s}^{2}dW_{s} \Bigg) $$
- $\Rightarrow$ $\sigma_{t}^{2}$ (resp. $\sigma_{t}$) is called instantaneous or spot variance (volatility)
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Spot and Integrated Volatility
SLIDE: Integrated Variance (IV)
CONTENU:
- Over an interval of time $[t-1,t]$ the log-return variance is hence

$$ IV_{t} = \int_{t-1}^{t}\sigma_{s}^{2}ds $$

also called Integrated Variance

- Assuming that the time length of one day is $t - (t - 1) = 1$

- ... $\sqrt{IV}$ represents the daily log-return volatility

- For any sequence of partitions $t-1 = t_{0} < t_{1} < \ldots < t_{M} = t$ with

- ... $\sup_{j}\{t_{j+1} - t_{j}\} \to 0$ for $M \to \infty$, the Quadratic Variation $(QV)$ can be defined as

$$ [p,p]_{t} = \underset{M \to \infty}{\operatorname{plim~}} \sum_{j = 0}^{M-1} (p_{t_{j+1}} - p_{t_{j}})(p_{t_{j+1}} - p_{t_{j}}) = IV_{t} $$
- Note In the particular constant volatility case, $IV_{t} = \sigma^{2} t$
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Spot and Integrated Volatility
SLIDE: Integrated Variance and semi-martingale
CONTENU:
- Now, consider a more general representation with $p_{t} \in \mathcal{SM}$

$$ p_{t} = A_{t} + M_{t} $$

where $A_{t}$ has finite variation and $M_{t}$ is a local martingale

- If $A_{t}$ is continous, it can be show that the $QV$

$$ [p,p]_{t} = M_{t} $$

even if $M_{t}$ is contaminated by discontinuities (jumps)

- However, one cannot ensure that $QV$ converges to $IV$
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Continuous-time models
SLIDE: Simple continuous-time models
CONTENU:
- Under the assumption that $S_{t} \in \mathcal{SM}$, many models can be considered

- The simplest one is

$$ S_{t} = S_{0} + \int_{0}^{t}\sigma_{s}dW_{s} $$

for which we have $IV_{t} = \int_{0}^{t}\sigma_{s}ds$ over interval $[0,t]$

- It appears as the solution of the SDE

$$ dS_{t} = \sigma_{t}dW_{t} $$

- However,

- $\Rightarrow$ more general integrators ($\mathcal{LI}$) can be considered in place of $W_{t}$

- $\Rightarrow$ many models exist for the stochastic dynamics of price ($\mathcal{SP}$)

- $\Rightarrow$ many models exist for the stochastic dynamics of volatility ($\mathcal{SV}$)
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Continuous-time models
SLIDE: $\mathcal{LI}$ : Lévy processes
CONTENU:
**Définition** : A càdlàg process $(X_{t})_{t\geq0}$ defined on $(\Omega, \mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$ is a Lévy process if $X_{0} = 0$ and

- For any increasing sequence $t_{0},\cdots,t_{n}$, the random variables $X_{t_{0}},X_{t_{1}}-X_{t_{0}},\cdots,X_{t_{n}}-X_{t_{n-1}}$ are independent

- The law of $X_{t+h}-X_{t}$ does not depend on $t$ such that increments are stationary

- $X_{t}$ is stochastically continuous, i.e. $\lim\limits_{h\to 0} \mathbb{P}(|X_{t+h} - X_{t}| \geq \varepsilon) = 0$

- Note The last point just rules out nonrandom occurrence of discontinuities

- $\Rightarrow$ $X_{t} \sim \mathcal{L}(.)$ can be discontinuous as we will see in a few slides

- Lévy processes are more general than Brownian motions and possibly have non-Gaussian increments
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Continuous-time models
SLIDE: $\mathcal{LI}$ : Lévy processes
CONTENU:
**Définition** : A càdlàg process $(X_{t})_{t\geq0}$ defined on $(\Omega, \mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$ is a Lévy process if $X_{0} = 0$ and

- For any increasing sequence $t_{0},\cdots,t_{n}$, the random variables $X_{t_{0}},X_{t_{1}}-X_{t_{0}},\cdots,X_{t_{n}}-X_{t_{n-1}}$ are independent

- The law of $X_{t+h}-X_{t}$ does not depend on $t$ such that increments are stationary

- $X_{t}$ is stochastically continuous, i.e. $\lim\limits_{h\to 0} \mathbb{P}(|X_{t+h} - X_{t}| \geq \varepsilon) = 0$
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Continuous-time models
SLIDE: $\mathcal{LI}$ : Infinite divisibility of Lévy processes
CONTENU:
- Let $X_{t} \sim \mathcal{L}(.)$ be sampled at regular time intervals $0,\Delta,2\Delta,\cdots,n\Delta$

- $\Rightarrow$ the resulting process is still a random walk as

$$ X_{n\Delta} = \sum_{k = 0}^{n-1} (X_{(k+1)\Delta} - X_{k\Delta}) = \sum_{k = 0}^{n-1} \Delta_{n}X_{k} $$

has i.i.d. increments $\Delta_{n}X_{k}$

- Moreover, their distribution is the same as the one of $X_{\Delta}$ whatever the sampling frequency

- For $n\Delta = t>0$ and $n \geq 1$, $X_{t}$ and $X_{\Delta = t/n}$ have the same distribution

- $\Rightarrow$ $X_{t}$ can be divided into $n$ i.i.d. parts : it is infinitely divisible

- A random walk can have arbitrary distribution whereas the distribution of increments of $X_{t} \sim \mathcal{L}(.)$ has to be infinitely divisible

- $\Rightarrow$ the most common eligible distributions are the Gaussian, the $\alpha$-stable and the Poisson distributions
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Continuous-time models
SLIDE: $\mathcal{SP}$ : Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) model
CONTENU:
- The OU model appears as the counterpart of an AR(1) process

$$ dX_{t} = \alpha(\theta - X_{t})dt + \sigma dW_{t} $$

with $\theta > 0$ and $\sigma > 0$

- The solution of the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck SDE is

$$ X_{t} = X_{0} e^{-\alpha t}+\theta \,(1-e^{-\alpha t})+\sigma \int _{0}^{t}e^{-\alpha (t-s)}\,dW_{s} $$
- In the financial literature, the OU coefficients can be interpreted as

- $\theta$ represents the asset equilibrium value

- $\sigma$ the volatility of shocks coming from the diffusion

- $\alpha$ the rate at which these shocks vanish & $X_{t}$ reverts towards the mean

- when is used to model interest rates, it is also known as Vasicek model
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Continuous-time models
SLIDE: $\mathcal{SP}$ : Hull-White (HW) model
CONTENU:
- The HW model extends the Vasicek model

$$ dX_{t} = \alpha(\theta(t) - X_{t})dt + \sigma(t) dW_{t} $$

with $\theta(t)$ a time-dependent coefficient

- The solution of the SDE is

$$ X_{t} = X_{0} e^{-\alpha t}+ \alpha\int_{0}^{t}e^{\alpha (s-t)}\theta_{s}ds + \sigma e^{-\theta t} \int _{0}^{t}e^{\theta s}\,dW_{s} $$
- As $\theta$ is time-dependent, one can use the Yield Curve for calibration

- Unfortunately, the HW model cannot ensure the positivity of $X_{t}$

- $\Rightarrow$ not suitable for interest rate (in normal periods) nor for volatility
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Continuous-time models
SLIDE: $\mathcal{SP}$ : Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) model
CONTENU:
- The CIR model is also designed to mimic the evolution of interest rates

$$ dX_{t} = \theta(\mu - X_{t})dt + \sigma {\sqrt {X_{t}}}\,dW_{t} $$

with

- $\theta(\mu - X_{t})$ the short term dynamics of $X_{t}$

- $\sigma$ the volatility of $X_{t}$

- Interestingly, as long as $2\theta \mu \geq \sigma^{2}$, $X_{t}$ will never reach 0 (Feller condition)

- This type of square-root SDE is hence useful to model volatility

- $\Rightarrow$ However, this SDE has no closed-form solution
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Continuous-time models
SLIDE: $\mathcal{SP}$ : Jump augmented models
CONTENU:
- Abrupt changes can occur in price dynamics

- $\Rightarrow$ such jumps in price cannot be modeled by Gaussian increments

- Counting processes $\mathcal{CM}$ are good candidates

- A counting process is a stochastic non-decreasing process $N_{t} \in \mathbb{N}$, $t \geq 0$

- $\Rightarrow$ As $N_{t} \in \mathbb{N}$, for $s \leq t$, $N_{t} - N_{s}$ is the number of events occurred in $(s,t]$
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Continuous-time models
SLIDE: $\mathcal{SP}$ : Poisson model
CONTENU:
- A Poisson point process $N_{t} \in \mathcal{CM}$ is defined as follows

- $N_{0} = 0$ and for $s \leq t$ where increments $N_{t} - N_{s}$ are independent

- the probability mass function of $N_{t}$ is

$$ \mathbb{P}(N_{t} = c) = \frac{(\lambda t)^{c}}{c!}\exp(-\lambda t) $$

with $\lambda$ the arrival intensity of events and $\ntxt{\mathbb{E}(N_{t}) = \lambda t}$

- $\Rightarrow$ $N_{t}$ will represent the jumps occurrence irrespective of the jumps size

- Consider $(N_{t} - \lambda t)_{t}$ a compensated process satisfying $\ntxt{\mathbb{E}(N_{t} - \lambda t) = 0}$

- $\Rightarrow$ Since it has centered and independent increments, $\tilde{N}_{t} = (N_{t} - \lambda t)_{t} \in \mathcal{M}$
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Continuous-time models
SLIDE: $\mathcal{SP}$ : Compound Poisson model
CONTENU:
- Let's define $J_{t}$ a compound Poisson process

$$ J_{t} = \sum_{i = 1}^{N_{t}} Y_{i}, $$

where $Y_{i}$ is i.i.d, square-integrable and generally Gaussian

- Defining $Y_{t^{-}} := \lim\limits_{s\to t} Y_{s}$, the jump size is hence

$$ \Delta J_{t} = Y_{t} - Y_{t^{-}} = dJ_{t} $$
- $\Delta J_{t}$ will be used latter to obtain an integral representation of $J_{t}$

- Notice that $\mathbb{E}(J_{t}) = \lambda t \; \mathbb{E}(Y)$ and hence the compensated process

$$ \tilde{J}_{t} = \big(J_{t} - \lambda t \; \mathbb{E}(Y) \big)_{t} $$

has centered and independent increments $\Rightarrow \tilde{J}_{t} \in \mathcal{M}$
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Continuous-time models
SLIDE: Stochastic integral representation of $J_{t}$
CONTENU:
- Let $f_{Y}(.) \in \mathbb{R}$ be the jump size distribution function and observe that

$$ \nu(dy) = \lambda f_{Y}(dy) $$

is the density of $J_{t}$ in the jump size interval $[y,y+dy]$

- $\btxt{\nu(dy)}$ is called Lévy or intensity measure but is not a probability measure since

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}} \nu(dy) = \lambda \neq 1 $$
- Now we call Poisson random measure, for $B = [t_{1},t_{2}]$,

$$ \mtxt{\mu(B,A)} = \#\{(J_{t_{2}} - J_{t_{1}}) \in A\} $$

a measure that counts the jumps in $B$ such that their sizes are in $A$

- Then, $J_{t}$ has a stochastic integral representation given by

$$ J_{t} = \sum_{s \in [0,t]} \Delta J_{s} = \int_{[0,t]\times \mathbb{R}} y \times \mu(ds\times dy) $$
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Continuous-time models
SLIDE: Lévy-Itô decomposition
CONTENU:
**Modèle** : Let $(X_{t})_{t\geq 0}$ be a Lévy process and $\nu(.)$ its Lévy measure verifying

$$ \int_{|x|\leq \kappa} |x|^{2} \nu(dx) < \infty \text{ and } \int_{|x|\geq \kappa}\nu(dx) < \infty $$

such that the intensity of jumps larger than $\kappa>\varepsilon>0$ is finite and denote $\mu(.)$ its Poisson random measure on $[0,\infty)\times \mathbb{R}$. Then, there exists a drift $\alpha$ and a Brownian motion $(W_{t})\geq 0$ with variance $\beta$ such that

$$ X_{t} = \alpha t + W_{t} + J_{t}^{l} + \lim\limits_{\varepsilon \to 0}\tilde{J}_{t}^{\varepsilon} $$

where large jumps with finite activity are modeled by

$$ J_{t}^{l} = \int_{0}^{t}\int_{|x|\geq \kappa} x \mu(ds\times dx) $$

and small jumps with possibly infinite activity by

$$ \tilde{J}_{t}^{\varepsilon} = \int_{0}^{t} \int_{\varepsilon\leq|x|< \kappa} x (\mu(ds\times dx) - \nu(dx)ds) $$
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Continuous-time models
SLIDE: Lévy characteristic triplet
CONTENU:
- The Lévy-Itô decomposition entails that every Lévy process

- 1 is a sum of (Brownian) continuous and discontinuous paths

- 2 is characterized by the triplet $X_{t} = \mathcal{L}(\alpha,\beta,\nu)$

- 3 has large jumps $J_{t}^{l}$ that follow a finite activity compound Poisson

- 4 has small jumps $J_{t}^{\varepsilon}$ that follow an infinite activity compound Poisson

- As $\nu < \infty$ is imposed only for $|x|\geq \kappa$, the Lévy process can diverge

- $\Rightarrow$ $J_{t}^{\varepsilon}$ needs to be compensated $\Rightarrow$ $\tilde{J}_{t}^{\varepsilon}$

- One can define a « pure-jump » Lévy process by setting $X_{t} = \mathcal{L}(0,0,\nu)$

- $\Rightarrow$ generally unrealistic in finance as it rules out the diffusion
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Continuous-time models
SLIDE: $\mathcal{SP}$ : Jump diffusion model and Exponential Lévy
CONTENU:
- A jump-diffusion process combines a Brownian diffusion with jumps

$$ dS_{t} = \mu S_{t^{-}} dt + \sigma S_{t^{-}} dW_{t} + S_{t^{-}}dJ_{t} $$
- $\Rightarrow$ it is an Exponential Lévy if $S_{t} = \exp(X_{t})$ with $X_{t} \sim \mathcal{L}(\mu,\sigma^{2},\nu)$

- Applying an Itô formula for jump, the SDE solution is $S_{t} = A_{t} + M_{t}$

- The martingale part is

$$ M_{t} = 1 + \int_{0}^{t}S_{t^{-}}\sigma dW_{s} + \int_{[0,t]\times \mathbb{R}} S_{t^{-}}(e^{y} - 1) \times \tilde{\mu}(ds\times dy) $$

and the continuous finite variation drift part is given by

$$ A_{t} = \int_{0}^{t}S_{t^{-}}\Big(\mu - \sigma^{2}/2 + \int_{\mathbb{R}} (e^{y} - 1 - y\mathds{1}_{|y|\leq\kappa}) \times \nu(dy)\Big)ds $$
- $S_{t}$ will be a martingale if $\mathbb{E}(S_{t}|S_{0}) = S_{0}$ and hence if

$$ \mu - \sigma^{2}/2 + \int_{\mathbb{R}} (e^{y} - 1 - y\mathds{1}_{|y|\leq\kappa}) \times \nu(dy) = 0 $$
- Note $S_{t}$ could be defined directly as a Lévy but without positivity constraint
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
slide_title: $\mathcal{SP}$ : Jump diffusion model and Exponential Lévy

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Continuous-time models
SLIDE: $\mathcal{SP}+\mathcal{SV}$ : Heston model
CONTENU:
- Previous models are unrealistic because $\sigma$ is constant over time

- Heston (1993) suggests the following stochastic volatility model

$$\begin{aligned}
dS_{t} &= \mu S_{t}dt + S_{t}\sigma_{t} dW_{1,t} \\
d\sigma^{2}_{t} & = -\theta(\sigma^{2}_{t} - \eta)dt + \gamma\sigma_{t} dW_{2,t}
\end{aligned}$$

with $W_{1,t}$ and $W_{2,t}$ two Brownian motions and $\theta,\eta,\gamma>0$

- $\Rightarrow$ The stochastic volatility is modeled as a CIR process

- The Heston model is a particular case of two-factor stochastic volatility model

$$\begin{aligned}
dS_{t} &= m_{t}S_{t}dt + \sigma_{t} S_{t} dW_{1,t} \\
d\sigma^{2}_{t} & = \alpha(t,\sigma^{2}_{t})dt + \beta(t,\sigma^{2}_{t}) dW_{2,t}
\end{aligned}$$

where $Cov(W_{1,t},W_{2,t}) = \rho t$ is possibly non-null

- In practice $d\sigma_{t}$ tends to be negatively correlated with $dS_{t} \Rightarrow \rho < 0$
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Continuous-time models
SLIDE: $\mathcal{SP}+\mathcal{SV}$ : Infinite activity jump diffusion stochastic volatility model
CONTENU:
- Let $p_{t} \in \mathcal{SM}$ be stated by the following general $\mathcal{SV}$ model

$$\begin{aligned}
p_{t} & = p_{0} + \underbrace{\int_{0}^{t}m_{s}ds + \int_{0}^{t}\sigma_{s}dW_{s}}_{\text{Continuous (1)}} + \underbrace{\int_{0}^{t}dJ_{s}}_{\text{Discontinuous}} \\
\int_{0}^{t}dJ_{s} & = \underbrace{\int_{0}^{t}\int_{|x|\geq \kappa} x \mu(ds\times dx)}_{\text{Big jumps (2)}} + \underbrace{\int_{0}^{t} \int_{\varepsilon\leq|x|< \kappa} x (\mu(ds\times dx) - \nu(dx)ds)}_{\text{Small jumps (3)}}
\end{aligned}$$
- As seen before, $p_{t}$ will always generate a finite number of big jumps

- ... but it may give rise to either a finite or infinite number of small jumps

- Each component of $p_{t}$ can be mapped into an economic source of risk

- Part 1 capture the normal risk of the asset, which is hedgeable

- Part 2 capture default risk, or more generally big news-related events

- Part 3 represent price moves which are large on a time scale of a few seconds, but generally not significant on a daily frequency
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
slide_title: $\mathcal{SP}+\mathcal{SV}$ : Infinite activity jump diffusion stochastic volatility model

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Continuous-time models
SLIDE: $\mathcal{SP}+\mathcal{SV}$ : Finite activity jump diffusion stochastic volatility model
CONTENU:
- Let $p_{t} \in \mathcal{SM}$ be stated as previously but impose $\kappa = 0$

- $\Rightarrow$ all jumps are qualified as being big jumps

- $\Rightarrow$ hence $p_{t}$ has finite activity and jumps are summable

$$ \sum_{s\leq t}|\Delta p_{s}| < \infty, \text{ where } \Delta p_{s} = p_{s} - p_{s^{-}} $$
- In such a case, on can rewrite $p_{t}$ as

$$ p_{t} = p_{0} + \underbrace{\int_{0}^{t}\tilde{m}_{s}ds + \int_{0}^{t}\sigma_{s}dW_{s}}_{\text{Continuous}} + \underbrace{\sum_{s\leq t}\Delta p_{s}}_{\text{Discontinuous}} $$

where $\tilde{m}_{s} = m_{s} - \int_{\mathbb{R}}yf(dy)$

- In practice, the jump activity is difficult to measure but index such as Blumenthal-Getoor (BG or $\beta$) index exist
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
slide_title: $\mathcal{SP}+\mathcal{SV}$ : Finite activity jump diffusion stochastic volatility model

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Continuous-time models
SLIDE: Finite versus Infinite activity : the Blumenthal-Getoor index
CONTENU:
- Finite varition of order $p$ means that for $\Delta X_{k} = X_{k\Delta} - X_{(k-1)\Delta}$: $\quad \sum_{k=1}^{[t/\Delta]}|\Delta X_{k}|^{p} < \infty \text{ as } \Delta \to 0$
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
slide_title: Finite versus Infinite activity : the Blumenthal-Getoor index

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Continuous-time models
SLIDE: $\mathcal{SP}+\mathcal{SV}$ : Bates model
CONTENU:
- Bates (1996) extends the Heston model to Poisson jump-diffusion

$$\begin{aligned}
dS_{t} &= \mu S_{t^{-}}dt + S_{t^{-}}\sigma_{t} dW_{1,t} + S_{t^{-}}dJ_{t} \\
d\sigma^{2}_{t} & = -\theta(\sigma^{2}_{t} - \eta)dt + \gamma\sigma_{t} dW_{2,t}
\end{aligned}$$
- In this model, the QV of $p_{t} = \log(S_{t})$ no-longer converges to IV

- $\Rightarrow$ For any sequence of partitions $t-1 = t_{0} < t_{1} < \ldots < t_{M} = t$ with

- ... $\sup_{j}\{t_{j+1} - t_{j}\} \to 0$ for $M \to \infty$, the Quadratic Variation $(QV)$ is

$$ [p,p]_{t} = \underset{M \to \infty}{\operatorname{plim~}} \sum_{j = 0}^{M-1} (p_{t_{j+1}} - p_{t_{j}})(p_{t_{j+1}} - p_{t_{j}}) = \btxt{IV_{t}} + \ntxt{JV_{t}} $$

where

$$ \btxt{IV_{t}} = \int_{t-1}^{t}\sigma_{s}^{2}ds \text{ and } \ntxt{JV_{t}} = \sum_{i = N_{t-1}+1}^{N_{t}} \xi_{i}^{2} = \sum_{t-1\leq s\leq t}|\Delta p_{s}|^{2} $$

with $\xi_{i} = \log(1 + Y_{i})$ and $Y_{i}$ the jump magnitude of the count $i$
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Continuous-time models
SLIDE: Quadratic variation of various processes
CONTENU:
- Overall, depending on the stochastic process we have :

$$ [p,p]_{t} = \btxt{IV_{t}} = \sigma^{2} t $$

if $p_{t}$ is a standard Brownian motion,

$$ [p,p]_{t} = \btxt{IV_{t}} = \int_{t-1}^{t}\sigma_{s}^{2}ds $$

if $p_{t}$ is a Brownian motion with stochastic volatility

$$ [p,p]_{t} = \btxt{IV_{t}} + \ntxt{JV_{t}} = \int_{t-1}^{t}\sigma_{s}^{2}ds + \sum_{t-1\leq s\leq t}|\Delta p_{s}|^{2} $$

if $p_{t}$ is a finite activity jump diffusion process

$$ [p,p]_{t} = \btxt{IV_{t}} + \ntxt{JV_{t}} = \int_{t-1}^{t}\sigma_{s}^{2}ds + \int_{0}^{t}\int_{\mathbb{R}} y^{2} \mu(ds\times dy) $$

if $p_{t}$ is a general Lévy process
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Continuous-time GARCH
SLIDE: Why continuous time models?
CONTENU:
- Observations are quite often irregularly spaced
- Observations quite often come in at a very high frequency
- Then a continuous time model may provide a better approximation to the discrete data than a discrete model

At the same time

- Continuous-time models are central to mathematical finance
- Most theoretical results on derivative pricing rely on continuous-time processes, obtained as solutions of diffusion equations

Aim: Construct continuous time models with features of GARCH (it is possible to establish connections between the two approaches: discrete-time and continuous-time models)

Note: In continuous time it is natural to model the logarithm of the asset price itself, that is $p_t$, rather than its increments $r_t$ as in discrete time
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Continuous-time GARCH
SLIDE: Continuous time GARCH approximations
CONTENU:
- A continuous time model may serve as an approximation to a GARCH process
- Main question: starting from the continuous model, how close would a process be to a GARCH process when sampled at discrete times?
- An optimal situation would be that the process itself is a GARCH process, whenever sampled at equidistant times $(kh)_{k\in \mathbb{N}_0}$, for each $h > 0$
- Issue: GARCH processes are not closed under temporal aggregation (Drost and Nijman, 1993)
- A continuous time process $(Y_t)_{t\geq0}$ which happens to be a GARCH(1,1) process when sampled at ${0, h, 2h, \ldots}$ for some frequency $h$ will not be GARCH when sampled at ${0, 2h, 4h, \ldots}$
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Continuous-time GARCH
SLIDE: The diffusion approximation of Nelson (1990)
CONTENU:
**Modèle** : The GARCH(1,1) diffusion limit satisfies

$$\begin{aligned}
d p_t &= \sigma_t dW_t^{(1)},\\
d\sigma^2_t &= (\omega-\theta\sigma_t^2)dt+ \lambda\sigma_t^2 dW_t^{(2)}, \ t\geq0
\end{aligned}$$

- Although the GARCH process is driven by a single noise sequence, the diffusion limit is driven by two independent Brownian motions $(W_t^{(1)})_{t\geq0}$ and $(W_t^{(2)})_{t\geq0}$
- The behavior of this diffusion limit is therefore rather different from that of the GARCH process itself since the volatility process $(\sigma^2_t)_{t\geq0}$ evolves independently of the driving process $(W_t^{(1)})_{t\geq0}$ in the first of the equations above
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Continuous-time GARCH
SLIDE: The diffusion approximation of Nelson (1990)
CONTENU:
**Modèle** : The GARCH(1,1) diffusion limit satisfies

$$\begin{aligned}
d p_t &= \sigma_t dW_t^{(1)},\\
d\sigma^2_t &= (\omega-\theta\sigma_t^2)dt+ \lambda\sigma_t^2 dW_t^{(2)}, \ t\geq0
\end{aligned}$$
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Continuous-time GARCH
SLIDE: The diffusion limit of Nelson
CONTENU:
Remarks:

- The equation of $d\sigma^2_t$ in the Theorem has a strictly stationary solution $(\sigma_t^2)_{t\geq 0}$ if
$$ 2\theta/\lambda^2 > -1\ \ \text{and}\ \ \omega> 0, $$
in which case the marginal stationary distribution of $\sigma_0^2$ is inverse Gamma distributed with parameters $1 +2\theta/\lambda^2$ and $2\omega/\lambda^2$
- The stationary limiting process $d\sigma^2_t$ has Pareto like tails
- The limit $(p_t, \sigma^2_t)$ is driven by two independent Brownian motions
- The processes $p_t$ and $\sigma^2_t$ are continuous. But empirical volatility can exhibit jumps

SLIDE: A continuous time GARCH model designed for option pricing\ (Kallsen and Taqqu, 1998)
CONTENU:
- Option pricing for Nelson's model (designed as limit of discrete time GARCH processes) may be demanding since the model gives rise to incomplete markets
- Kallsen and Taqqu (1998) developed a continuous time process which is a GARCH process when sampled at integer times
- This process is driven by a single Brownian motion only

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Continuous-time GARCH
SLIDE: A continuous time GARCH model designed for option pricing\ (Kallsen and Taqqu, 1998)
CONTENU:
**Définition** : Let $\omega,\lambda>0$, $\delta\geq0$ and $(B_t)_{t\geq0}$ be a standard Brownian motion. For some starting random variable $\sigma_0^2$, define the volatility process $(\sigma_t)_{t\geq0}$ by $\sigma_t^2 = \sigma_0^2$ for $t\in [0, 1)$ and

$$ \sigma_t^2 =\omega +\lambda \big(\int_{\lfloor t \rfloor -1}^{\lfloor t \rfloor} \sigma_{s^-}dB_s\big)^2+\delta \sigma^2_{\lfloor t \rfloor -1}, \ t\geq 1 $$

The continuous-time GARCH process $(p_t)_{t\geq0}$ then models the log-price process, and is given by

$$ p_t=p_0+\int_0^t (\mu(\sigma_{s^-})-\sigma^2_{s^-}/2)ds+\int_0^t \sigma_s dB_s $$
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
slide_title: A continuous time GARCH model designed for option pricing\ (Kallsen and Taqqu, 1998)

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Continuous-time GARCH
SLIDE: A continuous time GARCH model designed for option pricing\ (Kallsen and Taqqu, 1998)
CONTENU:
- the drift function $\mu$ is assumed to have continuous derivatives
- the volatility process $(\sigma_t)_{t\geq0}$ is constant on intervals $[n, n+ 1)$ for $n\in \mathbb{N}_0$
- the process $(p_t -p_{t-1}, \sigma_{t-1})_{t\geq1}$, when sampled at integer times, gives rise to a discrete time GARCH(1,1)-M process

$$\begin{aligned}
p_n-p_{n-1} &=\mu(\sigma_{n-1}) -\sigma^2_{n-1}/2 +\sigma_{n-1}(B_n-B_{n-1}), \ n\in \mathbb{N},\\
\sigma^2_{n} &= \omega+\lambda\sigma^2_{n-1}(B_n-B_{n-1})^2+\delta\sigma^2_{n-1}, \ n\in\mathbb{N}
\end{aligned}$$
- This differs from a usual GARCH(1,1) process only by the term $\mu(\sigma_{n-1}) - \sigma^2_{n-1}/2$, which vanishes if the function $\mu$ is chosen as $\mu(x) = x^2/2$
- If we are not in the classical GARCH situation but rather have
$$ \lim \sup_{x\to\infty} \mu(x)/x < \infty, $$
then Kallsen and Taqqu (1998) show that the continuous time model is arbitrage free and complete. This is then used to derive pricing formulas for contingent claims such as European options.

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
All CT GARCH slides are based on Lindner paper and slides

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Realized volatility measures
SLIDE: GARCH is Slow: A Thought Experiment
CONTENU:
- Suppose a sudden change in the true latent volatility

$$ \sqrt{\mathrm{var}(r_{t}|\mathcal{F}_{t-1})}=\begin{cases}
0.2 & \qquad t\leq T\\
0.4 & \qquad t>T
\end{cases} $$
- With $\alpha+\beta=1$ (e.g. $\alpha=0.05$ and $\beta=0.95$), GARCH(1,1)
implies

$$ \mathbb{E}(\sigma^{2}_{T+k})=\alpha\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\beta^{j}\mathbb{E}(r_{T+k-j}^{2})=\alpha\sum_{j=0}^{\ntxt{k-1}}\beta^{j}(0.4)^{2}+\alpha\sum_{j=\ntxt{k}}^{\infty}\beta^{j}(0.2)^{2} $$

- How quickly does $\sigma^{2}_{t}$ converge to the new level of $\mathrm{var}(r_{t}|\mathcal{F}_{t-1})$?

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Realized volatility measures
SLIDE: Realized Variance
CONTENU:
- In practice IV is unobservable and one only observe asset prices

- Moreover, log price data are only available in discrete time at frequency

$$ \Delta\tau = t_{i} - t_{i-1} $$

where sampling rates $\Delta\tau$ can be seconds or minutes

- $\Rightarrow$ For a given sampling rate, $r_{t_{i}} = p_{t_{i}} - p_{t_{i-1}}$ are intradaily log-returns

- We assume $M$ intradaily observations $t-1 = t_{0} < t_{1} < \ldots < t_{M} = t$

- $\Rightarrow$ the daily Realized Variance (RV) is given by

$$ RV_{t} = \sum_{i = 1}^{M} r_{t_{i}}^{2} $$

and one can show that in absence of jumps

$$ \sqrt{n}\Bigg(\sum_{i = 1}^{M} r_{t_{i}}^{2} - \int_{t-1}^{t}\sigma_{s}^{2}ds\Bigg)\Bigg(2\underbrace{\int_{t-1}^{t}\sigma_{s}^{4}ds}_{\ntxt{IQ}}\Bigg)^{-1/2} \,{\buildrel d \over \longrightarrow}\, \mathcal{N}(0,1) $$

with $IQ$ the Integrated Quarticity (the limit behavior of the vol-of-vol)
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Realized volatility measures
SLIDE: Realized Semi-Variance
CONTENU:
- The behavior of $r_{t}$ in the lower tail of their distribution is of interest

- ... as it often differs from the behavior in the upper tail

- $\Rightarrow$ requires an asymmetric treatment of the downside and upside risks

- Barndorff-Nielsen et al. (2010) suggest the Realized Semi-variance

$$ RS_{t}^{+} = \sum_{i = 1}^{M} r_{t_{i}}^{2}\mathds{1}_{r_{t_{i}} \geq 0} \text{ and } RS_{t}^{-} = \sum_{i = 1}^{M} r_{t_{i}}^{2}\mathds{1}_{r_{t_{i}} \leq 0} $$
- As for $RV_{t}$ in presence of finite activity jumps, they no-longer converge to $IV_{t}$ as

$$ RS_{t}^{+} \,{\buildrel p \over \longrightarrow}\, \frac{1}{2}\int_{t-1}^{t}\sigma_{s}^{2}ds + \ntxt{\sum_{t-1<s\leq t} |\Delta p_{s}|^{2}\mathds{1}_{r_{t_{i}}} \geq 0} $$

and

$$ RS_{t}^{-} \,{\buildrel p \over \longrightarrow}\, \frac{1}{2}\int_{t-1}^{t}\sigma_{s}^{2}ds + \ntxt{\sum_{t-1<s\leq t} |\Delta p_{s}|^{2}\mathds{1}_{r_{t_{i}}} \leq 0} $$
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Realized volatility measures
SLIDE: Realized Multipower Variation
CONTENU:
- In presence of jumps, $RV_{t} \,{\buildrel p \over \longrightarrow}\, QV_{t}$ instead of the $IV_{t}$ as $M \to \infty$

- As jumps cannot be easily distinguished from the continuous part,

- ... if $IV_{t}$ is of interest, robust realized measures are needed

- $\Rightarrow$ Barndorff-Nielsen et al. (2006) introduce the Multipower Variation

$$ MV_{t}^{\{\gamma_{1},\ldots,\gamma_{m}\}} = \bigg(\frac{1}{M}\bigg)^{1-\sum \gamma_{k}/2} \sum_{j = m}^{M}\prod_{i=1}^{m} |r_{t_{j-i+1}}|^{\gamma_{i}} $$

- The simplest case is the Bipower Variation (BV) with $\gamma_{1} = \gamma_{2} = 1$

$$ BV_{t}^{\{1,1\}} = BV_{t} = \frac{\pi}{2}\sum_{j = 2}^{M} |r_{t_{j}}||r_{t_{j-1}}| $$
- Conversely to $RV_{t}$, this measure is jump robust as $M \to \infty$ :

$$ BV_{t} \,{\buildrel p \over \longrightarrow}\, \int_{t-1}^{t}\sigma_{s}^{2}ds $$
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Realized volatility measures
SLIDE: Microstructure noise
CONTENU:
- The most striking feature of the empirical prices is their discreteness

- $\Rightarrow$ price movement cannot be smaller than one tick

- At the opposite, theoretical $\mathcal{M}$-based models are continuous in time

- $\Rightarrow$ efficient log-price are unobservable due to microstructure noise, i.e.

- frictions in the trading process : tick limit, rounding error

- informational effects : gradual response of prices to a block trade

- recording errors : prices entered as zero or misplaced decimal points
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Realized volatility measures
SLIDE: Realized Kernel
CONTENU:
- Let $p_{t}^{*} = p_{t} + \varepsilon_{t}$ be the observed price

- $\Rightarrow$ $\varepsilon_{t}\perp p_{t}$ acts as microstructure noise and is defined as a white noise

- Barndorff-Nielsen et al. (2008) suggest the Realized Kernel (RK)

$$ RK_{t} = \underbrace{\gamma_{0}(p_{t}^{*})}_{RV} + \underbrace{\sum_{h = 1}^{\mtxt{H}}\btxt{\mathcal{K}\Big(\frac{h}{H}\Big)}(\gamma_{h}(p_{t}^{*}) +\gamma_{-h}(p_{t}^{*}))}_{\text{noise correction}} \,{\buildrel p \over \longrightarrow}\, \int_{t-1}^{t}\sigma_{s}^{2}ds +\ntxt{\sum_{t-1<s\leq t} |\Delta p_{s}|^{2}} $$

with $\gamma_{h}(p_{t}^{*}) = \sum_{j = 1}^{M} (p_{t_{j}}^{*} - p_{t_{j-1}}^{*})(p_{t_{j-h}}^{*} - p_{t_{j-1-h}}^{*})$ and $\mathcal{K}(.)$ a kernel

- The recommended kernel $\btxt{\mathcal{K}(.)}$ is Parzen’s kernel

$$ \btxt{\mathcal{K}(x)} = \begin{cases} 1-6x^2+6x^3, \ \ 0>x\geq \frac{1}{2}\\
2(1-x)^3, \ \ \frac{1}{2}>x\geq 1 \\
0, \ \ x>1
\end{cases} $$
- The preferred choice for the bandwidth is $\mtxt{H} = 3.5134\times \hat{\xi}^{4/5} M^{3/5}$ with

$$ \hat{\xi} = q^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{q}\hat{\omega}^{2}_{(i)}/RV_{\text{sparse}} \text{ and } \hat{\omega}^{2}_{(i)} = RV_{\text{dense}}^{(i)}/(2M_{(i)}) $$

where $RV_{\text{sparse}}$ ($RV_{\text{dense}}^{(i)}$) are based on 20 min (2 min independent) $r_{t_{i}}$
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Realized volatility measures
SLIDE: Jumps identification and Realized Jumps ($RJ$)
CONTENU:
- It is hard to disentangle the continuous and jump parts of the $QV$

- Consider for instance $RK_{t} \,{\buildrel p \over \longrightarrow}\, IV_{t}$ and $BV_{t} \,{\buildrel p \over \longrightarrow}\, QV_{t}$ as $M \to \infty$

- $\Rightarrow$ Hence, we have $RJ_{t} = RK_{t} - BV_{t} \,{\buildrel p \over \longrightarrow}\, - J_{t} = - \ntxt{\sum_{t-1<s\leq t} |\Delta p_{s}|^{2}}$

- Based on that result, several test statistics can be defined ...

- ... e.g. the one of Barndorff-Nielsen and Shephard (2006) :

$$ T_{M} = \Bigg(1-\frac{BV_{t,M}}{RV_{t,M}}\Bigg) \Bigg(\frac{1}{M}\frac{\vartheta_{BV} MV_{t,M}^{\{1,1,1,1\}}}{BV_{t,M}^{2}}\Bigg)^{-1/2} \,{\buildrel d \over \longrightarrow}\, \mathcal{N}(0,1) $$

under the null $H_{0} :$ no jump, with $\vartheta_{BV} \approx 2.609$ and as $M \to \infty$

- $\Rightarrow$ The rejection of the null at 5% is thus given by $T_{M} > 1.64$

- ... and allows to identify insignificant Realized Jumps
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Realized volatility measures
SLIDE: Nonparametric realized measure
CONTENU:
- $RV_{t}$, $RS_{t}$, $BV_{t}$ and $RK_{t}$ are ex-post realized measures ($\mathcal{RM}$) of volatility

- ... at the opposite GARCH-type models estimate ex-ante volatility

- Realized measures are nonparametric estimators of $IV_{t}$ or $QV_{t}$

- $\Rightarrow$ without conditional models, parametric forecasts are infeasible

- $\mathcal{RM}$ are highly persistent with hyperbolic decay of autocorrelations

- $\Rightarrow$ one could use this stylized fact to forecast volatility
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Realized volatility measures
SLIDE: Modelling realized measures with ARFIMA
CONTENU:
- Autocorrelations of ARMA models decay at exponential rate

- $\Rightarrow$ only ARMA$(\infty)$ can mimic an hyperbolic decay

- Such a slow decay reflects the presence of Long Memory ($\mathcal{LM}$)

- $\Rightarrow$ the simplest parametric model of $\mathcal{LM}$ is the ARFIMA$(p,\delta,q)$

$$ (1 - L)^{\delta} \underbrace{\Phi(L) (x_{t} - \mu) = \Theta(L)}_{\text{ARMA}(p,q)} \varepsilon_{t} \Rightarrow \varepsilon_{t} = \sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\Xi_{i} x_{t-i} $$

with $\delta \in (-1/2,1)$ and $x_{t} \in \btxt{\log(\mathcal{RM})}$ or $x_{t} \in \btxt{(\mathcal{RM})^{1/2}}$
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Realized volatility measures
SLIDE: Estimating and forecasting with ARFIMA models
CONTENU:
- Under Gaussian assumption (reasonable if $x_{t} \in \btxt{\log(\mathcal{RM})}$), the exact log-likelihood is

$$\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{L}_{E}(\vartheta;\bm{x}) & = -\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi) -\frac{1}{2} \log |\Sigma(\vartheta)| -\frac{1}{2}\bm{x}'\Sigma(\vartheta)^{-1}\bm{x}
\end{aligned}$$

with $\bm{x} = (x_{1},\cdots,x_{n})'$, $\vartheta = (\delta,\phi_{1},\cdots,\phi_{p},\theta_{1},\cdots,\theta_{p})$ and

$$ \Sigma(\vartheta) = \gamma_{x}(r - s;\vartheta), \text{ for } r,s = 1,\cdots,n $$
- As the fractional polynomial $(1 - L)^{\delta}$ implies an infinite dependence

$$ (1 - L)^{\delta} = \sum_{j=0}^{\ntxt{\infty}}\frac{\Gamma(j+\delta)}{\Gamma(j+1)\Gamma(\delta)}L^{j} $$
- ... the MLE $\widehat{\vartheta} = \arg\min\limits_{\vartheta \in \Theta} \mathcal{L}_{E}(\vartheta;\bm{x})$ is time consuming

- The log-variance forecasts are then obtained by

$$ \hat{x}_{t+h} \equiv \mathbb{E}_{t}(x_{t+h}) = \sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\Xi_{i} x_{t+h-i} \approx \sum_{i=0}^{\btxt{r}}\Xi_{h+i} x_{t-i} $$

where in practice the infinite sum is truncated at lag $\btxt{r}$
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
slide_title: Estimating and forecasting with ARFIMA models

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Realized volatility measures
SLIDE: Modelling realized measures with HAR
CONTENU:
- Corsi (2008) suggests an Heterogeneous AR model that mimics $\mathcal{LM}$

$$ x_{t+1}= c+\underbrace{\beta_d x_{t}}_{\text{day}}+\underbrace{\beta_w x^{w}_{t}}_{\text{week}}+\underbrace{\beta_m x^{m}_{t}}_{\text{month}} + \varepsilon_{t+1}, \ \varepsilon_t \sim \operatorname{~i.i.d.~}, $$

where $x^{w}_{t}=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{j=1}^{4}x_{t-j}$ and $x^{m}_{t}=\frac{1}{22}\sum_{j=1}^{21}x_{t-j}$ and $x_{t} \in \btxt{(\mathcal{RM})^{1/2}}$

- A log-HAR version is possible if $x_{t} \in \btxt{\log(\mathcal{RM})}$

- The HAR is simple and flexible $\Rightarrow$ can model additional stylized facts
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Realized volatility measures
SLIDE: Extensions of the HAR model : LHAR
CONTENU:
- Define aggregated negative and positive returns at given frequency $s$

$$ (r_{t}^{s})^{-} =\frac{1}{s}\sum_{j=1}^{s}r_{t-j}\mathds{1}_{\sum_{j=1}^{s}r_{t-j}<0} \text{ and } (r_{t}^{s})^{+} =\frac{1}{s}\sum_{j=1}^{s}r_{t-j}\mathds{1}_{\sum_{j=1}^{s}r_{t-j}\geq 0} $$
- We allow for the leverage effect to impact each market component

$$\begin{aligned}
x_{t+1} & = c + \beta_{d} x_{t}+ \beta_w x^{w}_{t} + \beta_m x^{m}_{t} \\
& + \gamma_{d}^{-}(r_{t})^{-} + \gamma_{w}^{-}(r_{t}^{w})^{-} + \gamma_{m}^{-}(r_{t}^{m})^{-} \\
& + \gamma_{d}^{+}(r_{t})^{+} + \gamma_{w}^{+}(r_{t}^{w})^{+} + \gamma_{m}^{+}(r_{t}^{m})^{+} + \varepsilon_{t+1}
\end{aligned}$$

- $\Rightarrow$ The Leverage HAR (LHAR) fits particularly well the asymmetric relationship between $r_{t}$ and $x_{t+1}$ with $x_{t} \in \btxt{(\mathcal{RM})^{1/2}}$
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
slide_title: Extensions of the HAR model : LHAR

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Realized volatility measures
SLIDE: Extensions of the HAR model : LHAR-CJ
CONTENU:
- Assume now that $J_{t,T_{M}}$ is the sequence of significant realized jumps

- In the spirit of the HAR let's define at given frequency $s$

$$ J_{t,T_{M}}^{s} =\frac{1}{s}\sum_{j=1}^{s}J_{t-j,T_{M}} $$
- The Leverage HAR with Continuous volatility and Jumps (LHAR-CJ) is given by

$$\begin{aligned}
x_{t+1} & = c + \beta_{d} x_{t}+ \beta_w x^{w}_{t} + \beta_m x^{m}_{t} \\
& + \alpha^{d} J_{t,T_{M}} + \alpha^{w}J_{t,T_{M}}^{w} + \alpha^{m}J_{t,T_{M}}^{m} \\
& + \gamma_{d}^{-}(r_{t})^{-} + \gamma_{w}^{-}(r_{t}^{w})^{-} + \gamma_{m}^{-}(r_{t}^{m})^{-} \\
& + \gamma_{d}^{+}(r_{t})^{+} + \gamma_{w}^{+}(r_{t}^{w})^{+} + \gamma_{m}^{+}(r_{t}^{m})^{+} + \varepsilon_{t+1}
\end{aligned}$$
- As the model is linear, one can use OLS to estimate all parameters

- This general model offers good in-sample and out-of-sample performances
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
slide_title: Extensions of the HAR model : LHAR-CJ

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Realized volatility measures
SLIDE: GARCH-X with realized measures
CONTENU:
- Engle (2002) (and many others)

$$ \sigma^{2}_{t}=\omega+\alpha r_{t-1}^{2}+\beta \sigma^{2}_{t-1}{\color{blue}+\gamma x_{t-1}} $$

$x_{t} \in \btxt{\mathcal{RM}}$ is a realized measure of the $QV$ (not $IV$)

- Leads to substantial empirical gains

- $\Rightarrow$ Typically

- $\hat{\gamma}\simeq0.5$

- $\hat{\alpha}\simeq0$ (ARCH parameter becomes insignificant)

- However, GARCH-X models are partial (incomplete) models that have nothing to say about returns and volatility beyond a single
period into the future.
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Realized volatility measures
SLIDE: Realized GARCH (Hansen, Huang, Shek, 2012)
CONTENU:
- The Realized GARCH is a complete model, contrary to GARCH-X

- $\Rightarrow$ It fully specifies the dynamic properties of both $r_{t}$ and $x_{t}$ :

$$\begin{aligned}
r_{t} & = & \overbrace{\mu+\sqrt{\sigma^{2}_{t}}z_{t}}^{\text{Return Equation}}\\
\log \sigma^{2}_{t} & = & \left. \alpha+\beta\log \sigma^{2}_{t-1}+\gamma\log x_{t-1} \right\} \text{ GARCH Equation }\\
\log x_{t} & = & \underbrace{\xi+\psi\log \sigma^{2}_{t}+\tau(z_{t})+u_{t}}_{\text{Measurement Equation}}
\end{aligned}$$
- $x_{t} \in \btxt{\mathcal{RM}}$ is a realized measure of the $QV$ (not $IV$)

- $\tau(z) = \tau_{1}z +\tau_{2}(z^2-1)$ models an asymmetric response in volatility to return shocks (leverage effect)

- $z_{t}\sim \operatorname{~i.i.d.~}(0,1)$, $u_{t}\sim \operatorname{~i.i.d.~}(0,\sigma_{u}^{2})$

- $\tau(z_t)+u_t$ are the volatility shocks
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Realized volatility measures
SLIDE: Realized GARCH estimation
CONTENU:
- Assume $z_t \sim \operatorname{~i.i.d.~} \mathcal{N}(0,1)$ and $u_t \sim \operatorname{~i.i.d.~} \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2_{u})$

- The quasi-log likelihood function is constructed based on

$$\begin{aligned}
\overbrace{f(r_{t},x_{t}|\mathcal{F}_{t-1})}^{\text{Joint density}} & =f(r_{t}|\mathcal{F}_{t-1})f(x_{t}|r_{t},\mathcal{F}_{t-1}),\\
l(r,x;\theta) & =-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{t=1}^{n} \Big(\log(\sigma^{2}_t) +r_{t}^2/\sigma^{2}_{t}\Big) -\frac{1}{2}\sum_{t=1}^{n}\Big( \log(\sigma^2_u) + u_{t}^2 / \sigma_{u}^2 \Big)
\end{aligned}$$
- Based on Straumann and Mikosch (2006) the authors conjecture that

$$ \sqrt{n}(\hat\theta_n-\theta) \,{\buildrel d \over \longrightarrow}\, \mathcal{N}(0,\Omega), $$

with $\Omega$ the usual QMLE covariance matrix
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling
SECTION: Realized volatility measures
SLIDE: Realized GARCH multi-period forecast
CONTENU:
- Predicts both the conditional return variance and the realized measure

- e.g. RGARCH(1,1) forecasts through the VARMA(1,1) structure

$$ \begin{pmatrix} \log \sigma^2_t \\ \log x_t\end{pmatrix}=
\begin{pmatrix} \beta &\gamma \\ \psi\beta & \psi\gamma \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} \log \sigma^2_{t-1} \\ \log x_{t-1} \end{pmatrix}+
\begin{pmatrix} \alpha \\ \psi\alpha+\xi \end{pmatrix}+
\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ \tau(z_t)+u_t \end{pmatrix} $$
- $h$-step ahead forecasts are obtained from

$$\begin{aligned}
\begin{pmatrix} \widehat{\log \sigma^2_{t+h}} \\ \widehat{\log x_{t+h}}\end{pmatrix}= &
\begin{pmatrix} \beta &\gamma \\ \psi\beta & \psi\gamma \end{pmatrix}^{h}
\begin{pmatrix} \log \sigma^2_{t-1} \\ \log x_{t-1} \end{pmatrix}+ \\ &
\sum_{j=0}^{h-1}
\begin{pmatrix} \beta &\gamma \\ \psi\beta & \psi\gamma \end{pmatrix}^{j}\Bigg(
\begin{pmatrix} \alpha \\ \psi\alpha+\xi \end{pmatrix}+
\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ \tau(z_{t+h-j})+u_{t+h-j} \end{pmatrix}\Bigg)
\end{aligned}$$
- One would have to account for distributional aspects of $\log \sigma^2_{t+h}$ in order to produce an unbiased forecast of it since $\mathbb{E}(\log x) \neq \log(\mathbb{E}(x))$
chapter: Chapter 2 — Finance Theory and High Frequency Modelling

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 3 — Multivariate Realized Mesures
SECTION: Multivariate realized models
CONTENU:
- There is growing theoretical and empirical interest in extending the results of the univariate processes discussed previously to a multivariate framework

- Multivariate volatility modelling is of particular importance in the areas of risk management, portfolio management and asset pricing

- We will discuss:

- Multivariate realized measures

- Modelling and forecasting multivariate realized measures

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Chapter 3 — Multivariate Realized Mesures
SECTION: Multivariate realized models
SLIDE: Multivariate realized measures
CONTENU:
1. Realized Covariance (Barndorff-Nielsen and Shephard, 2004)

- Suppose that along day $t$ the log-prices of financial assets follow a $k$-variate continuous time diffusion process

$$ d\boldsymbol{p}_{t+\tau} = \boldsymbol{\mu}_{t+\tau}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma^{1/2}}_{t+\tau} d\boldsymbol{W}_{t+\tau}, \ \ 0\leq\tau\leq 1, \ t=1,2, \ldots, $$

where

- $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t+\tau}$ is the multivariate drift component
- $\boldsymbol{\Sigma^{1/2}}_{t+\tau}$ is the instantaneous $k\times k$ co-volatility matrix
- $\boldsymbol{W}_{t+\tau}$ is the standard multivariate Brownian
motion
- $\bm{\Sigma^{1/2}}_{t+\tau}$ is orthogonal to $\bm{W}_{t+\tau}$

- A generic element of $\bm{\Sigma}_{t+\tau}$ is given by ${\Sigma}_{t+\tau}^{(u)(s)}$

1. Realized Covariance (Barndorff-Nielsen and Shephard, 2004)

**Définition** : The realized covariance over the arbitrary interval between 0 and 1 (representing day $t$) is computed using the outer-product of high-frequency returns

$$ \bm{\mathrm{RCov}}_t^{(ALL)}=\sum\limits_{j=1}^{M} \bm{r}_{t_j}\bm{r}'_{t_j}, $$

where $\bm{r}_{t_j}$ is the j-th return on day $t$ and it is a consistent estimator for the sum of the integrated covariance matrix and the realized jump variability
$\int_0^1 \bm{\Sigma}_{t+\tau}d\tau + \int_{0}^{1} \xi_{\tau} \xi'_{\tau}dN(\tau)$

- Barndorff-Nielsen and Shephard (2004) showed that when the price process is Brownian motion with drift, as $M \rightarrow \infty$

$$ M^{1/2}\Big[vech(\bm{\mathrm{RCov}}_t^{(ALL)})- vech(\int_0^1 \bm{\Sigma}_{t+\tau}d\tau) \Big] \,{\buildrel d \over \longrightarrow}\, \mathcal{N}_{k}(0,\bm\Pi_t) $$
- In principle prices should be sampled as frequently as possible to maximize the precision of the realized covariance estimator

second term in the definition=> QV, i.e. with the jumps

JUMP VARIATION : $N_t$ counting process, $\xi_{\tau}$ jump size which gives the contribution of the $\tau$ th jump in [t,t+1] to the price diffusion

QV -$\Sigma$ can be nonstationary, have long-memory, jumps, no moments, and include intra-day effects

Gaussian limit theory : square-root convergence to Gaussian distribution with random covariance matrix

Vech form allows one to avoid that the random cov matrix is singular, due to the symmetric nature of realized cov and QV

The matrix $\Pi_i$ is a function of the path of $\Sigma$ and so, as we argue conditionally on $\Sigma$ ,$\Pi_i$ is deterministic

1. Realized Covariance (Barndorff-Nielsen and Shephard, 2004)

In practice:

- Prices, especially transaction prices (trades), are contaminated by noise (e.g. bid-ask spread, non-trading, price discreteness, trades occurring on different markets or
networks, rounding errors)
- Bandi and Russell (2005) showed that in the presence of microstructure noise
the realized covariation estimator is not consistent

Solutions:

- The standard method to address these concerns is to sample relatively infrequently, for example every 5 minutes
- An improved method is to use modified realized covariance estimators (e.g. using subsampling)

- Difficult to avoid singular covariance matrices issue when $k$ is large

2. Realized Semi-Covariance (Bollerslev, Patton, Quaedvlieg, 2020)

- Let $r_{t,j,i}$ denote the return over the $j$-th intra-daily time on day $t$ for asset $i$ and $\bm{r}_{t,j}$ the vector returns
- With $\mathbb{I}\{.\}$ is the indicator function and $\odot$ the Hadamard product, the vectors of $k$ signed returns are

$$ \bm{r}_{t,j}^{+} = \bm{r}_{t,j}\odot \mathbb{I}\{\bm{r}_{t,j}>0 \}, \ \ \ \bm{r}_{t,j}^{-} = \bm{r}_{t,j}\odot \mathbb{I}\{\bm{r}_{t,j}\leq 0 \}, $$

**Définition** : Therefore, the standard realized covariance matrix can be decomposed in four realized semi-covariance matrices:

$$\begin{aligned}
\bm{P}_t^{(M)}& \equiv \sum_{j=1}^{M}\bm{r}_{t,j}^{+}\bm{r}_{t,j}^{+'},\ \
\bm{Q}_t^{(M)+} \equiv \sum_{j=1}^{M}\bm{r}_{t,j}^{+}\bm{r}_{t,j}^{-'},\\
\bm{Q}_t^{(M)-}& \equiv \sum_{j=1}^{M}\bm{r}_{t,j}^{-}\bm{r}_{t,j}^{+'},\ \
\bm{N}_t^{(M)} \equiv \sum_{j=1}^{M}\bm{r}_{t,j}^{-}\bm{r}_{t,j}^{-'},
\end{aligned}$$

where $\bm{P}$, $\bm{N}$ and $\bm{Q}$ correspond to « positive », « negative » and « mixed » vector signs, such that the realized covariance matrix is given by

$$ RCov_t^{M}=\bm{P}_t^{(M)}+\bm{N}_t^{(M)} + \bm{Q}_t^{(M+)}+ \bm{Q}_t^{(M-)} $$

2. Realized Semi-Covariance (Bollerslev, Patton, Quaedvlieg, 2020)

- Since $RCov_t^{M}$, $\bm{P}_t^{(M)}$ and $\bm{N}_t^{(M)}$ are all defined as sums of vector outerproducts, these matrices are all positive semidefinite
- Since the diagonal elements of $\bm{Q}_t^{(M)+}$ and $\bm{Q}_t^{(M)-}$ are identically zero by construction, these matrices are necessarily indefinite
- If the assets have a clear ordering, the two realized semicovariances may have different economic interpretations
- If the ordering is arbitrary, they may convey the same information, combined in a single semi-covariance matrix $\bm{Q}_t^{(M)}=\bm{Q}_t^{(M)+} +\bm{Q}_t^{(M)-}$

- E.g. In a bivariate case

$\bm{P}_t^{(M)}=\begin{pmatrix} \mathcal{P}_{1,t}^{(M)+} & \mathcal{P}_{12,t}^{(M)}\\
\bullet & \mathcal{P}_{2,t}^{(M)+} \end{pmatrix}, \ \
\bm{N}_t^{(M)}=\begin{pmatrix} \mathcal{N}_{1,t}^{(M)-} & \mathcal{N}_{12,t}^{(M)}\\
\bullet & \mathcal{N}_{2,t}^{(M)-} \end{pmatrix}$

$\bm{Q}_t^{(M)}=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & \mathcal{Q}_{12,t}^{(M)}\\
\bullet & 0 \end{pmatrix}$

2. Realized Semi-Covariance (Bollerslev, Patton, Quaedvlieg, 2020)

- Daily realized semicovariances averaged across 500 randomly-selected pairs of S&P 500 stocks over the 1993-2014 period (smoothed by a moving average of 50 obs)

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
To illustrate, Figure 1 plots the off-diagonal elements of the daily realized
semicovariance matrices averaged across 500 randomly-selected pairs of S&P 500
stocks over the 1993-2014 period.

The mixed Qt component is, of course, always negative, while Pt + Nt is always positive.

The “concordant” (Pt + Nt) and « discordant » (Qt) terms are typically fairly similar in magnitude.

In periods of high volatility, however, Pt + Nt increases substantially more than Qt declines,
in line with the widely held belief that during periods of financial market stress
correlations and tail dependencies among most financial assets tend to increase.

Correspondingly, the off-diagonal element of RCOVt (denoted RCOVt) is almost
exclusively determined by the two concordant realized semicovariance components
in high volatility periods.

Further corroborating the idea that the concordant semicovariances are related to notions of market stress, we find that the average correlation of Pt and Nt with the VIX volatility index, popularly interpreted as a market « fear gauge », equal 0.484 and 0.477, respectively, compared to 0.285 for RCOVt.

2. Realized Semi-Covariance (Bollerslev, Patton, Quaedvlieg, 2020) asymptotic theory ($k=2$)

**Définition** : Assume that the bivariate log-price process evolves continuously through time according to the semimartingale
$\bm{p}_t=\bm{p}_0+\int_0^t \bm{m}_s ds + \int_0^t \bm{\sigma}_s d\bm{W}_s, \ \ 0\leq t \leq 1,$
where $\bm{W}_s$ denotes a 2-dimensional Brownian motion, $\bm{m}_s$
is a 2-dimensional locally bounded predictable drift process, and $\bm{\sigma}$ is a $\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2}$-valued càdlàg volatility process.
Then for $\bm r_{j,i} \equiv \bm{p}_{j/M,i} - \bm{p}_{(j-1)/M,i}$, $M\rightarrow \infty$, with
$\sigma^2_{s,i}$ and $\rho_s$ the spot variance and correlation respectively,

$$ \bm{V}^{(M)}= \begin{bmatrix}
\mathcal{P}_{1}^{(M)+} \\
\mathcal{P}_{2}^{(M)+} \\
\mathcal{N}_{1}^{(M)-} \\
\mathcal{N}_{2}^{(M)-} \\
\mathcal{P}_{12}^{(M)} \\
\mathcal{N}_{12}^{(M)} \\
\mathcal{Q}_{12}^{(M)+} \\
\mathcal{Q}_{12}^{(M)-} \\
\end{bmatrix}\,{\buildrel p \over \longrightarrow}\, \int_{0}^{1}
\begin{bmatrix}
\sigma^2_{s,1} /2 \\
\sigma^2_{s,1} /2 \\
\sigma^2_{s,2} /2 \\
\sigma^2_{s,2} /2 \\
\sigma^2_{s,1}\sigma^2_{s,2}\Big(\rho_s \arccos(-\rho_s) +\sqrt{1-\rho_s^2}\Big) /(2\pi) \\
\sigma^2_{s,1}\sigma^2_{s,2}\Big(\rho_s \arccos(-\rho_s) +\sqrt{1-\rho_s^2}\Big) /(2\pi) \\
\sigma^2_{s,1}\sigma^2_{s,2}\Big(\rho_s \arccos\rho_s -\sqrt{1-\rho_s^2}\Big) /(2\pi) \\
\sigma^2_{s,1}\sigma^2_{s,2}\Big(\rho_s \arccos\rho_s -\sqrt{1-\rho_s^2}\Big) /(2\pi) \\
\end{bmatrix}ds \equiv \bm{V} $$

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
in the absence of jumps the positive and negative realized semivariance measures each converge in probability to onehalf times the integrated variance

so large dfferences between the two realized semivariance measures, + and - , are naturally interpreted as evidence for discontinuities, or jumps

Differences in the values of P(M) and N(M) may similarly be attributed to the presence of discontinuities occurring at the same time in the two assets, or so-called cojumps, which could affect the measures differently or arise from asymmetries in correlations between positive and negative returns.

As is standard in the in-fill asymptotic high-frequency data setting, the
limiting distribution is random, so that its variance depends on the realization of
the underlying process (see, e.g., Mykland and Zhang, 2009).

2. Realized Semi-Covariance (Bollerslev, Patton, Quaedvlieg, 2020)

Asymptotic theory ($k=2$ and a unit time interval)

**Définition (CLT and feasible CLT)** : Assume that the bivariate log-price process evolves continuously through time according to slide (), with the $\bm{\sigma}_{t}$ volatility process determined by $\bm{\sigma}_{t}=\bm{\sigma}_{0}+\int_{0}^{t} \nu'_sd\bm{W}^{*}_{s}$, with $\nu'_s$ an adapted càdlàg process, and $\bm{W}^{*}_{s}$ a $2\times2$-dimensional Brownian motion independent of $\bm{W}_{s}$. Then for $M\rightarrow \infty$,

$$ \sqrt{M} (\bm{V}^{(M)}-\bm{V})\overset{d_{st}}{\longrightarrow} \int_{0}^{1} \bm{\alpha}_s d\bm{W}_s + \int_{0}^{1} \bm{\beta}_s d \bm{\tilde W}_{s} \equiv \bm{U}, $$

where $d_{st}$ denotes stable convergence in distribution, $\bm{\alpha}_s$ and $\bm{\beta}_s$ are $8\times2$-dimensional processes.
With
$$ \bm{\Pi} \equiv Var(\bm{U}) =\int_{0}^{1}(\bm{\alpha}_s \bm{\alpha}'_s + \bm{\beta}_s \bm{\beta}'_s) ds, $$

$$ \bm{\Pi}^{(M)} \,{\buildrel p \over \longrightarrow}\, \bm{\Pi}, $$

$$ \{\bm{\Pi}^{(M)} \}^{-1/2}\sqrt{M}(\bm{V}^{(M)}-\bm{V}) \,{\buildrel d \over \longrightarrow}\, \mathcal{N}_{2}(0,\bm{I}) $$

3. Realized Bipower Covariation (Barndorff-Nielsen and Shephard, 2004b)

**Définition** : The realized bipower covariation over the arbitrary interval between 0 and 1 (representing day $t$) computed as

$$\begin{aligned}
RBPCov_t =& \frac{1}{4}\Big (\sum_{j=2} ^{M} |r_{(v),t_j}+ r_{(l),t_j}||r_{(v),t_{j-1}}+ r_{(l),t_{j-1}}| \\ & - |r_{(v),t_j}- r_{(l),t_j}||r_{(v),t_{j-1}}- r_{(l),t_{j-1}}| \Big )
\end{aligned}$$

where $r_{(v),t_j}$ is the $v$-th component of the return vector $\bm{r}_{t_j}$,
is an estimator of the integrated covariance matrix (robust to jumps)

$$ RBPCov_t \underset{\Delta \rightarrow 0}{\,{\buildrel p \over \longrightarrow}\,} \int_{0}^{1} \bm{\Sigma}_{t+\tau} d\tau $$

- Compared to the univariate case, the additional issue of synchronicity arises for multivariate measures

- The asynchronous nature of intraday prices biases realized covariances toward 0, unless an appropriate adjustment is made

- The downward bias occurs because when trading is infrequent, news that affect a pair of assets will be incorporated at different times simply as a result of asynchronous trading

**Définition (Epps effect, Epps, 1979)** : Information arrives at different frequencies for different assets, therefore introducing additional microstructure effects that are related to the nonsynchronicity in the process of price formation.

Even when there is no microstructure friction as previously discussed, nonsynchronous trading introduces a downward bias in the realized covariance estimates when sampling returns in calendar time at high frequencies.

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
Prices are typically not recorded at equispaced time points, while e.g. many realized volatility measures rely on equispaced returns

An approach to tackle the problem of asynchronous trading :

- previous tick aggregation : forces prices to an equispaced grid by taking the last price realized before each grid point or, alternatively, the interpolation of the 1st and last price in the interval
- But, at least one quote should be available for both assets in the chosen time interval for this algorithm to be applicable

- Empirical work use heuristically chosen 5 or 30 minutes return interval to try to avoid the bias and market microstructure effects

- But this type of correction will increase the variance of the realized covariance estimator and no rule to choose an optimal frequency exists

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
the optimal choice of the frequency of the returns and the number of leads and lags covariances would substantially lower the RMSE compared to the heuristic choices, these optimal values are unknown in empirical application (Martens 2004).

A better approach: Refresh-time sampling (Harris and Wood, 1995)

- Each $\{\tau_j\}$ with $j = 1, \ldots, M$ is the time it has taken for all the assets to (re)-trade.

- This procedure forces the time series to synchronize but not necessarily on equispaced time grid

- Some realized measures are based on this time clock $\{\tau_j\}$ while showing that stale pricing errors have no impact on the asymptotic distribution of the measures

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
Denoting by $\tau(1)$ the first point in time when both assets have changed their price at least one time since market opening; as soon as we have identified $\tau(1)$ we repeat the exercise and denote by $\tau(2)$ the first point in time when both assets have changed their prices again

We iterate this time labeling algorithm until the end of the day, obtaining $\tau(j)$ data points with $j = 1, \ldots, M$

4. Realized Kernel (Barndorff-Nielsen, Hansen, Lunde, and Shephard, 2011)

**Définition** : The multivariate realized kernel over the arbitrary interval between 0 and 1 (representing day $t$) defined as

$$\begin{aligned}
RK_t =& \Gamma_0 + \sum_{h=1}^{H} \mathcal{K}\Big(\frac{h}{H} \Big)(\Gamma_{h} + \Gamma_{h}'),\\
\Gamma_{h} =& \sum_{j=h+1}^{\tilde M} \tilde{\bm{r}}_{t_{j}} \tilde{\bm{r}}_{t_{j-h}},
\end{aligned}$$

with $\tilde{\bm{r}}_{t_j}$ refresh-time returns, $\mathcal{K}$ a kernel weighting function (e.g. Parzen), $\tilde M$ is the refresh-time sample size after jittering (averaging observations on the boundaries of the sample) and $H$ is a parameter which controls the bandwidth.

- Simultaneously guarantees consistency, positive semi-definiteness and robustness to microstructure noise
- Accounts for nonsynchroneity of observations by using refresh-time returns

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
similar to realized covariance
except that realized kernels use a weighting function similar to that in a Newey and West (1987) covariance estimator $\Gamma_h$ is the h-th realised autocovariance, symmetric function (has the same form as a standard HAC covariance matrix estimator), but Unlike the situation in the standard HAC literature, an estimator based on the Bartlett
kernel will not be consistent for the QV.

H choice $H$ controls the number of leads and lags used for all the series

JITTERING: asymptotic theory dictates that we need to average $m$ prices at the very beginning and end of the day to obtain a consistent estimator. So $\tilde M -1 + 2m = M$, with $M$ refresh-time sample and $m$ genrally =2 for financial data (jittered observations record the efficient price without much error, as the error is averaged away).

$\Gamma_{h} = \Gamma_{-h}'$

\Gamma_{h} =& \sum_{j=h+1}^{\tilde M} \tilde{\bm{r}}_{t_{j}} \tilde{\bm{r}}_{t_{j-h}},
\end{aligned}$$

with $\tilde{\bm{r}}_{t_j}$ refresh-time returns, $\mathcal{K}$ a kernel weighting function (e.g. Parzen), $\tilde M$ is the refresh-time sample size after jittering (averaging observations on the boundaries of the sample) and $H$ is a parameter which controls the bandwidth.

**Théorème (Asymptotic theory)** : $$\begin{aligned}
& \frac{H^{2}}{\tilde M} RK_{t} \,{\buildrel p \over \longrightarrow}\, |\mathcal{K}^{\prime \prime}(0)|\Omega,\ \text{if}\ \eta<1/2,\\
&RK_{t} = \int_{0}^{1}\bm{\Sigma}(s)ds + c_0^{-2} |\mathcal{K}^{\prime \prime}(0)|\Omega + O_p(1),\ \text{if} \ \eta=1/2,\\
&RK_{t} \,{\buildrel p \over \longrightarrow}\, \int_{0}^{1}\bm{\Sigma}(s)ds\ if\ \eta>1/2,
\end{aligned}$$

where $H=c_0 \tilde M^{\eta}$, $c_0 >0$, $\eta \in (0,1)$, and $\Omega$: average long run variance of the noise

$$ \tilde M^{1/5} \Big(RK_{t} - \int_{0}^{1}\bm{\Sigma}(s)ds \Big) \overset{d_{st}}{\longrightarrow} \mathcal{MN}(c_0^{-2}|\mathcal{K}^{\prime \prime}(0)|\Omega, 4c_0\mathcal{K}_{\bullet}^{0,0})IQ), $$

with $\mathcal{K}_{\bullet}^{0,0}=\int_{0}^{\infty} \mathcal{K}(s)^2 ds$
and $IQ$s the multivariate integrated quarticity

- The bandwidth $H$ plays a crucial role, as it has to increase with $\tilde M$
quite quickly to remove the influence on the estimator of the noise

$|k^{\prime \prime}(0)|$ is absolute value of. second derivative of kernel function

This is the multivariate CLT, yielding a limit theorem for the consistent multivariate estimator in the presence of noise.

The bias is determined by the long-run variance $\Omega$ whereas the variance depends solely on the integrated quarticity.

In this paper we have assumed that Y is a pure BSM. The analysis could be extended to the situation where Y is a pure BSMplus a finite activity jump process. The analysis in Barndorff- Nielsen et al. Bandwidth choice

- It must grow with $\tilde M$ at rate $\tilde M^{3/5}$

- Solutions for estimating a good constant of proportionality in this multivariate case:

- i) Apply the univariate optimal mean square error bandwidth selection to each asset price individually, i.e. $\hat H_{(i)}=c_0\hat \xi_{(i)}^{4/5}\tilde M^{3/5}$, for $i=1,2, \ldots, k$, with $c_0=3.5134$ for Parzen kernel

One then gets $k$ bandwidths and constructs some ad hoc rules for choosing the global $\hat H$, such as Min(.), Max(.) or Average(.)

- ii) Construct a sort of equally weighted « market portfolio’’

Once prices are converted into Refresh Time, one computes the market return and then carries out a univariate analysis on it, choosing an optimal $\hat H$ for the market

This single $\hat H$ is then applied to the multivariate problem

2. Realized correlation and realized beta

- Realized Correlation is the realized analogue of the usual correlation estimator, but defined in terms of realized covariance (RC)

$$ RCorr = \frac{RC_{vl}}{\sqrt{RC_{vv}RC_{ll}}} $$
- Suppose
$$ RC= \begin{pmatrix}RV_v & RC'_{fv}\\ RC_{fv} & RC_{ff} \end{pmatrix} $$
is the realized covariance matrix of an asset with a set of observable factors. The realized beta is defined as
$$ R\beta= RC_{ff}^{-1}RC_{fv} $$
- Realized betas are similar to other realized measures in that they are model free and, as long as prices can be sampled frequently and have little market microstructure noise, is an accurate measure of the current exposure to changes in the market

1. VARFIMA approach (Chiriac and Voev, 2010)

- $X_t$ is modeled as a vector autoregressive fractionally integrated
moving average (VARFIMA($p,\delta,q$)) process

$$ \Phi(L)D(L)[X_t-BZ_t] =\Theta(L)\varepsilon_t, \ \varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\Omega) $$
- where $Z_t$ is a $n\times 1$ vector of exogenous variables

- $B$ is a $g\times n$ matrix of coefficients

- $\Phi(L)=I_g-\Phi_1 L-\Phi_2 L^2-\ldots -\Phi_p L^p$
and $\Theta(L)=I_g-\Theta_1 L-\Theta_2 L^2-\ldots -\Theta_q L^q$ are matrices of lag AR and MA polynomial, respectively

- $D(L)=diag\{(1-L)^{\delta_1}, \ldots, (1-L)^{\delta_g} \}$ with $d_1,\ldots, \delta_g$ the degrees of fractional integration of each of the $g$ elements of $X_t$

- We assume that the roots of $\Phi(L)$ and $\Theta(L)$ lie outside the unit circle

- $Z_t$ could include exogenous variables (trading volume, corporate bond returns, short-term interest rates, etc.)

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
Since a single exogenous regressor implies $g$ additional parameters
in the model, in order to keep the model tractable, restrictions might need to be imposed by structuring the matrix B appropriately. This is an empirical question

1. VARFIMA approach (Chiriac and Voev, 2010)

- Advantages of Choleski factors VARFIMA

- No need to impose parameter restrictions on the model

- The out-of-sample covariance matrice is always positive definite by the `reverse' Cholesky transformation

$$ Y_{ij,t}=\sum_{l=1+i(i-1)/2}^{i(i-1)/2} X_{l,t}X_{l+j(j-1)/2 - i(i-1)/2,t}, \ i,j=1,\ldots,k,\ j\geq i, $$

where $X_{l,t}$ is the $l$-th element of $X_t$
- Parsimonious VARFIMA (1,d,1) model for forecasting

$$ (1-\phi L)D(L)[X_t-c] =(1-\theta L)\varepsilon_t, \ \varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\Omega), $$

where $c$ is a $g\times 1$ vectors of constants
- Estimation under the assumption of normally distributed errors by the approximate ML approach in the spirit of Beran (1995), which is also applicable for non-stationary processes ($\delta > 0.5$)

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
The estimation effectively minimizes the sum of squared residuals, circumventing the estimation of $\Omega$, which is irrelevant for the purposes of constructing a point forecast

In order to assess whether the matrix decomposition method makes a difference empirically, we also apply the VARFIMA model to the log-volatility series $a_t=vech(A_t)$ with $A_t=B_t \log G_t B'_t$, where $B_t$ and $G_t$ result from the spectral decomposition of $Y_t=B_t G_t B'_t$. The empirical results are similar, but this makes more sense for the gaussian MLE hypothesis.

Approximate MLE:

set $d=m+\delta$, $\-1/2<\delta<1/2$,$m\geq 0$ is an integer (it is the number of times that $X_t$ must be differenced to achieve stationarity

The only restriction for aMLE is that we consider invertible processes, i.e. $d > -1/ 2$

$d$ can be estimated by an approximate maximum likelihood method based on the estimated residual process

The estimator is optimal for Gaussian fractional and non-fractional ARIMA processes

ARIMA (p,d,q) $\phi(L)(1-L)^{m}Y_t=\theta(L)\varepsilon_t$ with $Y_t=(1-L)^{\delta}X_t$
can be estimated by usual Box-Jenkins ARIMA(p,m,q) methods after passing $X_t$ through the linear filter $(1-L)^{\delta}$ to get $Y_t$

from ARIMA(p,m,q) coefficients estimated and the fractional filter one computes the coefficients of the infinite AR representation of the process ARIMA (p,d,q), and then obtains the residuals

They have to be corrected for unknown mean based on the fact that $m$-differenced $X_t$ is stationary (mean exists)

The aMLE estimates model parameters by minimizing ssq residuals

1. Forecasting with the VARFIMA model for the Cholesky factors

- From the VAR($\infty$) representation of the model

$$ \Phi(L)D(L)\Theta(L)^{-1}X_t = \sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\Xi_i X_{t-i}, $$

one obtains multi-step-ahead forecasts by truncation at $r$ lags

$$ \hat X_{t+s} = \mathbb{E}_t (X_{t+s}) = \sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\Xi_i X_{t+s-i} \approx \sum_{i=0}^{\btxt{r}} \Xi_{i+s} X_{t-i} $$
- The forecast is unbiased

- Having obtained $\hat X_{t+s}$, we construct the forecast $\hat Y_{t+s}$ by applying the `reverse' Cholesky transformation on the previous slide

- Since $\hat Y_{ij,t+s}$ is a quadratic transformation of $\hat X_{t+s}$, it is biased by $\sigma_{s,ij}^{\ast}=\sum_{l=1+i(i-1)/2}^{i(i+1)/2} \sigma_{s(l,l+ j(j-1)/2-i(i-1)/2)}$ where $j\geq i$, $i=1,\ldots,k$ and $\sigma _{s(u,v)}$ is the $(u,v)$-element of $\Omega_s=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty} \Psi_i \Omega \Psi'_i$ with $\Psi_i$ the coefficients of the VMA($\infty$) representation of the model

Recall: it means the forecast errors have zero mean

Economic value of volatility forecasts : portfolio optimization

- Suppose the return distribution is completely characterized by its first two moments

- $\Rightarrow$ Portfolio optimization reduces to finding asset weights which minimize the portfolio volatility for a given expected return (Markowitz, 1952)

- Denote by $\mu_p$ the annualized expected return

- The optimal portfolio is given by the solution to the following quadratic problem

$$ \min_{w_{t+s|t}} w'_{t+s|t}\hat H_{t:t+s}w'_{t+s|t}, \ \mathrm{s.t.}\ w'_{t+s|t}\mathbb{E}_t[r_{t:t+s}]=\frac{s\mu_p}{250}, \ w'_{t+s|t}\mathds{1}_{k}=1, $$

with

$\bullet$ $w_{t+s|t}$ the $k\times 1$ vector of portfolio weights chosen at $t$ and held until $t+s$,

$\bullet$ $\hat H_{t:t+s}$ a covariance matrix forecast

$\bullet$ $\frac{s\mu_p}{250}$ the target return scaled to the investment horizon $s$

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
oracle forecast: the cumulated RCov matrix computed over the actual period $t:t+s$

oracle forecast has a superior mean–variance trade-off

VARFIMA and HAR-based plots almost overlap (similar performance)

A natural point to be considered is the level of return corresponding to the global
minimum variance portfolio (GMVP), accentuated in Figure 1 by a particular symbol for each
model.

3. Multivariate Realized GARCH approach (Hansen et al. 2014)

Marginal model for the market return

$$\begin{aligned}
r_{0,t} & = & \mu_0+\sqrt{\sigma^{2}_{0,t}}z_{0,t}\\
\log \sigma^{2}_{0,t} & = & a_0+b_0\log \sigma^{2}_{0,t-1}+c_0\log x_{0,t-1} \\
\log x_{0,t} & = & \xi_0+ \psi_0\log \sigma^{2}_{0,t}+\tau_0(z_{0,t})+u_{0,t}
\end{aligned}$$

- $z_{0,t}\sim \operatorname{~i.i.d.~}(0,1)$, $u_{0,t}\sim \operatorname{~i.i.d.~}(0,\sigma_{u_0}^{2})$ for the estimation

- A simple second-order polynomial is used for the leverage effect function

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
Tying the realized measure, xt, to the conditional variance, ht, is motivated by the fact that conventional GARCH models imply $\log (rt_-\mu)^2 = \log h_t +\log z_t$ and $x_t$ is similar to $r_t^2$
