3. Multivariate Realized GARCH approach (Hansen et al. 2014)

Conditional model for an individual asset return and its realized measures ($i>0$)

$$ r_{i,t} = \mu_i+\sqrt{\sigma^{2}_{i,t}}z_{i,t}\ \ \text{Return Eq.} $$

- where the dependence on $(r_{0,t}, x_{0,t})$ operates through $\rho_{i,t}=\operatorname{cov}(z_{0,t},z_{i,t}|I_{t-1})$

- $\Rightarrow$ i.e. there is a “factor” structure
$z_{i,t}=\rho_{i,t}z_{0,t} + \sqrt{1- \rho_{i,t}^2w_{i,t}},$
where $w_{i,t}$ has mean zero, unit variance and is uncorrelated with $z_{0,t}$

$$ \Bigg. \begin{array}{c}
\log \sigma^{2}_{i,t} = a_i+b_i\log \sigma^{2}_{i,t-1}+c_i\log x_{i,t-1} +
d_i\log \sigma^{2}_{0,t-1}\\
\digamma(\rho_{i,t}) = a_{i,0}+ b_{i,0}\digamma(\rho_{i,t-1})+c_{i,0}\digamma(\varrho_{i,t-1})
\end{array} \Bigg\} \ \ \text{GARCH Eq.} $$

$$ \Bigg. \begin{array}{c} \log x_{i,t} = \xi_i+ \psi_i\log \sigma^{2}_{i,t}+\tau_i(z_{i,t})+u_{i,t}\\
\digamma(\varrho_{i,t}) = \xi_{i,0}+ \psi_{i,0}\digamma(\rho_{i,t})+v_{i,t}
\end{array} \Bigg\}\ \ \text{Measurement Eq.} $$

Fisher transform, $\digamma$, is a 1 to 1 mapping from (-1,1) to $\mathbb{R}$

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
Hence, the studentized returns for the individual asset is not iid, it is a linear combination of the
studentized market return and the idiosyncratic component $w$, where the relative weighting (defined by $\rho$) is time varying.

The parameter $d_1$ can be interpreted as a spillover effect that measures the extend to
which the market’s volatility affects the volatility of the individual asset while accounting for the asset-specific volatility dynamics

Fisher transform is a 1 to 1 mapping from (-1,1) to $\mathbb{R}$ $\digamma(\rho)=\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{1+\rho}{1-\rho}$

3. Multivariate Realized GARCH approach (Hansen et al. 2014)

Estimation

- The joint density of the observables conditional on the information set can be decomposed

$$\begin{aligned}
f(r_{0,t},x_{0,t},r_{i,t},x_{i,t},y_{i,t}|\mathcal{F}_{t-1}) &=f(r_{0,t},x_{0,t}|\mathcal{F}_{t-1})
f(r_{i,t},x_{i,t},y_{i,t}|r_{0,t},x_{0,t},\mathcal{F}_{t-1})\\
&=f(r_{0,t}|\mathcal{F}_{t-1})f(x_{0,t}|r_{0,t},\mathcal{F}_{t-1})\times\\
& f(r_{i,t}|r_{0,t},x_{0,t},\mathcal{F}_{t-1})f(x_{i,t},y_{i,t}|r_{i,t},r_{0,t},x_{0,t},\mathcal{F}_{t-1})
\end{aligned}$$

- As $z_{0,t}\sim \operatorname{~i.i.d.~}(0,1)$, $u_{0,t}\sim \operatorname{~i.i.d.~}(0,\sigma_{u_0}^{2})$, the four components of the likelihood function corresponding to the four conditional densities above are easy to explicitate

- The parameters of the model, generally denoted by $\theta$ are hence estimated by

$$ \hat\theta=\underset{\theta \in \Theta}{\arg \max}\log L(r_{0,t},x_{0,t},r_{i,t},x_{i,t},y_{i,t}|\theta) $$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: RM
SLIDE: Risk Management
CONTENU:
- **Définition** : Risk is defined as « hazard, a chance of bad consequences, loss or exposure to mischance » (the Concise Oxford English Dictionary)

- A bank’s attitude to risk is not passive and defensive; a bank actively and willingly
takes on risk, because it seeks a return and this does not come without risk

- Risk management can be seen as the core competence of an insurance company
or a bank

- Financial risk management is mainly concerned with downside risk : « the quantifiable likelihood of loss or less-than-expected results »

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: RM
SLIDE: Risk Management
CONTENU:
**Définition** : Risk is defined as « hazard, a chance of bad consequences, loss or exposure to mischance » (the Concise Oxford English Dictionary)

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: RM
SLIDE: Risk Management
CONTENU:
Distinguish

- Market risk
- Credit risk
- Operational risk
- and
- Liquidity risk
- Model risk

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
market risk, the risk of a change
in the value of a financial position due to changes in the value of the underlying
components on which that position depends, such as stock and bond prices, exchange rates, commodity prices,

credit risk, the risk of
not receiving promised repayments on outstanding investments such as loans and
bonds, because of the “default” of the borrower.

operational risk, the risk of losses resulting from inadequate or failed internal processes, people and systems, or from external events.

Liquidity risk could be roughly defined as the risk
stemming from the lack of marketability of an investment that cannot be bought or
sold quickly enough to prevent or minimize a loss. Liquidity can be thought of as
“oxygen for a healthy market”

The latter is the risk associated with using a misspecified
(inappropriate) model for measuring risk.

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: RM
SLIDE: Risk Management
CONTENU:
- Although risk management has been described as « one of the most important innovations of the 20th century » by Steinherr (1998), some concepts that are used in modern risk management, in particular derivatives, have been around for longer

- e.g. Dunbar (2000) interprets a passage in the Code of Hammurabi from Babylon of 1800 BC as being early evidence of the use of the option concept to provide financial cover in the event of crop failure

- Before the 1950s the desirability of an investment was mainly equated to its return

- Black–Scholes–Merton formula appeared in 1973; the methodology developed for the rational pricing and hedging of financial derivatives changed finance

- General public mistrust these modern tools of finance because of their perceived triggering effect for crashes and bubbles

- The present regulatory risk-management framework originates from the
Basel Committee of Banking Supervision - established by the Central-Bank Governors of the Group of Ten (G-10) at the end of 1974

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
A very explicit mention of options
appears in Amsterdam towards the end of the seventeenth century and is beautifully
narrated by Joseph de la Vega in his 1688 Confusion de Confusiones, a discussion
between a lawyer, a trader and a philosopher observing the activity on the Beurs
of Amsterdam.

in 1952 Harry Markowitz laid the foundation of the theory of portfolio selection by mapping the desirability of an investment onto a risk–return diagram,

The famous Black–Scholes–Merton formula for the price of (to value) a European call option appeared in 1973 ==== 1997 Nobel Price

The methodology developed for the rational pricing and hedging of financial derivatives changed finance

technological developments (mainly on the IT side) also laid the foundations for an explosive growth in the volume of new risk-management and investment products.

This development was further aided by worldwide deregulation in the 1980s.

Thus it is imperative that mathematicians take a serious interest in derivatives
and the risks they generate.

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: RM
SLIDE: Risk Management tools timeline
CONTENU:
- The first Basel Accord of 1988 on Banking Supervision
(Basel I) took an important step towards an international minimum capital standard.

- 1993 seminal report addressing off-balance-sheet products and the industry identifies the need for a proper risk management of these new products

- At JPMorgan the Value-at-Risk (VaR) is born as a market risk measure and RiskMetrics set an industry-wide standard (1994 RiskMetrics Technical Document)

- 1996 Amendment to Basel I prescribed a so-called standardized
model for market risk based on internal models

- 1997: Artzner et al. « Coherent Measures of Risk »

- 2001: Rockafellar, Uryasev, Acerbi and Tasche, define the Expected Shortfall (ES, or CVaR) - coherent risk measure

- Since the 2000's VaR and ES are used as complementary tools

- 2013: Basel Committee replaces $VaR_{1\%}$ with $ES_{2.5\%}$

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
Basel I main emphasis was on credit risk, by then clearly the most important source of risk in the banking industry; measured risk in an insufficiently differentiated
way. Also the treatment of derivatives was considered unsatisfactory.

Legal implementation of the amendment was to be achieved by the year 2000

In practice risk measures are used for a variety of purposes. Among the most
important are the following.
1 Regulatory purposes: Determination of risk capital and capital adequacy.
One of the main functions of risk management in the financial sector is to
determine the amount of capital a financial institution needs to hold as a buffer
against unexpected future losses on its portfolio in order to satisfy a regulator, who
is concerned with the solvency of the institution.

A related problem is the determination of appropriate margin requirements for investors trading at an organized exchange, which is typically done by the clearing house of the exchange.

2. Management tool. Risk measures are often used by management as a tool for limiting the amount of risk a unit within a firm may take. For instance, traders in
a bank are often constrained by the rule that the daily 95% Value-at-Risk of their
position should not exceed a given bound.

3. fInsurance premiums. Insurance premiums compensate an insurance company for bearing the risk of the insured claims. The size of this compensation can be viewed as a measure of the risk of these claims.

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: RM
SLIDE: Risk Management tools
CONTENU:
- Notional-amount approach

- Scenario analysis

- Risk measures based on loss distribution

Most modern measures of the risk in a portfolio are statistical quantities describing the conditional or unconditional loss distribution of the portfolio over some predetermined horizon

Examples include:

- the variance (previous chapters)

- the Value-at-Risk

- the Expected Shortfall

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
notional-amount approach: weighted nominal value nominal value as substitute for outstanding amount at risk

-weighting factor representing riskiness of associated asset class as substitute for riskiness of individual asset
- component of standardized approach of Basel capital adequacy framework

- advantage: no individual risk assessment necessary - applicable even without empirical data

-weakness: diversification benefits and netting unconsidered, strong
simplification

Scenarios: define possible future economic scenarios (stock market crash of -20
percent in major economies, default of Greece government securities,...) derive associated losses

- determine risk as specified quantile of scenario losses (5th largest loss, worst loss, protection against at least 90 percent of scenarios,...)

- since scenarios are not accompanied by statements about likelihood of occurrence, probability dimension is completely left unconsidered

-scenario analysis can be conducted without any empirical data on the sole grounds of expert knowledge

loss distribution
- incorporates all information about both probability and magnitude of losses

- includes diversification and netting effects

- usually relies on empirical data

-full information of distribution function reduced to charateristics of distribution for better comprehensibility

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk
CONTENU:
**Définition** : VaR summarizes the worst loss over a target horizon that will not be exceeded with a given level of confidence(Jorion, 2007)

- VaR is the worse potential loss over a given time horizon such that there is a low, pre-specified probability that the actual loss will be larger

- e.g. A bank might announce that the daily VaR on its trading portfolio is $50 million at the 99% CI.
$\Rightarrow$ There is only one chance in 100, under normal market conditions, for a loss greater than $50 million to occur.

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk
CONTENU:
**Définition** : VaR summarizes the worst loss over a target horizon that will not be exceeded with a given level of confidence(Jorion, 2007)

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk
CONTENU:
Statistical Definition

- A VaR defined for a coverage rate $\alpha\%$ corresponds to the $\alpha$ quantile of the P&L distribution associated with holding an asset or a portfolio over a fixed period

- typical values for $\alpha$ : $\alpha=0.95$, $\alpha=0.99$ or $\alpha=0.999$

- e.g. VaR p.d.f. under the Normal distribution

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk computation
CONTENU:
Elements required to compute the VaR

- the P&L distribution for the asset or the portfolio

- the coverage rate (1- the confidence level) e.g. 5%

- the holding period (time-horizon)

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk computation
CONTENU:
The P&L distribution

- is associated with the log-return series
$$ R_t = ln\big(\frac{P_t +D_t}{P_{t-1}}\big) $$

- Hence, if the return distribution is known, the VaR can be immediately derived as the $\alpha$ quantile of the P&L distribution
$VaR_t (\alpha) = F^{-1}_{R_t}(\alpha)$

- Otherwise, estimate the parameters of the underlying loss distribution, and evaluate the inverse cdf at required quantile

- Remark Modelling the loss distribution inevitably entails model risk

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk computation
CONTENU:
The coverage rate and holding period

- The probability to observe a loss greater than the VaR over a fixed horizon is equal by definition to the coverage rate:

$$ \mathrm{Pr}[R_t<VaR_t(\alpha)] = \alpha, \ \mathrm{where} \ VaR_t (\alpha)= F^{-1}_{R_t}(\alpha) $$

- There is no rule so as to the choice of the holding period for computing the $VaR$

- Remark: Temporal aggregation issue

– the frequency of P&L (intra-day, daily, weekly, monthly,…) doesn’t correspond to the risk horizon

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk computation
CONTENU:
Single asset or portfolio ?

In the second case there are 2 ways:

- Consider the return of the portfolio as that of an asset and compute the VaR on this aggregated return

- Simple to implement, but neglecting the covariances between asset returns means not accounting for any possible risk diversification

- Account for the correlations between assets when computing the VaR (multivariate approach)

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk computation
CONTENU:
Estimation methods

- Non-parametric methods (Historical Simulation, Weighted Historical Simulation, Filtered historical Simulation)

- Semi-parametric methods: CAViaR [EM2004], extreme value theory [MF2000]

- Parametric methods (ARCH, univariate GARCH, multivariate GARCH, RiskMetrics)

- Remark: In the rest of the slides, the VaR will be expressed as a positive number, like it is done in the literature

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk estimation
CONTENU:
Nonparametric methods: Historical Simulation

- Very simple, the VaR is the empirical quantile of the past returns

- Example: If we have a sample of 1000 observations of past returns, the VaR for a 95% confidence interval is the return value corresponding to the 50st largest loss

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
no parametric distribution is imposed a priori

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk estimation
CONTENU:
Nonparametric methods: Historical Simulation

- Let $R_1, R_2,\ldots, R_T$ be a sequence of returns observed at time $t=1\ldots T$

- At each date, the return $R_t$ is a random variable drawn from a certain distribution for which the associated $VaR_t (\alpha)$ can be deduced

- However, we only observe one realization of this distribution, $R_t$.
Without any further assumptions, it is hence impossible to estimate the quantile of the P&L at date $t$, i.e., the VaR.

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk estimation
CONTENU:
Nonparametric methods: Historical Simulation

- Hypotheses

- Suppose that the unconditional distribution of the returns is the same for all $t=1,\ldots,T$
$$ f_{R_t}(w) = f_{R}(w) $$

- It follows that the quantile of the unconditional distribution (the VaR) is also identical
$$ VaR_t(\alpha) = VaR(\alpha) \forall t $$

- Suppose that the returns $R_1, R_2,, \ldots, R_T$ are independently distributed

- Under this hypothesis of i.i.d.-ness of the returns, we obtain a sample of $T$ realizations of the random variable that follow the same distribution and hence admit the same VaR.

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk estimation
CONTENU:
Nonparametric methods: Historical Simulation

**Définition** : Under the previous hypotheses, a convergent estimator of the VaR for a coverage rate $\alpha\%$ is defined by the $\alpha$ empirical quantile of the historical realizations of the returns, denoted by ${r_1,r_2,\ldots, r_T}$

$$ \widehat{VaR}(\alpha) = percentile\big( \{r_j\}_{j=1}^{T}, 100\alpha\big) $$

$$ \widehat{VaR}(\alpha) \pto VaR(\alpha) $$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk estimation
CONTENU:
**Définition** : Under the previous hypotheses, a convergent estimator of the VaR for a coverage rate $\alpha\%$ is defined by the $\alpha$ empirical quantile of the historical realizations of the returns, denoted by ${r_1,r_2,\ldots, r_T}$

$$ \widehat{VaR}(\alpha) = percentile\big( \{r_j\}_{j=1}^{T}, 100\alpha\big) $$

$$ \widehat{VaR}(\alpha) \pto VaR(\alpha) $$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk estimation
CONTENU:
HS numerical example :

- Let us consider the daily returns of the Nikkei index from 05.01.2020 to 02.05.2022 (a total of 5550 observations)

- We sort the observations in ascending order $\{r_1,\ldots, r_{5550}\}$

- Compute the 1% VaR-HS as the 56th observation

$$ \widehat{VaR}_t(1\%) = -0.01507\% $$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk estimation
CONTENU:
HS simulation study: examine the properties of estimated sample quantiles

- assume t-distributed losses with degrees-of-freedom parameter $\nu=3$ and mean shifted by -0.004 :

- $VaR_{0.99}$= 4.54
- $VaR_{0.995}$= 5.84
- $VaR_{0.999}$ = 10.22
- Estimate the VaR for 100000 simulated samples of size 2500
(approximately 10 years in trading days)

- Compare the distribution of estimated VaR values with the real value of
applied underlying loss distribution in each case

- Even with sample size 2500, only 2.5 values occur above the 0.999 quantile on average $\Rightarrow$ high MSE

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk estimation
CONTENU:
HS simulation study: examine properties of estimated sample quantiles

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk estimation
CONTENU:
HS simulation study: examine properties of estimated sample quantiles

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk estimation
CONTENU:
Nonparametric methods: Historical Simulation

How to obtain a sequence of VaR-HS forecasts ?

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
Pros. Easy to implement. No statistical estimation of the
distribution of X necessary.

Cons. It may be difficult to collect sufficient quantities of relevant,
synchronized data for all risk factors. Historical data may not
contain examples of extreme scenarios.

Monte Carlo method: Instead we make inference about L using Monte Carlo methods,
which involves simulation of new risk factor data.

Pros. Very general. No restriction in our choice of distribution for Xt+1.

Cons. Can be very time consuming if loss operator is difficult to evaluate, which depends on size and complexity of portfolio.

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk estimation
CONTENU:
Nonparametric methods: Historical Simulation

- Rolling VaR-HS

$$ VaR_{t|t-1}=percentile\big( \{r_j\}_{j=t-T_e}^{t-1}, 100\alpha\big), $$

for a fixed window size $T_e$

- $\Rightarrow$ VaR-HS forecasts (for Nasdaq, June 2005-June 2006) are relatively invariant to changes in the economic environment, i.e. VaR-HS forecasts are `flat’ or `relatively flat' (in the case of rolling estimates).

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
Plus la taille de la fenêtre Te est petite, plus les prévisions de
VaR seront volatiles

Plus la taille de la fenêtre Te est grande, plus la VaR prévue
convergera vers la VaR non conditionnelle et sera par
conséquent quasi "constante" dans le temps.

boostrapped HS: take average of VaR on bootstrapped samples - from each window for rolling forecasts

wheighted HS: do not give same weight to the recent and old observations / or depending on volatility level, or correlation level

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk estimation
CONTENU:
Parametric methods: steps

1. Stipulate a parametric distribution for the P&L (normal, Student, GED,…)

2. Find the estimators of the parameters of that distribution (estimation)

3. Compute the appropriate quantile

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk estimation
CONTENU:
Parametric methods : hypothesis H1

- H1 Assume normally distributed losses with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$, $R_t \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$

**Définition** : VaR under the normality of the P&L hypothesis for a coverage rate of $\alpha\%$ is

$$ VaR_t (\alpha) = -\mu -\sigma \Phi^{-1}(\alpha), $$

with $\Phi$ the standard normal cumulative distribution function (Recall VaR is taken as a positive number here)

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk estimation
CONTENU:
**Définition** : VaR under the normality of the P&L hypothesis for a coverage rate of $\alpha\%$ is

$$ VaR_t (\alpha) = -\mu -\sigma \Phi^{-1}(\alpha), $$

with $\Phi$ the standard normal cumulative distribution function (Recall VaR is taken as a positive number here)

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk estimation
CONTENU:
Proof

$$\begin{aligned}
&\Pr[R_t<-VaR_t(\alpha)] =\alpha\\
\Leftrightarrow &\Pr[\frac{R_t-\mu}{\sigma}<\frac{-VaR_t(\alpha)-\mu}{\sigma}] = \alpha
\end{aligned}$$

where the standardized variable follows a standard normal distribution by H1

Therefore,

$$\begin{aligned}
&\Phi\Big(\frac{-VaR_t(\alpha)-\mu}{\sigma}\Big) =\alpha\\
\Rightarrow &\frac{-VaR_t(\alpha)-\mu}{\sigma}] = \Phi^{-1}(\alpha)
\end{aligned}$$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk estimation
CONTENU:
Parametric methods: numerical example 1

- $R_t \sim N(0.01, 1.5^2)$

- $\Rightarrow$ the 1% and 5% VaR are

- $VaR_t (0.01) = -0.01 -1.5 \Phi^{-1}(0.01) =3.479$

- $VaR_t (0.05) = -0.01 -1.5 \Phi^{-1}(0.05) = 2.457$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk estimation
CONTENU:
Parametric methods: numerical example 1

In practice, the assumption of normally distributed returns usually can be rejected both for loss distributions associated with credit and operational risk, as well as for loss distributions associated with market risk at high levels of confidence

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk estimation
CONTENU:
Parametric methods: hypothesis H2

- H2 We suppose that the P&L follows a Student distribution with $\nu$ degrees of freedom
$$ R_t \sim t(\nu) $$

**Définition** : VaR under the Student distribution for an $\alpha\%$ coverage rate is

$$ VaR_t(\alpha) = G(\alpha;\nu)^{-1} $$

Where $G(\alpha;\nu)^{-1}$ represents the cumulative distribution function for a Student distribution with $\nu$ degrees of freedom

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk estimation
CONTENU:
**Définition** : VaR under the Student distribution for an $\alpha\%$ coverage rate is

$$ VaR_t(\alpha) = G(\alpha;\nu)^{-1} $$

Where $G(\alpha;\nu)^{-1}$ represents the cumulative distribution function for a Student distribution with $\nu$ degrees of freedom

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk estimation
CONTENU:
Parametric methods: numerical example 2

- $R_t \sim t(5)$

- $\Rightarrow$ the 1% and 5% VaR are

- $VaR_t (0.01) = G^{-1}(0.01, 5) =4.032$

- $VaR_t (0.05) =G^{-1}(0.05, 5) = 2.570$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk estimation
CONTENU:
Parametric methods: conditional distribution

- We generally work with the conditional distribution of P&L instead of the marginal one

- $\Rightarrow$ P&L Density function conditional on the set of information available at time t, $\Omega_t$, with $r_t$ a realization (observation) from the sample of return process $R_t$

**Définition** : Conditional VaR for a coverage rate $\alpha\%$ conditional on $\Omega_t$ corresponds to the $\alpha$ quantile of the conditional distribution of the P&L

$$ VaR_t (\alpha | \Omega_t)=F^{-1} R_t (\alpha | \Omega_t) $$

where $F_{R_t}(\alpha |\Omega_t)$ is the conditional CDF of returns.

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk estimation
CONTENU:
**Définition** : Conditional VaR for a coverage rate $\alpha\%$ conditional on $\Omega_t$ corresponds to the $\alpha$ quantile of the conditional distribution of the P&L

$$ VaR_t (\alpha | \Omega_t)=F^{-1} R_t (\alpha | \Omega_t) $$

where $F_{R_t}(\alpha |\Omega_t)$ is the conditional CDF of returns.

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk estimation
CONTENU:
Parametric methods: conditional distribution example

- Suppose the P&L at time $t+1$ denoted by $R_{t+1}$ are normally distributed

- The conditional distribution of the P&L is

$$ R_{t+1| \Omega_t} \sim N(\hat\mu_{t+1|t}, \hat\sigma^2_{t+1|t} ), $$

with
$$ \hat\mu_{t+1|t} = \mathbb{E}(R_{t+1}| \Omega_t) $$

$$ \hat\sigma^2_{t+1|t} )= \mathbb{V}(R_{t+1}| \Omega_t) $$

- The VaR forecast at $t+1$ for a coverage rate $\alpha$ is

$$ VaR_{t+1|t} (\alpha) = -\hat\mu_{t+1|t} -\hat\sigma_{t+1|t} \Phi^{-1}(\alpha) $$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk advantages and inconvenients
CONTENU:
Advantages of the VaR as a risk measure

- Single number that indicates the extent of risk in a given portfolio and is measured in either price or as a percentage, making understanding VaR easy

- Simple to compute and interpret

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk advantages and inconvenients
CONTENU:
Inconvenients of the VaR as a risk measure

General ones

- Subjected to model risk (e.g. specification error in the P&L distribution)

- Subjected to implementation risk

Specific ones

- Does not provide any information about the losses beyond the VaR

- Misleading; different methods can lead to different results

- Can lead agents to take more risk

- Can be difficult to calculate the VaR for large portfolios

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
While VaR is useful for predicting the risks facing an investment, it can be misleading. One critique is that different methods give different results: you might get a gloomy forecast with the historical method while Monte Carlo Simulations are relatively optimistic. It can also be difficult to calculate the VaR for large portfolios: you can't simply calculate the VaR for each asset, since many of those assets will be correlated. Finally, any VaR calculation is only as good as the data and assumptions that go into it

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: Value-at-Risk advantages and inconvenients
CONTENU:
Two portfolios can have the same VaR but different extreme risk levels
(no information about the size of extreme loss is given by the VaR)

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
Note also that we focus on the univariate case here

Given only information about $VaR^A$ of random variable A and $VaR^B$ of random variable B, there is in general no sufficient information to calculate VaR for a function of both:
$VaR^{f(A;B)} \neq g(VaR^A; VaRB)$

- In such cases, in order to calculate $VaR^{f(A;B)}$, we have to derive the distribution of $f(A; B)$ first
despite the marginal distributions of the constituting parts, the transformed distribution under f is affected by the way that the margins are related with each other: the dependence structure between individual assets is crucial to the determination of $VaR^{f (A;B)}$

- As multi-period returns can be calculated as simple sum of sub-period returns in the logarithmic case, we aim to model $VaR^{f (A;B)} = VaR^{A+B}$

even though our object of interest relates to a simple sum of random variables, easy analytical solutions apply only in the very restricted cases where summation preserves the distribution: $A, B$ and $A + B$
have to be of the same distribution this property is fulfilled for the case of jointly normally distributed
random variables

- while portfolio returns can be calculated as weighted sum of individual assets for discrete returns, such an easy relation does not exist for the case of logarithmic returns

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR

The Coherent risk measure theory of Artzner et al. 1997, 1999

text:
COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: VaR
SLIDE: What is a good risk measure?
CONTENU:
The Coherent risk measure theory of Artzner et al. 1997, 1999

**Définition** : Let $X$ and $Y$ be two $P\&L$ distributions associated with two portfolios and $\rho(.)$ a risk measure over a given horizon

The risk measure $\rho(.)$ is said to be coherent if and only if it satisfies the following axioms:

1. Monotonicity $Y \succ X \Rightarrow \rho(Y) \leq \rho(X)$

2. Subadditivity $\rho(X+Y) \leq \rho(X) + \rho(Y)$

3. Homogeneity $\rho(hX) = h\rho(X)$ for $h>0$

4. Translation invariance $\rho(X+n) = \rho(X) + n, \ \forall n$

CONTENU:
**Définition** : Let $X$ and $Y$ be two $P\&L$ distributions associated with two portfolios and $\rho(.)$ a risk measure over a given horizon

The risk measure $\rho(.)$ is said to be coherent if and only if it satisfies the following axioms:

1. Monotonicity $Y \succ X \Rightarrow \rho(Y) \leq \rho(X)$

2. Subadditivity $\rho(X+Y) \leq \rho(X) + \rho(Y)$

3. Homogeneity $\rho(hX) = h\rho(X)$ for $h>0$

4. Translation invariance $\rho(X+n) = \rho(X) + n, \ \forall n$

Proof of coherency under Gaussian dist.

For any two random variables $X$ and $Y$,

$$\begin{aligned}
\sigma^2_{X+Y} &= Var[X+Y]=\mathbb{E}[(X+Y)^2]- (\mathbb{E}[(X+Y)])^2\\
&=\mathbb{E}[X^2]+\mathbb{E}[Y^2]+2\mathbb{E}[XY]-\mathbb{E}[X]^2-\mathbb{E}[Y]^2-2\mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y]\\
&=Var[X]+Var[Y]+2(\mathbb{E}[(X+Y)]- \mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y])\\
&=Var[X]+Var[Y]+2(\mathbb{E}[(X-\mathbb{E}[X])(Y-\mathbb{E}[Y])]\\
&\leq Var[X]+Var[Y]+2 \sqrt{\mathbb{E}[(X-\mathbb{E}[X])^2]}\sqrt
{\mathbb{E}[(Y-\mathbb{E}[Y])^2]}\\
&=(\sqrt{Var[X]} + \sqrt{Var[Y]} )^2
\end{aligned}$$

where we applied the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.

If $X$ and $Y$ are Gaussian,

$$\begin{aligned}
VaR_{X+Y}& =-\mu_{X+Y} - \sigma_{X+Y} \Phi^{-1}(\alpha)\\
&=-\mu_{X}-\mu_{Y} - \sigma_{X+Y} \Phi^{-1}(\alpha)\\
&\leq -\mu_{X}-\mu_{Y} - (\sigma_X+\sigma_Y) \Phi^{-1}(\alpha)\\
&=VaR_{X}+VaR_{Y}
\end{aligned}$$

SLIDE: Expected Shortfall
CONTENU:
**Définition** : The Expected Shortfall associated with an $\alpha\%$ coverage rate
denotes the conditional expected loss given that the realized loss is equal to or exceeds the corresponding value of the $VaR(\alpha)$

$$ ES(\alpha) = \mathbb{E}(L| L\geq VaR(\alpha)) $$

Otherwise said, it corresponds to the average of the $\alpha\%$ largest expected losses

$$ ES(\alpha) = -\frac{1}{\alpha}\int_{0}^{\alpha} F^{-1}_{R_t} (p)dp $$

where $F^{-1}_{R_t}$ stands for the cumulative distribution function of the returns series

It hence coincides with the Tail Value at Risk

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: ES
SLIDE: Expected Shortfall computation
CONTENU:
- Example In the case of a normal distribution, the ES associated with an $\alpha\%$ coverage rate is

$$ ES_t (\alpha) = -\mu -\sigma\frac{\phi(\Phi^{-1}(\alpha) )}{1-\alpha} $$

SECTION: ES
SLIDE: Expected Shortfall computation
CONTENU:
- In general the underlying distribution is not known

- Two estimation methods or ES

- Directly estimate the mean of all values greater than the associated
quantile of historical data

- Estimate a model for underlying loss distribution, and calculate
expectation of conditional loss distribution

If $R_t$ $i.i.d$ $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ then $R_{t,t+n-1}^{\log}$ $i.i.d$ $N(n\mu,n\sigma^2)$

- $\mathbb{E}[R^{\log} _{t,t+n-1}] = \mathbb{E}[\sum\limits_{i=0}^{n-1} R^{\log} _{t+i}] = \sum\limits_{i=0}^{n-1} \mu = n\mu$

- $\mathbb{V}[R^{\log} _{t,t+n-1}] =\mathbb{V}[\sum\limits_{i=0}^{n-1} R^{\log} _{t+i}] = \sum\limits_{i=0}^{n-1} \mathbb{V}(r_{t+i}^{\log}) + 0 = n\sigma^2$

- $\sigma_{t,t+n-1} = \sqrt{n}\sigma$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: ES
SLIDE: Multi-period risk measures computation
CONTENU:
Square-root-of-time scaling

Denote $\mu_n = n \mu$ and $\sigma_n = \sqrt{n} \sigma$

The multi-period $VaR^{(n)} (\alpha)$ can be expressed as a function of the one-period $VaR(\alpha)$:

$$\begin{aligned}
VaR^{(n) }(\alpha) &= -\mu_n - \sigma_n \Phi^{-1}(\alpha) \\
&=(\sqrt{n}-n)\mu + \sqrt{n} VaR(\alpha)
\end{aligned}$$

For $\mu=0$, $VaR^{(n) }(\alpha) = \sqrt{n} VaR(\alpha)$

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
requirements:

returns are independent through time: no autocorrelation

returns are normally distributed with zero mean

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)

SLIDE: Multi-period risk measures computation
CONTENU:
Square-root-of-time scaling

The multi-period $ES^{(n)} (\alpha)$ can be expressed as a function of the one-period $ES(\alpha)$:

$$\begin{aligned}
ES^{(n) }(\alpha) &= -\mu_n - \sigma_n \frac{\phi(\Phi^{-1}(\alpha))}{1-\alpha} \\
&=(\sqrt{n}-n)\mu + \sqrt{n} ES(\alpha)
\end{aligned}$$

For $\mu=0$, $ES^{(n) }(\alpha) = \sqrt{n}ES(\alpha)$

- Traditionally, we compare the forecast (ex-ante) with the ex-post realization

- The test hence relies on a criterion based on the distance between the true and forecasted values (loss function), e.g. Mean-Square Error, or information criteria (AIC, BIC).

Forecast evaluation test

**Définition** : A VaR violation (hit, exception) is a situation where the observed loss at time $t$ is larger than the forecasted VaR

The hit function (hit variable) is a dummy variable $I_t(\alpha)$ associated with the observation of an $\alpha\%$ VaR violation at time $t$

$$ I_t(\alpha) =\begin{cases} 1, \mathrm{if}\ R_t<VaR_{t|t-1}(\alpha)\\ 0\ \mathrm{otherwise} \end{cases} $$

Note that the VaR is the true, negative quantile here

Backtesting in practice

- The main tools used in backtesting are violation ratios

$$ VR = \frac{\mathrm{Observed\ Nº\ of \ violations}}{\mathrm{Expected\ Nº\ of\ violations}} $$

- The observed number of VaR violations are compared with the expected

- If the violation ratio is greater than one the VaR model underforecasts risk

- If smaller than one the model overforecasts risk

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
- 250*5 - 500 = 750 oos 1 period ahead VaR forecasts

- Expected Nº of violations = theoretical proba of occurrence $\alpha$ times the OOS sample size

- VaR violations are infrequent events: With a 1% VaR, a violation is expected once every 100 days, so that 2.5 violations are expected per year

- So the actual sample size of violations is quite small, Causing difficulties for statistical inference

- Need at least 10 violations for reliable statistical analysis, or 4 years of data, Preferably more

- VR=1 is expected, A useful rule of thumb is

If VR in [0.8, 1.2] the model is good

If VR in [0.5, 0.8] or VR in [1.2, 1.5] the model is acceptable

If VR in [0.3, 0.5] or VR in [1.5, 2] the model is bad

If VR < 0.3 or VR>2 the model is useless

Backtesting VaR-calculations based on the assumption of independent normally distributed losses generally may lead to two patterns

- percentage frequencies of VaR-exceedances are higher than the confidence levels specified: normal distribution assigns a too small probability to large losses

- VaR-exceedances occur in clusters: given an exceedance of VaR today, the likelihood of an additional exceedance in the following days is larger than average

- $\Rightarrow$ VaR evaluation is therefore based on statistical tests (not simple criteria) for the two main hypotheses that the VaR violation process must fulfill:

- Unconditional coverage hypothesis (test the Nº of violations)

- Independence hypothesis (test clustering)

Christoffersen (1998) strategy

**Définition (Unconditional coverage)** : The Unconditional coverage hypothesis is satisfied when the probability to observe an ex-post excess loss relative to the ex-ante VaR forecast is precisely equal to the coverage rate $\alpha$

$$ \Pr[I_t (\alpha)=1] = \mathbb{E}[I_t (\alpha)] = \alpha $$

- Example:

In the case of a 1%VaR used as a reference over a period of 500 observations, the expected value of the number of violations should equal 5.

Christoffersen (1998) strategy

**Définition (Independence)** : The Independence hypothesis is satisfied when VaR violations observed at two different dates, for the same coverage rate, are independently distributed.

Formally, $I_t (\alpha)$ associated with a VaR violation at time $t$ for a coverage rate $\alpha$ is independent of $I_{t\pm k} (\alpha), \forall k \neq0$

**Corollaire** : Under the independence hypothesis there are no clusters of violations

Kupiec (1995) UC test

- Denote

- $VaR_{t|t-1} (\alpha)$ the VaR forecast for an $\alpha\%$ coverage rate

- $I_t (\alpha)$ the associated VaR violation process

- $M$ the number of violations for a sample of $T$ consecutive VaR forecasts
$$ M= \sum\limits_{t=1}^{T} I_t (\alpha) $$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: Backtesting
SLIDE: Backtesting
CONTENU:
Kupiec (1995) UC test

- Denote

- $VaR_{t|t-1} (\alpha)$ the VaR forecast for an $\alpha\%$ coverage rate

- $I_t (\alpha)$ the associated VaR violation process

- $M$ the number of violations for a sample of $T$ consecutive VaR forecasts
$$ M= \sum\limits_{t=1}^{T} I_t (\alpha) $$
- The ratio $M/T$ is the empirical frequency of violations

- Under $H_0$ of UC, the failure rate is a consistent estimator of the coverage rate

$$ \frac{M}{T} \pto \alpha $$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: Backtesting
SLIDE: Backtesting
CONTENU:
Kupiec (1995) UC test

- Supposing that $I_t (\alpha)$ are i.i.d., under $H_0$ UC the total number of violations $M$ follows a Binomial distribution $M\sim B(T,\alpha)$ with
$\mathbb{E}(M)=\alpha T$ and $\mathbb{V}(M)=\alpha (1-\alpha)T$

- Therefore, the UC hypothesis:
$H_0$ $\mathbb{E}(I_t) = \alpha$ vs $H_1$ $\mathbb{E}(I_t)\neq \alpha$
can be tested through a likelihood-ratio statistic

$$ LR_{UC}= -2\ln [(1-\alpha)^{T-M}\alpha^M ] + 2 \ln\Big[\Big(1-\frac{M}{T} \Big)^{T-M} \Big(\frac{M}{T} \Big)^M \Big] \dto \chi^2 (1) $$

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
If, violations are observed more often the VaR model is underestimating risk

And similarly if we observe too few violations

As $I_t (\alpha) \sim Bernoulli(\alpha)$, $M\sim Binomial(T,\alpha)$, $T$ oos sample size here

$LRT= -2 (LR_{H0} - LR_{H1})$
with

$LR_{H1} = \prod\limits_{t=1}^{T}(1-\hat\alpha)^{1-I_t} (\hat\alpha)^{I_t}$ = unrestricted likelihood function based on Bernoulli iid variable

$LR_{H0}= \prod\limits_{t=1}^{T}(1-\alpha)^{1-I_t} (\alpha)^{I_t}$ use true $\alpha$

Kupiec calls the LR test the proportion of failures (PF) test.

Choosing a 5% significance level for the test, the null hypothesis is rejected if
LR > 3.84

As the author remarks, the test presents low power in small samples:
there is a significant probability of not rejecting the null hypothesis when it is false.
Like Basel criterion, this test is exclusively based on the frequency of tail losses
and it also neglects potentially important information as the size of tail losses and
the temporal dependence in exceptions behavior.

Christoffersen (1995) test

- Suppose the violations cluster

- The violation process can be represented as a Markov chain with two states and
transition probability matrix

$$ \Pi =\Big( \begin{array}{cc} p_{00} & p_{01}\\
p_{10} & p_{11}
\end{array} \Big), $$

$\mathrm{with}\ p_{ij}= \Pr(I_{t}(\alpha)=j| I_{t-1}(\alpha)=i),\ \mathrm{for}\ i,j\in\{0,1\}$

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
violates ind property

a good VaR model should increase the VaR forecast after a violation and do not lead to a second consecutive violation

$p_{01}$ = proba of a violation if there was no violation on the previous day

$p_{11}$ = proba of a violation if there was violation on the previous day

so $\hat\alpha = p = p_{01}=p_{11}$ under the CC hypothesis

under the null hypothesis of no clustering, the probability of a violation tomorrow
does not depend on today being a violation and besides overall we have $\alpha$ chances of a violation

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: Backtesting
SLIDE: Backtesting
CONTENU:
Christoffersen (1995) IND test

- The likelihood function under $H_1$ is

- $L(\Pi_{1})= (1-p_{01})^{v_{00}}p_{01}^{v_{01}}(1-p_{11})^{v_{10}} p_{11}^{v_{11}}$

- where $v_{ij}$ is the number of observations where $j$ follows $i$

- and the estimated transition probability matrix is

$$ \hat\Pi_{1} =\Big( \begin{array}{cc} \frac{v_{00}}{v_{00}+v_{01}} & \frac{v_{01}}{v_{00}+v_{01}}\\
\frac{v_{10}}{v_{10}+v_{11}} & \frac{v_{11}}{v_{10}+v_{11}}
\end{array} \Big) $$

- Under H0 of no clustering $p_{01}=p_{11}=p$, which is not necessarily equal to $\alpha$

- Therefore $\hat\Pi_{0}$ simplifies to
$$ \hat\Pi_{0} =\Big( \begin{array}{cc} 1-\hat p & \hat p\\
1-\hat p & \hat p
\end{array} \Big) $$

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
under the null hypothesis of no clustering, the probability of a violation tomorrow
does not depend on today being a violation

p not necessarily equal to the unconditional coverage rate $\alpha$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: Backtesting
SLIDE: Backtesting
CONTENU:
Christoffersen (1995) test

- The LR test for the independence hypothesis is

$$ LR_{IND} = -2\Big(\log L(\hat\Pi_{0}) -\log L(\hat\Pi_{1}) \Big) \dto \chi^2 (1) $$
- The main problem with tests of this sort is that they must specify the particular
way in which independence is breached

- And there are many possible ways in which the independence property is not fulfilled

- The LR test for the UC hypothesis, $I_t(\alpha) = p = \alpha$, is

$$ LR_{UC} = -2\Big(\log L(\Pi_{\alpha}) -\log L(\hat\Pi_{0}) \Big) \dto \chi^2 (1) $$

with
$$ \Pi_{\alpha} =\Big( \begin{array}{cc} 1-\alpha & \alpha\\
1-\alpha & \alpha
\end{array} \Big) $$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)
SECTION: Backtesting
SLIDE: Backtesting
CONTENU:
Christoffersen (1995) joint test (of CC)

- $H_0$ $\mathbb{E}(\hat I_t(\alpha)| \hat I_{t-1}(\alpha))=\alpha$, i.e.
$p_{01}=p_{11}=p=\alpha$,

- $LR_{joint} = LR_{UC} + LR_{IND} \dto \chi^2 (2)$

- The joint test has less power to reject a VaR model which only satisfies one of the
two properties

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
Note that the LRcc test only takes into account the first order autocorrelation of the hit sequence in a particular way - markov chain.

l'utilisation d'une chaine de Markov ne permet pas de mesurer le role d'autres variables que la seule sequence des violations passées dans une possible dependance des violations.

IND: the independence statistic based on testing whether $I_t (\alpha)$ are iid $Ber (\alpha)$ random variables against the alternative of first order Markov dependence.

Other issues:------

Escanciano and Olmo (2010) show that the use of standard unconditional and independence
backtesting procedures can be misleading, because they do not take into account the uncertainty associated with parameter estimation.

They show that one of the main determinants of the corrected asymptotic variance is the forecasting scheme used to generate the VaR forecasts, i.e., whether one uses recursive, rolling or fixed parameter estimates.

Escanciano and Olmo (2011) analyze the effects of model misspecification on the UC and LRcc tests, and propose using a block-bootstrap procedure to implement robust backtests.

Martingale difference hypothesis test

- Under $H_0$ of CC, $\mathbb{E}[I_t (\alpha)|\mathcal{I}_{t-1}] = \alpha$

- So if $I_{t-k}(\alpha)\in \mathcal{I}_{t-1},$

$$ \mathbb{E}[I_t (\alpha)-\alpha | {I}_{t-k}(\beta) - \beta] = 0, \ \forall (\alpha,\beta), \ \forall k\neq 0 $$

COURS: Financial_Econometrics (M2)

CONTENU:
Martingale difference hypothesis test

Berkowitz (2005)

- Define $\delta_{t}(\alpha )= I_t (\alpha)-\alpha$

- Ljung-Box test of null autocorrelation

$$ LB(K) = T(T+2)\sum\limits_{i=1}^{K} \frac{\hat \rho_i ^2}{T-i} \dto \chi^2 (K), $$

with $\hat \rho_i ^2$ the empirical autocorrelation of order $i$ of the $\delta (\alpha)$ process

- Based on the idea of Mincer Zarnowitz (1969) regression-based forecast evaluation

The predictive performance of point forecasts is commonly measured in terms of the average realized score $1/n\sum^n_{t=1} S(X_t,Y_t)$ for some loss or scoring function S, using the orientation the smaller the better.

If a functional admits a strictly consistent score, it is called elicitable; ES is not elicitable, but VaR and ES are jointly elicitable (Fissler Ziegel 2016) (VaR is elicitable, based on the check function, it is a quantile).

Variance and ES are not elicitable, but bijections of an elicitable/identifiable functional is elicitable/identifiable. So the pair mean-variance or VaR-ES are elicitable and identifiable.

results show that both, the GARCH-N and GJR-GARCH-N are rejected for almost
all the stocks (in more than 80% of the cases) uniformly over the different estimation

Independent of the sample length and
refitting frequency, this supports the well-known finding that Gaussian residuals generally
fail to capture the riskiness of financial assets, especially in the tails of the distribution.

In contrast, for the two GARCH specifications with Student-t distributed
innovations, the rejection frequencies are considerably lower and for almost all choices
of the refitting frequency and the estimation window length, they are below the nominal
significance level of 5%.

Furthermore, refitting the models more frequently tends to
slightly decrease the rejection frequency for the models with Student-t distributed innovations,
however, it tends to increase the rejection frequency for the Gaussian models.

Overall, this implies that the refitting frequency is not a key factor in the model performance.

Increasing the size of the estimation window tends to decrease the rejection
frequency, whereas the results stabilize for lengths above 1000 days.

Interestingly,
employing the GJR-GARCH model, which accounts for a potential leverage effect in the
volatility process, does not perform better than the standard GARCH model.

Overall, the results of this application which are diversified over 200 individual stocks,
imply that using a fat-tailed residual distribution and an estimation window above
1000 days (roughly four years) suffices to obtain rejection rates uniformly below 1%.

**Définition** : A linear time series $\{X_{t}\}_{t \in \mathbb{Z}}$ is an ARMA$(p,q)$ if

$$ X_{t} = \sum_{j = 1}^{p}\varphi_{j} X_{t-i} + \varepsilon_{t} + \sum_{j = 1}^{q} \theta_{j}\varepsilon_{t-j} \Longleftrightarrow \varphi(B) X_{t} = \theta(B)\varepsilon_{t} $$

where $\varepsilon_{t}$ is a SWN, $\varphi(B) = I - \sum_{j = 1}^{p}\varphi_{j}B^{j}$ and $\theta(B) = I - \sum_{j = 1}^{q}\theta_{j}B^{j}$

- $X_{t}$ is stationary if $\varphi(B)$ and $\theta(B)$ have no common roots and

$$ \varphi(z) = 0 \Rightarrow |z| \neq 1, \;\;\; \forall z \in \mathbb{C} $$
- $\Rightarrow$ no root on the unit circle or equivalently $\varphi(z) \neq 0$ for all $|z| = 1$

- Obviously, $X_{t}B^{j} = X_{t-j}$. Later we will also use $X_{t}F^{j} = X_{t + j}$, $F = B^{-1}$

- Consider $X_{t+1} = \check{\varphi}_{1} X_{t} + \check{\varepsilon}_{t+1}$

- It follows that $X_{t} = \check{\varphi}_{1}^{-1}\check{\varphi}_{1} X_{t} = \check{\varphi}_{1}^{-1}X_{t+1} - \check{\varphi}_{1}^{-1}\check{\varepsilon}_{t+1}$ and iterating

$$ X_{t} = - \sum_{j = 0}^{\infty} \check{\varphi}_{1}^{-j-1}\check{\varepsilon}_{t+j+1} = \btxt{\sum_{j = 0}^{\infty} \varphi_{1}^{j}\varepsilon_{t+j}}, \;\;\; \varphi_{1} = \check{\varphi}_{1}^{-1}, \;\;\; \varepsilon_{t} = - \varphi_{1} \check{\varepsilon}_{t+1} $$

where $\sum_{j = 0}^{\infty} \varphi_{1}^{j} F^{j}$ has absolutely summable coefficients

- $\Rightarrow$ Future shocks drive the dynamics : $X_{t} = \varphi_{1} X_{t+1} + \varepsilon_{t}$ is **non-causal**

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Outline
SLIDE: Non-Causal ARMA processes
CONTENU:
**Définition** : Let $X_{t}$ be a stationary ARMA$(p,q)$. Then, $X_{t}$ is non-causal if $\varphi(z) \neq 0$ for all $|z| \geq 1$ or equivalently $\varphi(z) = 0 \Rightarrow |z| < 1, \;\;\; \forall z \in \mathbb{C}$.

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Outline
SLIDE: Non-Causal AR and stationary solution
CONTENU:
Let $X_{t}$ be a non-causal AR$(1)$ defined by $X_{t} = \check{\varphi}_{1} X_{t - 1} + \check{\varepsilon}_{t}$

- Recall that $X_{t} = \check{\varphi}_{1}^{-1}X_{t+1} - \check{\varphi}_{1}^{-1}\check{\varepsilon}_{t+1}$ and that iterating we have

$$ X_{t} = - \check{\varphi}_{1}^{-1}\check{\varepsilon}_{t+1} - \cdots - \check{\varphi}_{1}^{-k-1}\check{\varepsilon}_{t+k+1} + \ntxt{\check{\varphi}_{1}^{-k-1}}X_{t+k+1} = \btxt{\sum_{j = 0}^{\infty} \varphi_{1}^{j}\varepsilon_{t+j}} $$
- If $X_{t}$ is stationary, $\mathbb{E}(X_{t}^{2})$ is finite and time independent so that

$$ \mathbb{E}\Big((X_{t} - \sum_{j = 0}^{k} \varphi_{1}^{j}\varepsilon_{t+j})^{2}\Big) = \ntxt{\varphi_{1}^{2k+2}}\mathbb{E}\Big((X_{t+k+1})^{2}\Big) \to 0 \text{ as } k \to \infty $$

which arises from the condition $|\varphi_{1}| = |\check{\varphi}_{1}^{-1}| < 1$

- $\Rightarrow$ $\sum_{j = 0}^{k} \varphi_{1}^{j}\varepsilon_{t+j}$ is the unique stationary solution of $X_{t}$

- However, $X_{t}$ depends on future shocks : not a Wold representation

- Remark In $X_{t} = \check{\varphi}_{1} X_{t-1} + \check{\varepsilon}_{t}$ the roots are **ill-located** whereas in $X_{t} = \varphi_{1}X_{t+1} + \varepsilon_{t}$ the roots are **well-located**

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Outline
SLIDE: Invertible ARMA
CONTENU:
**Définition** : Let $X_{t}$ be a stationary ARMA$(p,q)$. Then, $X_{t}$ is invertible if $\theta(z) \neq 0$ for all $|z| \leq 1$ or equivalently $\theta(z) = 0 \Rightarrow |z| > 1, \;\;\; \forall z \in \mathbb{C}$.

Illustration with an ARMA$(1,1)$ : $X_{t} - \varphi_{1} X_{t - 1} = \varepsilon_{t} + \theta_{1}\varepsilon_{t-1}$, $|\theta_{1}| < 1$

- The power expansion of $\theta$ is $\zeta(z) = \sum_{j = 0}^{\infty} -\theta_{1}^{j}z^{j}$ and hence
$$ \varepsilon_{t} = \zeta(B)\varphi(B)X_{t} = \pi(B)X_{t} $$
with $\sum_{j = -\infty}^{\infty} |\pi_{j}| < \infty$ as $|\theta_{1}| < 1$
- $\Rightarrow$ The invertible solution of $X_{t}$ is
$$ \varepsilon_{t} = X_{t} - (\varphi_{1} + \theta_{1}) \sum_{j = 1}^{\infty} -\theta_{1}^{j-1}X_{t-j} $$
as $\varepsilon_{t}$ is expressed in terms of present and past values of $X_{s}$, $s \leq t$

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Outline
SLIDE: Invertible ARMA
CONTENU:
**Définition** : Let $X_{t}$ be a stationary ARMA$(p,q)$. Then, $X_{t}$ is invertible if $\theta(z) \neq 0$ for all $|z| \leq 1$ or equivalently $\theta(z) = 0 \Rightarrow |z| > 1, \;\;\; \forall z \in \mathbb{C}$.

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Outline
SLIDE: Non-invertible ARMA
CONTENU:
**Définition** : Let $X_{t}$ be a stationary ARMA$(p,q)$. Then, $X_{t}$ is non-invertible if $\theta(z) \neq 0$ for all $|z| \geq 1$ or equivalently $\theta(z) = 0 \Rightarrow |z| < 1, \;\;\; \forall z \in \mathbb{C}$.

Illustration with an ARMA$(1,1)$ : $X_{t} - \varphi_{1} X_{t - 1} = \varepsilon_{t} + \theta_{1}\varepsilon_{t-1}$, $|\theta_{1}| > 1$

- Applying a similar reasoning to noncausal ARMA we obtain
$$ \varepsilon_{t} = -\varphi_{1}\theta_{1}^{-1}X_{t} + (\varphi_{1} + \theta_{1}) \sum_{j = 1}^{\infty} -\theta_{1}^{-j-1}X_{t+j} $$
- $\Rightarrow$ $X_{t}$ is noninvertible as $\varepsilon_{t}$ is expressed in terms of present and **future** values of $X_{s}$, $s \geq t$

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Outline
SLIDE: Non-invertible ARMA
CONTENU:
**Définition** : Let $X_{t}$ be a stationary ARMA$(p,q)$. Then, $X_{t}$ is non-invertible if $\theta(z) \neq 0$ for all $|z| \geq 1$ or equivalently $\theta(z) = 0 \Rightarrow |z| < 1, \;\;\; \forall z \in \mathbb{C}$.

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Mixed-Phase processes
SLIDE: Minimum phase and Non-Minimum phase processes
CONTENU:
- Let $X_{t}$ be a stationary ARMA$(p,q)$

**Définition** : If $\varphi(z) = 0 \Rightarrow |z| > 1, \;\;\; \forall z \in \mathbb{C}$ and $\theta(z) = 0 \Rightarrow |z| > 1, \;\;\; \forall z \in \mathbb{C}$, $X_{t}$ is causal and invertible. Such a process is called **minimum phase**

**Définition** : If $\varphi(z) = 0 \Rightarrow |z| < 1, \;\;\; \forall z \in \mathbb{C}$ and $\theta(z) = 0 \Rightarrow |z| < 1, \;\;\; \forall z \in \mathbb{C}$, $X_{t}$ is non-causal and non-invertible. Such a process is called **non-minimum phase**

- Let $X_{t}$ be a stationary AR$(p+q)$

**Définition** : If $\varphi(z) = 0 \Rightarrow |z| \neq 1, \;\;\; \forall z \in \mathbb{C}$ with some zeros inside and outside the unit circle, $X_{t}$ is mixed-causal/noncausal. Such a process is called Mixed-AR or MAR$(p,q)$ with $p$ and $q$ denoting the number of non-causal and causal lags respectively. The MAR enters the class of **mixed phase** processes.

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Mixed-Phase processes
SLIDE: Mixed phase AR processes
CONTENU:
**Définition** : A linear time series $\{X_{t}\}_{t \in \mathbb{Z}}$ is an AR$(p+q)$ if it is strictly stationary and satisfies the equation

$$ \varphi(B) X_{t} = \varepsilon_{t} $$

where

$$ \varphi(B) = 1 - \sum_{j = 1}^{p+q}\varphi_{j}B^{j} = 0 \Rightarrow |z| \neq 1 $$

and $\varepsilon_{t}$ is a strong white noise

- Here we clearly allow the roots of $\varphi(B)$ to be **outside and/or inside the unit circle**

- When $\varphi(B)$ has zeros both outside and inside the unit circle the process is **mixed phase** and called a MAR$(p,q)$

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Mixed-Phase processes
SLIDE: Mixed phase AR processes
CONTENU:
**Définition** : A linear time series $\{X_{t}\}_{t \in \mathbb{Z}}$ is an AR$(p+q)$ if it is strictly stationary and satisfies the equation

$$ \varphi(B) X_{t} = \varepsilon_{t} $$

where

$$ \varphi(B) = 1 - \sum_{j = 1}^{p+q}\varphi_{j}B^{j} = 0 \Rightarrow |z| \neq 1 $$

and $\varepsilon_{t}$ is a strong white noise

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Mixed-Phase processes
SLIDE: The MAR$(p,q)$
CONTENU:
**Définition** : A linear time series $\{X_{t}\}_{t \in \mathbb{Z}}$ is a MAR$(p,q)$ if $\varphi(B) X_{t} = \varepsilon_{t}$ can be decomposed as

$$ \varphi^{\circ}(F)\varphi^{\bullet} (B) X_{t} = \varepsilon_{t} $$

where

$$ \varphi^{\circ}(F) = 1 - \sum_{j = 1}^{p}\varphi^{\circ}_{j}F^{j}, \;\;\; \varphi^{\circ}(z) \neq 0 \text{ for all } |z| \leq 1 $$

and

$$ \varphi^{\bullet} (B) = 1 - \sum_{j = 1}^{q}\varphi^{\bullet} _{j}B^{j}, \;\;\; \varphi^{\bullet} (z) \neq 0 \text{ for all } |z| \leq 1 $$

- Defining $\varepsilon_{t}$ as a Gaussian noise would lead to an identification issue

- $\Rightarrow$ In the following, $\varepsilon_{t}$ will be assumed to be **Non-Gaussian**

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
There is no common root between $\varphi^{\circ}(F)$ and $\varphi^{\bullet} (B)$

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Mixed-Phase processes
SLIDE: The MAR$(p,q)$
CONTENU:
**Définition** : A linear time series $\{X_{t}\}_{t \in \mathbb{Z}}$ is a MAR$(p,q)$ if $\varphi(B) X_{t} = \varepsilon_{t}$ can be decomposed as

$$ \varphi^{\circ}(F)\varphi^{\bullet} (B) X_{t} = \varepsilon_{t} $$

where

$$ \varphi^{\circ}(F) = 1 - \sum_{j = 1}^{p}\varphi^{\circ}_{j}F^{j}, \;\;\; \varphi^{\circ}(z) \neq 0 \text{ for all } |z| \leq 1 $$

and

$$ \varphi^{\bullet} (B) = 1 - \sum_{j = 1}^{q}\varphi^{\bullet} _{j}B^{j}, \;\;\; \varphi^{\bullet} (z) \neq 0 \text{ for all } |z| \leq 1 $$

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Mixed-Phase processes
SLIDE: MAR$(1,1)$
CONTENU:
**Exemple** : Let $X_{t}$ be a MAR$(1,1)$ defined by $\varphi(B) X_{t} = \varepsilon_{t}$. Then, $X_{t}$ can be decomposed as

$$ (1 - \check{\varphi}^{\circ} B)(1 - \varphi^{\bullet} B) X_{t} = \check{\varepsilon}_{t}, \;\;\; |\check{\varphi}^{\circ}|>1, \;\;\; |\varphi^{\bullet}|<1 $$

or equivalently

$$ (1 - \varphi^{\circ} F)(1 - \varphi^{\bullet} B) X_{t} = \varepsilon_{t}, \;\;\; \varphi^{\circ} = 1/\check{\varphi}^{\circ}, \;\;\; \varepsilon_{t} = - \varphi^{\circ}\check{\varepsilon}_{t+1} $$

- Then, the stationary solution of $X_{t}$ is given by

$$ X_{t} = \sum_{j = 1}^{\infty}\frac{(\varphi^{\circ})^{k}}{1 - \varphi^{\circ}\varphi^{\bullet}}\varepsilon_{t+k} + \frac{\varepsilon_{t}}{1 - \varphi^{\circ}\varphi^{\bullet}} + \sum_{j = 1}^{\infty}\frac{(\varphi^{\bullet})^{k}}{1 - \varphi^{\circ}\varphi^{\bullet}}\varepsilon_{t-k} $$

or equivalently by the **two-sided** MA$(\infty)$ representation

$$ X_{t} = \sum^{\infty}_{j = -\infty} \psi_{j} \varepsilon_{t - j}, \text{ where } \psi(L) = \frac{1}{\varphi(B)} = \frac{1}{\varphi^{\circ}(F)\varphi^{\bullet}(B)} $$

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Mixed-Phase processes
SLIDE: MAR$(1,1)$
CONTENU:
**Exemple** : Let $X_{t}$ be a MAR$(1,1)$ defined by $\varphi(B) X_{t} = \varepsilon_{t}$. Then, $X_{t}$ can be decomposed as

$$ (1 - \check{\varphi}^{\circ} B)(1 - \varphi^{\bullet} B) X_{t} = \check{\varepsilon}_{t}, \;\;\; |\check{\varphi}^{\circ}|>1, \;\;\; |\varphi^{\bullet}|<1 $$

or equivalently

$$ (1 - \varphi^{\circ} F)(1 - \varphi^{\bullet} B) X_{t} = \varepsilon_{t}, \;\;\; \varphi^{\circ} = 1/\check{\varphi}^{\circ}, \;\;\; \varepsilon_{t} = - \varphi^{\circ}\check{\varepsilon}_{t+1} $$

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Mixed-Phase processes
SLIDE: The generalized Mixed Phase ARMA
CONTENU:
**Définition** : A linear time series $\{X_{t}\}_{t \in \mathbb{Z}}$ is a generalized ARMA$(p^{\circ},p^{\bullet},q^{\circ},q^{\bullet})$ if $\varphi(B) X_{t} = \theta(B)\varepsilon_{t}$ can be decomposed as

$$ \varphi^{\circ}(F)\varphi^{\bullet}(B) X_{t} = \theta^{\circ}(F)\theta^{\bullet}(B)\varepsilon_{t} $$

implying the stationary solution $X_{t} = \sum^{\infty}_{j = -\infty} \psi_{j} \varepsilon_{t - j}$ if

$$ \varphi^{\circ}(F) = 1 - \sum_{j = 1}^{p^{\circ}}\varphi^{\circ}_{j}F^{j}, \;\;\; \varphi^{\bullet}(B) = 1 - \sum_{j = 1}^{p^{\bullet}}\varphi^{\bullet}_{j}B^{j}, \;\;\; \varphi^{\circ}(z),\varphi^{\bullet}(z) \neq 0, \;\forall |z| \leq 1 $$

and

$$ \theta^{\circ}(F) = 1 - \sum_{j = 1}^{q^{\circ}}\theta^{\circ}_{j}F^{j}, \;\;\; \theta^{\bullet}(B) = 1 - \sum_{j = 1}^{q^{\bullet}}\theta^{\bullet}_{j}B^{j}, \;\;\; \theta^{\circ}(z) ,\theta^{\bullet}(z) \neq 0, \;\forall |z| \leq 1 $$

where $\psi(B) = \varphi(B)^{-1}\theta(B)$

- $X_{t}$ is purely causal when $p^{\circ} = 0$ and purely non-causal when $p^{\bullet} = 0$

- ... purely invertible when $q^{\circ} = 0$ and purely non-invertible when $q^{\bullet} = 0$

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
- Both $\varphi^{\circ}(z)$ and $\varphi^{\bullet}(z) \neq 0 \text{ for all } |z| \leq 1$ because $\varphi^{\circ}(z)$ is written in terms of forward operator $F$ so that the roots of $\varphi^{\circ}(z)$ are already inversed (also true for $\theta^{\circ}(z) \text{ and } \theta^{\bullet} \neq 0 \text{ for all } |z| \leq 1$)

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Mixed-Phase processes
SLIDE: The generalized Mixed Phase ARMA
CONTENU:
**Définition** : A linear time series $\{X_{t}\}_{t \in \mathbb{Z}}$ is a generalized ARMA$(p^{\circ},p^{\bullet},q^{\circ},q^{\bullet})$ if $\varphi(B) X_{t} = \theta(B)\varepsilon_{t}$ can be decomposed as

$$ \varphi^{\circ}(F)\varphi^{\bullet}(B) X_{t} = \theta^{\circ}(F)\theta^{\bullet}(B)\varepsilon_{t} $$

implying the stationary solution $X_{t} = \sum^{\infty}_{j = -\infty} \psi_{j} \varepsilon_{t - j}$ if

$$ \varphi^{\circ}(F) = 1 - \sum_{j = 1}^{p^{\circ}}\varphi^{\circ}_{j}F^{j}, \;\;\; \varphi^{\bullet}(B) = 1 - \sum_{j = 1}^{p^{\bullet}}\varphi^{\bullet}_{j}B^{j}, \;\;\; \varphi^{\circ}(z),\varphi^{\bullet}(z) \neq 0, \;\forall |z| \leq 1 $$

and

$$ \theta^{\circ}(F) = 1 - \sum_{j = 1}^{q^{\circ}}\theta^{\circ}_{j}F^{j}, \;\;\; \theta^{\bullet}(B) = 1 - \sum_{j = 1}^{q^{\bullet}}\theta^{\bullet}_{j}B^{j}, \;\;\; \theta^{\circ}(z) ,\theta^{\bullet}(z) \neq 0, \;\forall |z| \leq 1 $$

where $\psi(B) = \varphi(B)^{-1}\theta(B)$

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Mixed-Phase processes
SLIDE: The generalized Mixed Phase ARFIMA
CONTENU:
**Définition** : A linear time series $\{X_{t}\}_{t \in \mathbb{Z}}$ is a generalized ARFIMA$(p^{\circ},p^{\bullet},q^{\circ},q^{\bullet})$ if $(1 - B)^{\delta}\varphi(B) X_{t} = \theta(B)\varepsilon_{t}$ can be decomposed as

$$ (1 - B)^{\delta}\varphi^{\circ}(F)\varphi^{\bullet}(B) X_{t} = \theta^{\circ}(F)\theta^{\bullet}(B)\varepsilon_{t} $$

implying the stationary solution $X_{t} = \sum^{\infty}_{j = -\infty} \psi_{j} \varepsilon_{t - j}$ if

$$ \varphi^{\circ}(F) = 1 - \sum_{j = 1}^{p^{\circ}}\varphi^{\circ}_{j}F^{j}, \;\;\; \varphi^{\bullet}(B) = 1 - \sum_{j = 1}^{p^{\bullet}}\varphi^{\bullet}_{j}B^{j}, \;\;\; \varphi^{\circ}(z), \varphi^{\bullet}(z) \neq 0, \;\forall |z| \leq 1 $$

and

$$ \theta^{\circ}(F) = 1 - \sum_{j = 1}^{q^{\circ}}\theta^{\circ}_{j}F^{j}, \;\;\; \theta^{\bullet}(B) = 1 - \sum_{j = 1}^{q^{\bullet}}\theta^{\bullet}_{j}B^{j}, \;\;\; \theta^{\circ}(z) ,\theta^{\bullet}(z) \neq 0, \;\forall |z| \leq 1 $$

where $\psi(B) = \varphi(B)^{-1}\theta(B)$ and $\delta \in (-1/2,1/2)$

- Generalized Mixed Phase ARMA and ARFIMA models are introduced by Wu and Davis (2010) and Wu (2014)

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
As in the traditional causal case, generalized Mixed Phase ARFIMA has squared summable autocovariance function for $\delta \in (0,1/2)$ and absolutely summable autocovariance function for $\delta \in (-1/2,0]$. As long as the autocovariance function is squared summable (i.e. $\delta < 1/2$), the process is stationary and as long as $\delta > -1/2$ the process has an infinite MA representation.

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Mixed-Phase processes
SLIDE: The generalized Mixed Phase ARFIMA
CONTENU:
**Définition** : A linear time series $\{X_{t}\}_{t \in \mathbb{Z}}$ is a generalized ARFIMA$(p^{\circ},p^{\bullet},q^{\circ},q^{\bullet})$ if $(1 - B)^{\delta}\varphi(B) X_{t} = \theta(B)\varepsilon_{t}$ can be decomposed as

$$ (1 - B)^{\delta}\varphi^{\circ}(F)\varphi^{\bullet}(B) X_{t} = \theta^{\circ}(F)\theta^{\bullet}(B)\varepsilon_{t} $$

implying the stationary solution $X_{t} = \sum^{\infty}_{j = -\infty} \psi_{j} \varepsilon_{t - j}$ if

$$ \varphi^{\circ}(F) = 1 - \sum_{j = 1}^{p^{\circ}}\varphi^{\circ}_{j}F^{j}, \;\;\; \varphi^{\bullet}(B) = 1 - \sum_{j = 1}^{p^{\bullet}}\varphi^{\bullet}_{j}B^{j}, \;\;\; \varphi^{\circ}(z), \varphi^{\bullet}(z) \neq 0, \;\forall |z| \leq 1 $$

and

$$ \theta^{\circ}(F) = 1 - \sum_{j = 1}^{q^{\circ}}\theta^{\circ}_{j}F^{j}, \;\;\; \theta^{\bullet}(B) = 1 - \sum_{j = 1}^{q^{\bullet}}\theta^{\bullet}_{j}B^{j}, \;\;\; \theta^{\circ}(z) ,\theta^{\bullet}(z) \neq 0, \;\forall |z| \leq 1 $$

where $\psi(B) = \varphi(B)^{-1}\theta(B)$ and $\delta \in (-1/2,1/2)$

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Mixed-Phase processes
SLIDE: Mixed phase baseline paths
CONTENU:
- For a given $t$ and $\tau$, a strong linear process can be represented as

$$ X_{t} = \sum_{\tau = -\infty}^{\infty} \varepsilon_{\tau}\mathds{1}_{\tau\leq t} \psi_{t - \tau} $$

if the process is causal and as

$$ X_{t} = \sum_{\tau = -\infty}^{\infty} \varepsilon_{\tau}\mathds{1}_{\tau\geq t} \psi_{t - \tau} $$

if the process is noncausal, that is a combination of baseline paths with stochastic $i.i.d.$ coefficients

- If the process is mixed phase we have

$$ X_{t} = \sum_{\tau = -\infty}^{\infty} \varepsilon_{\tau}\mathds{1}_{\tau\leq t} \psi_{t - \tau} + \sum_{\tau = -\infty}^{\infty} \varepsilon_{\tau}\mathds{1}_{\tau\geq t} \psi_{t - \tau} $$

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Mixed-Phase processes
SLIDE: Mixed phase baseline paths
CONTENU:
- $X_{t} = \varphi^{\bullet} X_{t - 1} + \varepsilon_{t}$ / $X_{t} = \varphi^{\circ} X_{t + 1} + \varepsilon_{t}$ / $X_{t} = \varphi^{\circ}X_{t + 1} +\varphi^{\bullet}X_{t - 1} + \varepsilon_{t}$, $\tau = 30$
