COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Mixed-Phase processes
SLIDE: Tracking error in minimum phase
CONTENU:
- Let $\varepsilon_{\tau}$ a large positive shock occuring at time $\tau$

- If $t \leq \tau$ the weight of that large shock increases exponentially as $t$ approaches $\tau$

- At $t = \tau + 1$ it looks like a brutal bubble burst

- For instance, consider a non-causal AR$(1)$ with $|\varphi| = |\check{\varphi}^{-1}| < 1$

$$\begin{aligned}
X_{t} & = \varepsilon_{t} + \varphi\varepsilon_{t+1} + \ldots + \varphi^{\tau-t-1}\varepsilon_{\tau - 1} + \btxt{\varphi^{\tau-t}}\ntxt{\varepsilon_{\tau}}, \;\;\; t < \tau \\
X_{t+1} & = \varepsilon_{t+1} + \varphi\varepsilon_{t+2} + \ldots + \btxt{\varphi^{\tau-t-1}}\ntxt{\varepsilon_{\tau}} + \varphi^{\tau-t}\varepsilon_{\tau + 1}, \;\;\; t + 1 < \tau \\
\vdots & \\
X_{\tau} & = \ntxt{\varepsilon_{\tau}} + \varphi\varepsilon_{\tau+1} + \ldots, \;\;\; t = \tau \\
X_{\tau+1} & = \varepsilon_{\tau+1} + \varphi\varepsilon_{\tau+2} + \ldots, \;\;\; t > \tau
\end{aligned}$$
- In a mixed phase process, if $t > \tau$, the bubble burst is smooth and the weight of that large shock decreases exponentially

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Identification
SLIDE: Conditional expectation
CONTENU:
- Let $X_{t+1}$ and $X_{t} = \mu + \rho(1)(X_{t-1} - \mu) + \varepsilon_{t}$ two stationary variables such that conditional distribution of $X_{t+1}$ given that $X_{t} = x_{t}$ is
$$ \mathcal{N}(\mu + \rho(1)(x_{t}-\mu),\sigma^{2}(1-\rho(1)^{2})) $$
with $\rho(h) = \gamma(h)/\gamma(0)$ and $|\rho(1)|<1$.

**Proposition** : For $g(.)$ a real function, the **best mean square** predictor of $X_{t+1}$ is

$$ \arg\min_{g(X_{t})} \mathbb{E}\Big( (X_{t+1} - g(X_{t}))^{2} \Big) = \btxt{\mu + \rho(1)(X_{t}-\mu)} = \mathbb{E}(X_{t+1}|X_{t}) $$

**Proposition** : For $g(X_{t}) = aX_{t} + b$, the best mean square **linear** predictor of $X_{t+1}$ is

$$ \arg\min_{g(X_{t})} \mathbb{E}\Big( (X_{t+1} - g(X_{t}))^{2} \Big) = \btxt{\mu + \rho(1)(X_{t}-\mu)} = \mathbb{EL}(X_{t+1}|X_{t}) $$

- $\Rightarrow$ In the Gaussian case, the **best mean square** predictor is **linear**

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
- Observed that $X_{t}$ could be specified as $X_{t} = \mu + \rho(1)(X_{t-1} - \mu) + \varepsilon_{t}$

- Notice that

$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}\Big( (X_{t} - g(Y_{t}))^{2} \Big) & = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} (x_{t} - g(y_{t}))^{2} f_{X|Y}(x|y)dx \\
& = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x_{t}^{2} f_{X|Y}(x|y)dx - 2g(Y_{t})\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x_{t} f_{X|Y}(x|y)dx \\
& + g(Y_{t})^{2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_{X|Y}(x|y)dx
\end{aligned}$$

With respect to the minimization program, $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x_{t}^{2} f_{X|Y}(x|y)dx$ does not matter and $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_{X|Y}(x|y)dx = 1$ and hence

$$\begin{aligned}
\arg\min_{g(Y_{t})}\mathbb{E}\Big( (X_{t} - g(Y_{t}))^{2} \Big) & = \arg\min_{g(Y_{t})} \Big(- 2g(Y_{t})\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x_{t} f_{X|Y}(x|y)dx + g(Y_{t})^{2}\Big) \\
& = \arg\min_{g(Y_{t})} \Big(- 2g(Y_{t})\mathbb{E}( X_{t}|Y_{t}) + g(Y_{t})^{2}\Big)
\end{aligned}$$

Then, the FOC trivially implies :

$$\begin{aligned}
\nabla \mathbb{E}\Big( (X_{n+h} - g(Y_{t}))^{2} \Big) & = - 2\mathbb{E}( X_{t}|Y_{t}) + 2g(Y_{t}) = 0 \Longleftrightarrow g(Y_{t}) = \mathbb{E}( X_{t}|Y_{t})
\end{aligned}$$

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Identification
SLIDE: Conditional expectation
CONTENU:
**Proposition** : For $g(.)$ a real function, the **best mean square** predictor of $X_{t+1}$ is

$$ \arg\min_{g(X_{t})} \mathbb{E}\Big( (X_{t+1} - g(X_{t}))^{2} \Big) = \btxt{\mu + \rho(1)(X_{t}-\mu)} = \mathbb{E}(X_{t+1}|X_{t}) $$

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Identification
SLIDE: Conditional expectation
CONTENU:
**Proposition** : For $g(X_{t}) = aX_{t} + b$, the best mean square **linear** predictor of $X_{t+1}$ is

$$ \arg\min_{g(X_{t})} \mathbb{E}\Big( (X_{t+1} - g(X_{t}))^{2} \Big) = \btxt{\mu + \rho(1)(X_{t}-\mu)} = \mathbb{EL}(X_{t+1}|X_{t}) $$

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Identification
SLIDE: Best linear predictor and errors
CONTENU:
- In Propositions and , $X_{t} = \mu + \rho(1)(X_{t-1} - \mu) + \varepsilon_{t}$

- It follows that the best linear predictor of $X_{t+1}$ is
$$ \mathbb{EL}(X_{t+1}|X_{t}) = \mu + \rho(1)(X_{t}-\mu) $$
- ... leading to the following prediction error
$$ \varepsilon_{t+1} = X_{t+1} - \mu + \rho(1)(X_{t}-\mu) $$
- The predictor $\mathbb{EL}(X_{t+1}|X_{t})$ will be uniquely determined if

$$ \mathbb{E}(\text{Error}\times\text{Predictor Variable}) = 0 $$
- $\Rightarrow$ As $\varepsilon_{t+1}$ is a SWN, this condition is fulfilled

$$ \mathbb{E}(\varepsilon_{t+1}X_{t}) = 0 $$
- Note $\mathbb{EL} \equiv$ best approximation of expectation as a linear function

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Identification
SLIDE: Non-Causal AR and causal representation
CONTENU:
$X_{t} = \varphi_{1} X_{t+1} + \varepsilon_{t}$ or $X_{t} = \check{\varphi}_{1} X_{t - 1} + \check{\varepsilon}_{t}$ leads to 3 types of errors (noises)

- 1 $\varepsilon_{t} = X_{t} - \varphi_{1} X_{t+1}$

- As $\btxt{\varepsilon_{t-1}} = - \varphi_{1} \check{\varepsilon}_{t} \not\perp \btxt{X_{t-1}}$, $\varepsilon_{t}$ is not the innovation of $X_{t}$ and

$$ \btxt{\varepsilon_{t}} \not\perp \btxt{X_{t}} - \mathbb{EL}(X_{t}|X_{s},s < t) $$

- 2 $\check{\varepsilon}_{t} = X_{t} - \check{\varphi}_{1} X_{t - 1}$ is just an equivalent representation $X_{t}$

- As $- \varphi_{1} \ntxt{\check{\varepsilon}_{t}} \not\perp \ntxt{X_{t-1}}$, $\check{\varepsilon}_{t}$ is not the innovation of $X_{t}$ and

$$ \ntxt{\check{\varepsilon}_{t}} \not\perp X_{t} - \mathbb{EL}(X_{t}|\ntxt{X_{s}},s < t) $$

- Note The best predictor in mean square sense, $\mathbb{E}(X_{t}|X_{s},s < t)$, will be nonlinear if $\check{\varepsilon}_{t}$ is non-Gaussian with finite variance (Rosenblatt, 2000, p. 101)

- 3 $\tilde{\varepsilon}_{t} = X_{t} - \varphi_{1} X_{t-1}$ is a **weak causal representation** of $X_{t}$

- $\tilde{\varepsilon}_{t} \sim WWN$ (except when $\varepsilon_{t}$ is Gaussian, $\tilde{\varepsilon}_{t} \sim SWN$)

- Moreover, $\tilde{\varepsilon}_{t}$ is the linear innovation of $X_{t}$ because one can show that
$$ \tilde{\varepsilon}_{t} = X_{t} - \mathbb{EL}(X_{t}|X_{s},s < t) $$

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
- $\check{\varepsilon}_{t}$ is often interpreted as a shock or innovation on $X_{t}$ but this is misleading ! By definition, an innovation is independent and unpredictable... Here, theoretically, $\check{\varepsilon}_{t}$ is predictable.

- As $|\check{\varphi}_{1}|>1$ and $\varphi_{1} = \check{\varphi}_{1}^{-1}$, $X_{t} = \varphi_{1} X_{t-1} + \tilde{\varepsilon}_{t}$ admits a causal stationary solution and $\tilde{\varepsilon}_{t}$ and $X_{t-1}$ are independent so that $\tilde{\varepsilon}_{t}$ indeed represents the innovations of $X_{t}$

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Identification
SLIDE: Non-Causal ARMA and causal representation
CONTENU:
**Définition** : Let $X_{t}$ be a stationary ARMA$(p,q)$ defined as $\check{\varphi}(B)X_{t} = \check{\theta}(B)\check{\varepsilon}_{t}$. Then, it is always possible to find polynomials $\varphi(B)$ and $\theta(B)$ and a weak white noise sequence $\tilde{\varepsilon}_{t}$ such that $\varphi(B) X_{t} = \theta(B)\tilde{\varepsilon}_{t}$.

- Accordingly, any noncausal ARMA has a **weak causal representation**

- Remark $\tilde{\varepsilon}_{t}$ will **not** be a Strong White Noise unless $\check{\varepsilon}_{t}$ is Gaussian

- In the Gaussian case, all representations are equivalent ($\varepsilon_{t}$, $\check{\varepsilon}_{t}$, and $\tilde{\varepsilon}_{t}$)

- $\Rightarrow$ Causal and Non-Causal ARMA processes are **indistinguishable**

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Identification
SLIDE: Non-Causal ARMA and causal representation
CONTENU:
**Définition** : Let $X_{t}$ be a stationary ARMA$(p,q)$ defined as $\check{\varphi}(B)X_{t} = \check{\theta}(B)\check{\varepsilon}_{t}$. Then, it is always possible to find polynomials $\varphi(B)$ and $\theta(B)$ and a weak white noise sequence $\tilde{\varepsilon}_{t}$ such that $\varphi(B) X_{t} = \theta(B)\tilde{\varepsilon}_{t}$.

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Identification
SLIDE: Non-uniqueness of Gaussian MA processes
CONTENU:
- To understand the identification issue in the MA representation

- ... consider the following Gaussian MA$(1)$ process

$$ X_{t} = \check{\varepsilon}_{t} + \check{\theta} \check{\varepsilon}_{t-1}, \;\;\; \check{\varepsilon}_{t} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{\check{\varepsilon}}^{2}) $$

- $\Rightarrow$ If $\theta \neq 0$ we easily see that **several representations coexist**

$$ X_{t} = \varepsilon_{t} + \frac{1}{\check{\theta}} \varepsilon_{t-1}, \;\;\; \varepsilon_{t} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{\check{\varepsilon}}^{2}\check{\theta}^{2}) $$

where both $\check{\varepsilon}_{t}$ and $\varepsilon_{t}$ are Strong White Noises

- $\Rightarrow$ Both MA$(\infty)$ representations have the same probability structure

$$ X_{t} = \sum_{j = -\infty}^{\infty} \check{\pi}_{j}\check{\varepsilon}_{t-j} = \sum_{j = -\infty}^{\infty} \pi_{j}\varepsilon_{t-j} $$

because $\check{\varepsilon}_{t}$ and $\varepsilon_{t}$ are two $i.i.d.$ Gaussian random variables

- Remark We have a **two-sided** MA$(\infty)$ because we do not say which representation is invertible or not

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Identification
SLIDE: Non-uniqueness of Gaussian MA processes
CONTENU:
- Proof We use the autocovariance functions that summarize all the probability structure in the Gaussian case:

$$\begin{aligned}
\gamma_{X,\check{\varepsilon}}(h) & = Cov(X_{t+h},X_{t}) = Cov(\check{\varepsilon}_{t+h} + \check{\theta} \check{\varepsilon}_{t+h-1},\check{\varepsilon}_{t} + \check{\theta} \check{\varepsilon}_{t-1}) \\
& = \gamma_{\check{\varepsilon}}(h) + \ntxt{\check{\theta}} \gamma_{\check{\varepsilon}}(h + 1) + \ntxt{\check{\theta}} \gamma_{\check{\varepsilon}}(h - 1) + \btxt{\check{\theta}^{2}} \gamma_{\check{\varepsilon}}(h) \\
& = \sigma_{\check{\varepsilon}}^{2}(1 + \btxt{\check{\theta}^{2}}) \mathds{1}_{h = 0} + \sigma_{\check{\varepsilon}}^{2}\ntxt{\check{\theta}}\mathds{1}_{|h| = 1} \\
& \\
\gamma_{X,\varepsilon}(h) & = Cov(X_{t+h},X_{t}) = Cov(\varepsilon_{t+h} + \check{\theta}^{-1} \varepsilon_{t+h-1},\varepsilon_{t} + \check{\theta}^{-1} \varepsilon_{t-1}) \\
& = \gamma_{\varepsilon}(h) + \ntxt{\check{\theta}^{-1}} \gamma_{\varepsilon}(h + 1) + \ntxt{\check{\theta}^{-1}} \gamma_{\varepsilon}(h - 1) + \btxt{\check{\theta}^{-2}} \gamma_{\varepsilon}(h) \\
& = \mtxt{\sigma_{\check{\varepsilon}}^{2}\check{\theta}^{2}}(1 + \btxt{\check{\theta}^{-2}})\mathds{1}_{h = 0} + \mtxt{\sigma_{\check{\varepsilon}}^{2}\check{\theta}^{2}}\ntxt{\check{\theta}^{-1}}\mathds{1}_{|h| = 1} \\
& = \sigma_{\check{\varepsilon}}^{2}(1 + \check{\theta}^{2})\mathds{1}_{h = 0} + \sigma_{\check{\varepsilon}}^{2}\check{\theta}\mathds{1}_{|h| = 1}
\end{aligned}$$

with $\mathds{1}_{(.)}$ the indicatrice function, $\check{\varepsilon}_{t} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{\check{\varepsilon}}^{2})$ and $\varepsilon_{t} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\mtxt{\sigma_{\check{\varepsilon}}^{2}\check{\theta}^{2}})$

- Hence, $\gamma_{X,\check{\varepsilon}}(h) = \gamma_{X,\varepsilon}(h)$ and given the Gaussian nature of $\check{\varepsilon}_{t}$ and $\varepsilon_{t}$, the two representations of $X_{t}$ have a identical probability structure

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Identification
SLIDE: Non-uniqueness of Gaussian ARMA processes
CONTENU:
- Consider the non-causal Gaussian ARMA$(1,1)$

$$ X_{t} - \check{\varphi}_{1} X_{t - 1} = \check{\varepsilon}_{t} + \check{\theta}_{1}\check{\varepsilon}_{t-1} := \check{\varphi}(B) X_{t} = \check{\theta}(B)\check{\varepsilon}_{t}, \;\;\; |\check{\varphi}_{1}|>1 , \;\;\; |\check{\theta}_{1}|>1 $$
- The spectral density of $X_{t}$ is
$$ f_{X}(\lambda) = \Big|\frac{\check{\theta}(e^{-i\lambda})}{\check{\varphi}(e^{-i\lambda})}\Big|^{2}f_{\check{\varepsilon}}(\lambda) = \Big|\frac{\check{\theta}(e^{-i\lambda})}{\check{\varphi}(e^{-i\lambda})}\Big|^{2}\frac{\sigma^{2}_{\check{\varepsilon}}}{2\pi} $$
- Use $\varphi(B) = 1 - \frac{1}{\check{\varphi}_{1}}B$ and $\theta(B) = 1 - \frac{1}{\check{\theta}_{1}}B$ in $\varepsilon_{t} = \ntxt{\theta(B)^{-1}\varphi(B) }\btxt{X_{t}}$

- Then, the **spectral density** of $\varepsilon_{t}$ is

$$ f_{\varepsilon}(\lambda) = \ntxt{\Big|\frac{1-\check{\theta}_{1}^{-1}e^{-i\lambda}}{1-\check{\varphi}_{1}^{-1}e^{-i\lambda}}\Big|^{2}}\btxt{\Big|\frac{1-\check{\theta}_{1}e^{-i\lambda}}{1-\check{\varphi}_{1}e^{-i\lambda}}\Big|^{2}}\frac{\sigma^{2}_{\check{\varepsilon}}}{2\pi} = \frac{\check{\theta}_{1}^{2}}{\check{\varphi}_{1}^{2}} \frac{\sigma^{2}_{\check{\varepsilon}}}{2\pi} = \frac{\varphi_{1}^{2}\theta_{1}^{-2}\sigma^{2}_{\check{\varepsilon}}}{2\pi} = \frac{\sigma^{2}_{\varepsilon}}{2\pi}, $$

constant and hence $\varepsilon_{t}$ is also a Gaussian (strong) white noise

- $\Rightarrow$ The **probability structure** is the same for
$$ \varphi(B) X_{t} = \theta(B)\varepsilon_{t} \text{ and } \check{\varphi}(B) X_{t} = \check{\theta}(B)\check{\varepsilon}_{t} $$
and their two MA$(\infty)$ representations coexist

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
$f_{\varepsilon}(\lambda)$ simplifies to a constant because the Euler formula implies

$$\begin{aligned}
\Big|1-\frac{1}{\check{\varphi}_{1}}e^{-i\lambda}\Big|^{2} & = \frac{1}{\check{\varphi}_{1}^{2}}\Big|\check{\varphi}_{1}-e^{-i\lambda}\Big|^{2} \\
& = \frac{|e^{i\lambda}|^{2}}{\check{\varphi}_{1}^{2}}\Big|\check{\varphi}_{1}-e^{-i\lambda}\Big|^{2} \\
& = \frac{1}{\check{\varphi}_{1}^{2}}\Big|\check{\varphi}_{1}e^{-i\lambda} - 1\Big|^{2} = \frac{1}{\check{\varphi}_{1}^{2}}|1-\check{\varphi}_{1}e^{-i\lambda}|^{2}
\end{aligned}$$

- Recall that any Gaussian process is entirely determined by its autocovariance function or equivalently its spectral density (as only the two first moments determine the probability structure). As we can see in the spectral domain, inversing the roots of the polynomials does not change the probability structure so that the phase information coming from the transfer function $f_{X}(\lambda)$ is not identifiable.
- The non-uniqueness of the representation and hence the fact that one cannot distinguish between causal and non-causal models (the coefficients of the polynomials are not identifiable) in the Gaussian case justifies why time-series analysis generally focuses only on the causal representation and hence, restricts the parameters space to the causal invertible region.

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Identification
SLIDE: Uniqueness of linear process representation
CONTENU:
**Définition** : - Uniqueness means that the only way for $X_{t}$, a linear process, to admit two MA$(\infty)$ representations is

- 1 the existence of a constant scaling factor $c \in \mathbb{R}$

- 2 and a shift in time $l \in \mathbb{Z}$

- ... such that
$$ X_{t} = \sum_{j = -\infty}^{\infty} \check{\psi}_{j}\check{\varepsilon}_{t-j} = \sum_{j = -\infty}^{\infty} \psi_{j}\varepsilon_{t-j} $$

with
$$ \varepsilon_{t} = c\check{\varepsilon}_{t-l} \text{ and } \psi_{j} = \frac{1}{c} \check{\psi}_{j+l} $$

- Uniqueness is not found for Gaussian processes... is it similar for Non-Gaussian processes ?

- $\Rightarrow$ For finite variance non-Gaussian noises, uniqueness has been demonstrated (Rosenblatt, 2000, Th. 1.3.1)

- $\Rightarrow$ For infinite variance noises, we will detail some results

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
- Uniqueness of Non-Gaussian ARMA representation is very complicated to demonstrate even for simple deviation to the Gaussian distribution...
- les équations du slide 36 ne sont pas liées via une translation temporelle ou un facteur d'échelle multiplicatif. Par conséquent, pour un processus Gaussien, on viole le théorème d'unicité qui dit que la translation temporelle et le facteur d'échelle sont les seules possibilités pour avoir deux représentations identiques d'un processus d'un point de vue probabiliste

CHAPITRE: Identification
SLIDE: Uniqueness of linear process representation
CONTENU:
**Définition** : - Uniqueness means that the only way for $X_{t}$, a linear process, to admit two MA$(\infty)$ representations is

- 1 the existence of a constant scaling factor $c \in \mathbb{R}$

- 2 and a shift in time $l \in \mathbb{Z}$

- ... such that
$$ X_{t} = \sum_{j = -\infty}^{\infty} \check{\psi}_{j}\check{\varepsilon}_{t-j} = \sum_{j = -\infty}^{\infty} \psi_{j}\varepsilon_{t-j} $$

with
$$ \varepsilon_{t} = c\check{\varepsilon}_{t-l} \text{ and } \psi_{j} = \frac{1}{c} \check{\psi}_{j+l} $$

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: $\alpha$-stable MAR
SLIDE: How fat should we go
CONTENU:
- Non-Gaussian distributions are crucial to identify non-causality

- As non-causality is appropriate to model explosive (bubble) behavior, heavy-tail distributions are of interest

- The literature has primarily focused on the Student's $t$ distribution

$$ f_{\varepsilon}(\sigma,\nu) = \frac{\Gamma(\frac{\nu + 1}{2})}{\Gamma(\nu / 2)\sqrt{\pi\nu}\sigma}\Bigg( 1 + \frac{1}{\nu}\Big( \frac{\varepsilon}{\sigma}\Big)^{2}\Bigg)^{-\frac{\nu + 1}{2}} $$

with $\sigma > 0$ and $\nu > 0$ but sufficiently small to depart from the Gaussian distribution

- $\Rightarrow$ Hecq, Lieb and Teg (2016) extensively discuss this approach and investigate the question « How fat should we go » in terms of heavy tails

- Remark The Student's $t$ distribution is symmetric and therefore not necessarily appropriate to model some financial or macro phenomena (typically, bubbles are generally positive, right tail events)

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: $\alpha$-stable MAR
SLIDE: Introduction to Stable distributions
CONTENU:
- If the tails of the Student's $t$ distribution are not sufficiently heavy

- ... the family of Stable laws offers an attractive alternative

**Définition** : A real probability measure $\mu$ is said to be $\alpha$-**stable** if $\forall \; k \in \mathbb{N} \; \exists b^{k} > 0$ such that

$$ X_{1} + \ldots + X_{k} \,{\buildrel d \over =}\, b_{k} X + e_{k} $$

where $\mathcal{L}(X_{1}) = \ldots = \mathcal{L}(X_{k}) = \mathcal{L}(X) = \mu$ and $X_{1} + \ldots + X_{k}$ are independent and where $\exists \alpha \in (0,2]$ such that $b^{k} = k^{1/\alpha}$

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
- Another important property of stable distributions is the role that they play in a generalized central limit theorem. The central limit theorem states that the sum of a number of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) random variables with finite non-zero variances will tend to a normal distribution as the number of variables grows.

- A generalization due to Gnedenko and Kolmogorov states that the sum of a number of random variables with symmetric distributions having power-law tails (Paretian tails) with tail index $0<\alpha < 2$ (and therefore having infinite variance), will tend to a stable distribution $\mathcal{S}(\alpha,0,c,0)$ as the number of summands grows. If $\alpha \geq 2$ then the sum converges to a stable distribution with stability parameter equal to 2, i.e. a Gaussian distribution $\mathcal{N}(0,2c^{2})$.

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: $\alpha$-stable MAR
SLIDE: Introduction to Stable distributions
CONTENU:
**Définition** : A real probability measure $\mu$ is said to be $\alpha$-**stable** if $\forall \; k \in \mathbb{N} \; \exists b^{k} > 0$ such that

$$ X_{1} + \ldots + X_{k} \,{\buildrel d \over =}\, b_{k} X + e_{k} $$

where $\mathcal{L}(X_{1}) = \ldots = \mathcal{L}(X_{k}) = \mathcal{L}(X) = \mu$ and $X_{1} + \ldots + X_{k}$ are independent and where $\exists \alpha \in (0,2]$ such that $b^{k} = k^{1/\alpha}$

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: $\alpha$-stable MAR
SLIDE: Some remarks on Stable distributions
CONTENU:
- If $\varepsilon_{t}$ is a random variable that follows a stable distribution, then

$$ \varepsilon_{t} \sim \mathcal{S}(\alpha,\beta,\sigma,m) $$

where

- the stability parameter $\alpha \in (0,2]$ is also a tail index

- $\beta \in [-1,1]$ is the asymmetry parameter

- $\sigma \in (0,\infty)$ is the scale parameter

- $m \in \mathbb{R}$ is the location parameter (if $m = 0$, $\varepsilon_{t}$ is strictly stable)

- If $z_{t} \sim \mathcal{S}(\alpha,\beta,1,0)$ then, $\varepsilon_{t} = z_{t}\sigma + m \sim \mathcal{S}(\alpha,\beta,\sigma,m)$

- Normal If $\varepsilon_{t} \sim \mathcal{S}(2,\beta,\sigma,m)$ then, $f_{\varepsilon}(2,\beta,1,0) = (\sqrt{2\pi})^{-1}\exp(-\varepsilon^{2}/2)$

- Cauchy If $\varepsilon_{t} \sim \mathcal{S}(1,0,\sigma,m)$ then, $f_{\varepsilon}(1,0,1,0) = \big(\pi( 1 + \varepsilon^{2}) \big)^{-1}$

- Lévy If $\varepsilon_{t} \sim \mathcal{S}(1/2,1,\sigma,m)$ then,
$$ f_{\varepsilon}(1/2,1,1,0) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\varepsilon^{3/2}}\exp(\frac{-1}{2\varepsilon})\mathds{1}_{\varepsilon>0} $$

with $f_{\varepsilon}(.)$ the density function

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
Observe that $\beta$ has no impact when $\alpha = 2$ (no longer an asymmetric parameter)

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: $\alpha$-stable MAR
SLIDE: Analytic representation of Stable distributions
CONTENU:
- In most cases, neither the probability density, $f_{\varepsilon}(.)$, nor the cumulative distribution, $F_{\varepsilon}(.)$, functions are analytically expressible

- Fortunately, the characteristic function $\varphi_{\varepsilon}(.) = \mathbb{E}(e^{-iu\varepsilon})$ has a tractable expression for $\alpha \neq 1$

$$ \log \varphi_{\varepsilon}(u) = -\sigma^{\alpha}|u|^{\alpha}\Big( 1 - i\beta(\operatorname{sign} u) \tan \bigg( \frac{\pi\alpha}{2} \bigg) \Big) + im u $$
- Remark If $f_{\varepsilon}(.)$ exists, $\varphi_{\varepsilon}(.) = \mathbb{E}(e^{-iu\varepsilon})$ is also the Fourier transform of $f_{\varepsilon}(.)$ and one can see that it completely defines its p.d.f.

- Remark When $\alpha = 1$, $\log \varphi_{\varepsilon}(.)$ simplifies to

$$ \log \varphi_{\varepsilon}(u) = -\sigma|u|\Big( 1 + i\beta(\operatorname{sign} u) \frac{2}{\pi} \log|u| \Big) + im u $$

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: $\alpha$-stable MAR
SLIDE: Numerical evaluation of Stable distributions
CONTENU:
- Using the inverse Fourier transform of $\varphi_{\varepsilon}(.)$, we obtain

$$ f_{\varepsilon}(\alpha,\beta,\sigma,m) = (2\pi)^{-1} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \exp\Big(-is(\varepsilon - m) \Big) \varphi_{\varepsilon}(\sigma s)ds $$
- $f_{\varepsilon}(.)$ has no closed form solution but a numerical evaluation is possible

- $\Rightarrow$ Setting $\sigma = 1$ and $m = 0$ we have

$$ f_{\varepsilon}(\alpha,\beta,1,0) = \pi^{-1} \int_{0}^{\infty} \exp(-s^{\alpha}) \cos \Big(s\varepsilon + \beta \tan \Big( \frac{\pi\alpha}{2} \Big)(s - s^{\alpha})\Big)ds $$

when $\alpha \neq 1$ and

$$ f_{\varepsilon}(\alpha,\beta,1,0) = \pi^{-1} \int_{0}^{\infty} \exp(-s) \cos \Big(s\varepsilon + s\beta\frac{2}{\pi}\log s \Big)ds $$

when $\alpha = 1$

- $\Rightarrow$ Numerical evaluation of these integrals is possible in $R$ and MATLAB

- Remark For any $\sigma>0$ and $m$ we have $f_{\varepsilon}(\alpha,\beta,\sigma,m) = \sigma^{-1}f_{\sigma^{-1}(\varepsilon-m)}(\alpha,\beta,1,0)$

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: $\alpha$-stable MAR
SLIDE: Numerical evaluation of Stable Laws probability density function
CONTENU:
[Figure]

- The tail index $\alpha \in (0,2)$ is such that for $c_{\alpha}>0$ and as $x \to \infty$,

$$ \mathbb{P}(X < -x) \sim c_{\alpha}(1 - \beta)x^{-\alpha} \text{ and } \mathbb{P}(X > x) \sim c_{\alpha}(1 + \beta)x^{-\alpha} $$
- Remark If $X \sim \mathcal{S}(\alpha,\beta,\sigma,m)$ with $\alpha \in (0,2)$, $\mathbb{E}|X|^{s} < \infty$ **if and only if** $s < \alpha$

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: $\alpha$-stable MAR
SLIDE: Domains of attraction of $\alpha$-stable distributions
CONTENU:
**Définition** : For $\mu$ an $\alpha$-stable distribution and $\varepsilon_{t}$ an i.i.d. sequence, we say that $\mathcal{L}(\varepsilon_{1})$ belongs to the domain of attraction of $\mu$, also denoted $\mathcal{L}(\varepsilon_{1}) \in \mathbb{D}_{\alpha}(\mu)$ if for some $x>0$

$$ \mathbb{P}(\varepsilon_{1} > x) \sim x^{-\alpha} L(x) $$

with $L(x)$ is a slowly varying function at infinity and $\alpha \in (0,2)$ and if there exists a constant $c \in [0,1]$ such that

$$ \lim\limits_{x \to \infty} \frac{\mathbb{P}(\varepsilon_{1} > x)}{\mathbb{P}(|\varepsilon_{1}| > x)} = c $$

- Corollary A necessary and sufficient condition for $\mathcal{L}(\varepsilon_{t})$ to belong to $\mathbb{D}_{\alpha}(\mu)$ is

$$ \log |\varphi_{\varepsilon}(s)| \sim -\sigma^{\alpha}|s|^{\alpha}L(1/|s|) \text{ as } s \to 0 $$

where $\varphi_{\varepsilon}(s)$ is the characteristic function of $\varepsilon_{t}$

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
- Remark Slowly varying functions are introduced in Chapter 3 of « Dynamic Econometrics », M2 EIPMC

- Recall that here, « $\sim$ » means that $\log |\varphi_{\varepsilon}(s)|$ is proportional to $-\sigma^{\alpha}|s|^{\alpha}L(1/|s|)$ in the limit $s \to 0$

CONTENU:

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: $\alpha$-stable MAR
SLIDE: Absolute convergence of infinite variance sequences
CONTENU:
**Proposition** : Let $\varepsilon_{t}$ be an i.i.d. sequence such that $\mathcal{L}(\varepsilon_{1}) \in \mathbb{D}_{\alpha}(\mu)$. If $\psi_{j}$ is a sequence of constants such that

$$ \sum_{j = -\infty}^{\infty}|\psi_{j}|^{s}<\infty \text{ for some } s \in (0,\alpha) \cap [0,1] $$

then the infinite series,

$$ \sum_{j = -\infty}^{\infty}\psi_{j}\varepsilon_{t-j} $$

converges absolutely with probability one.

- This proposition due to Cline (1983) establishes **strict stationary** conditions for any MA$(\infty)$ linear sequence with infinite variance

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
- Proof 2.1 We first consider the case $1<\alpha<2$ for which the i.i.d. $\alpha$-stable sequence $\varepsilon_{t}$ satisfies $\mathbb{E}(\varepsilon_{1})<\infty$ altough $\mathbb{E}(\varepsilon_{1}^{2}) = \infty$ and hence, if $\psi_{j}<\infty, \forall j$

$$ \mathbb{E}\Bigg( \sum_{j = -\infty}^{\infty}|\psi_{j}\varepsilon_{t-j}|\Bigg) = \sum_{j = -\infty}^{\infty}|\psi_{j}|\mathbb{E}(|\varepsilon_{t-j}|) = \sum_{j = -\infty}^{\infty}|\psi_{j}|\mathbb{E}(|\varepsilon_{1}|) < \infty $$

thereby proving that $\sum_{j = -\infty}^{\infty}|\psi_{j}\varepsilon_{t-j}|<\infty$ with probability one.

- Proof 2.2 Now suppose that $0<\alpha < 1$ and hence $0 < s < \alpha \leq 1$. By applying the triangular inequality $|x+y|^{s} \leq |x|^{s} + |y|^{s}$ to the MA$(\infty)$ sequence we find that

$$ \mathbb{E}\Bigg( \sum_{j = -\infty}^{\infty}|\psi_{j}\varepsilon_{t-j}|\Bigg)^{s} \leq \mathbb{E}\Bigg( \sum_{j = -\infty}^{\infty}|\psi_{j}|^{s}|\varepsilon_{t-j}|^{s}\Bigg) = \sum_{j = -\infty}^{\infty}|\psi_{j}|^{s}\mathbb{E}(|\varepsilon_{t-j}|^{s}) < \infty $$

thereby proving that $\sum_{j = -\infty}^{\infty}|\psi_{j}\varepsilon_{t-j}|<\infty$ with probability one as long as $s \in (0,\alpha) \cap [0,1]$. This results is due to the fact that $\mathbb{E}(|\varepsilon_{1}|^{s}) = \infty$ if $s \geq \alpha$ and $\mathbb{E}(|\varepsilon_{1}|^{s}) < \infty$ if $s < \alpha$.
slide_title: Absolute convergence of infinite variance sequences

text:
COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: $\alpha$-stable MAR
SLIDE: Absolute convergence of infinite variance sequences
CONTENU:
**Proposition** : Let $\varepsilon_{t}$ be an i.i.d. sequence such that $\mathcal{L}(\varepsilon_{1}) \in \mathbb{D}_{\alpha}(\mu)$. If $\psi_{j}$ is a sequence of constants such that

$$ \sum_{j = -\infty}^{\infty}|\psi_{j}|^{s}<\infty \text{ for some } s \in (0,\alpha) \cap [0,1] $$

then the infinite series,

$$ \sum_{j = -\infty}^{\infty}\psi_{j}\varepsilon_{t-j} $$

converges absolutely with probability one.
slide_title: Absolute convergence of infinite variance sequences

text:
COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)

SLIDE: $\alpha$-stable MA$(\infty)$ process

**Proposition** : Let $\varepsilon_{t}$ and $\check{\varepsilon}_{t}$ be two i.i.d. processes such that

$$ \varepsilon_{t} = \sum_{j = -\infty}^{\infty} \check{\psi}_{j}\check{\varepsilon}_{t-j} $$

where $\mathcal{L}(\varepsilon_{1}) \in \mathbb{D}_{\alpha}(\mu)$ with $\alpha \in (0,2)$. Then, if

$$ \sum_{j = -\infty}^{\infty} |\check{\psi}_{j}|^{s} < \infty \text{ for } s \in (0,\alpha) \cap [0,1] $$

the MA representation is trivial (all except one MA coefficients $\check{\psi}_{j}$ have to be null)

- Gouriéroux and Zakoian (2015) prove Propositions and

- $\Rightarrow$ An $\alpha$-stable MA$(\infty)$ process cannot be i.i.d.

- Remark This result is very important in view of proving the uniqueness of the strong MA representation under of stable laws with $\alpha \in (0,2)$

**Proposition** : Let $\varepsilon_{t}$ and $\check{\varepsilon}_{t}$ be two i.i.d. processes such that

where $\mathcal{L}(\varepsilon_{1}) \in \mathbb{D}_{\alpha}(\mu)$ with $\alpha \in (0,2)$ and

Now suppose that $\check{\psi}(B)$ is invertible with

$$ \check{\psi}(B) ^{-1} = \sum_{j = -\infty}^{\infty} \tilde{\psi}_{j}B^{j} \text{ such that } \sum_{j = -\infty}^{\infty} |\tilde{\psi}_{j}|^{s} < \infty $$

Then, for some constants $c \in \mathbb{R}$ and $l \in \mathbb{Z}$, $\varepsilon_{t} = c\check{\varepsilon}_{t-l}$ and $\psi_{j} = \frac{1}{c} \check{\psi}_{j+l}$

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: $\alpha$-stable MAR
SLIDE: Stable Noncausal AR$(1)$ and unconditional stationary distribution
CONTENU:
- Let $X_{t}$ be a **stable** strong noncausal AR$(1)$

$$ X_{t} = \varphi X_{t+1} + \varepsilon_{t}, \;\;\; |\varphi| < 1, \;\;\; \varepsilon_{t} \sim \mathcal{S}(\alpha,\beta,\sigma,0), \;\;\; \alpha \in (0,2) $$
- We know that $X_{t}$ has the following strictly stationary solution

$$ X_{t} = \sum_{j = 0}^{\infty} \varphi^{j}\varepsilon_{t+j} $$

and we can now compute the unconditional **stable** distribution of $X_{t}$

$$\begin{aligned}
X_{t} & \sim \mathcal{S}\Big(\alpha,\beta,\frac{\sigma}{(1 - |\varphi|^{\alpha})^{1/\alpha}},0\Big), \text{ if } \alpha \neq 1 \text{ and } \varphi \geq 0 \\
X_{t} & \sim \mathcal{S}\Big(\alpha,\beta\frac{1 - |\varphi|^{\alpha}}{1 + |\varphi|^{\alpha}},\frac{\sigma}{(1 - |\varphi|^{\alpha})^{1/\alpha}},0\Big), \text{ if } \alpha \neq 1 \text{ and } \varphi \leq 0\\
X_{t} & \sim \mathcal{S}\Big(1,\beta\frac{1 - |\varphi|}{1 + |\varphi|},\frac{\sigma}{1 - |\varphi|},-\beta\sigma\frac{2}{\pi}\frac{\varphi \log |\varphi|}{(1-\varphi)^{2}}\Big), \text{ if } \alpha = 1
\end{aligned}$$

and state that $\mathbb{E}(|X_{t}|^{u}) < \infty \text{ if and only if } \ntxt{u} < \alpha$

- Remark When $\varphi \leq 0$, $X_{t}$ is **less asymmetric** than $\varepsilon_{t}$ because $\varphi$ affects $\beta$
slide_title: Stable Noncausal AR$(1)$ and unconditional stationary distribution

text:
COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: $\alpha$-stable MAR
SLIDE: Stable Noncausal AR$(1)$ and conditional moments
CONTENU:
- Let $X_{t}$ be a strong **stable** noncausal AR$(1)$

$$ X_{t} = \varphi X_{t+1} + \varepsilon_{t}, \;\;\; |\varphi| < 1, \;\;\; \varepsilon_{t} \sim \mathcal{S}(\alpha,\beta,\sigma,0), \;\;\; \alpha \in (0,2) $$
- Gouriéroux & Zakoian (2017): for the backward conditional density

$$ \mathbb{E}(|X_{t}|^{b}|X_{t+1}) < \infty \text{ iff } \mtxt{b} < \alpha $$
- Gouriéroux & Zakoian (2017): for the forward conditional density

$$ \mathbb{E}(|X_{t+h}|^{c}|X_{t-1}) < \infty, \; a.s., \text{ iff } \btxt{c} < 2\alpha + 1, \;\;\; \alpha \in (0,2), $$

for any $h \geq 0$ and $\beta \neq 1$, or $|\beta| = 1$ if $\varphi^{h+1} < 0$. If $\beta \neq 1$ and $\varphi^{h+1} > 0$

$$ \mathbb{E}(|X_{t+h}|^{c}|X_{t-1}) < \infty \; a.s. \; \forall \btxt{c} > -1 $$
- $X_{t}$ is also a causal homogeneous Markov process as
$$ \mathcal{L}(X_{t}|X_{t-1},X_{t-2},\ldots) = \mathcal{L}(X_{t}|X_{t-1}) $$
- Remark The number of finite forward conditional moments is $\btxt{c} > (\mtxt{b} = \ntxt{u})$
slide_title: Stable Noncausal AR$(1)$ and conditional moments

text:
COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: $\alpha$-stable MAR
SLIDE: Stable Noncausal AR$(1)$ and forward conditional expectation
CONTENU:
- The forward (causal) conditional expectation always exists...

- ... but the unconditional and backward (noncausal) conditional expectations exist only if $\alpha > 1$

- Gouriéroux & Zakoian (2017) : if $\beta = 0$ (symmetric stable laws : S$\alpha$S)

$$ \mathbb{E}(X_{t+h}|X_{t-1}) = |\varphi|^{(h+1)(\alpha - 1)}X_{t-1} , \;\;\; \forall h \geq 0, \;\;\; \alpha \in (0,2), $$

with $|\varphi|^{0} = \operatorname{sign}(\varphi)$ so that in the Cauchy case ($\alpha = 1$)

$$ \mathbb{E}(X_{t+h}|X_{t-1}) = \operatorname{sign}(\varphi)X_{t-1} , \;\;\; \forall h \geq 0 $$

and when $\varphi > 0$, $X_{t}$ behaves as a **stationary martingale !**

- Remark when $\varphi > 0$ and $\alpha \in (0,1)$, $X_{t}$ is a **stationary submartingale**

- Fries & Zakoian (2019) : if $\alpha \in (0,2)$ and $\beta \in (-1,1)$

$$ \mathbb{E}(X_{t+h}|X_{t-1}) = |\varphi|^{(h+1)(\alpha - 1)}X_{t-1} - \mathds{1}_{\alpha = 1} (h+1)\frac{2}{\pi}\beta\sigma\frac{\varphi\log \varphi}{1 - \varphi} , \;\;\; \forall h \geq 0 $$

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
- In the Cauchy case, the process has a unit-root if $\varphi > 0$ although $X_{t}$ is stationary : stationary martingale

- A submartingale satisfies $\mathbb{E}(X_{t+h}|X_{t-1}) \geq X_{t-1}$ and hence $X_{t}$ is a submartingale if $\alpha \in (0,1)$ because $|\varphi| < 1$ and

$$ |\varphi|^{(h+1)(\alpha - 1)}X_{t-1} \geq X_{t-1} , \;\;\; \forall h \geq 0 $$
slide_title: Stable Noncausal AR$(1)$ and forward conditional expectation

text:
COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: $\alpha$-stable MAR
SLIDE: Cauchy Noncausal AR$(1)$ and forward conditional moments
CONTENU:
- Let $X_{t}$ be a strong **Cauchy** noncausal AR$(1)$

- Gouriéroux & Zakoian (2017) : the causal predictive density is

$$ f_{X}(X_{t}|X_{t-h}) = \frac{1}{\sigma_{h}\pi} \frac{\sigma_{h}^{-2}}{(X_{t-h} - \varphi^{h}X_{t})^{2}} \frac{\sigma^{2} + (1 - |\varphi|)^{2}X_{t-h}^{2}}{\sigma^{2} + (1 - |\varphi|)^{2}X_{t}^{2}}, \sigma_{h} = \frac{1 - |\varphi|^{h}}{1 - |\varphi|} $$
- $\Rightarrow$ the second order conditional moment is heteroscedastic

$$ \mathbb{E}(X_{t}^{2}|X_{t-1}) = \frac{1}{|\varphi|}X_{t-1}^{2} + \frac{\sigma^{2}}{|\varphi|(1 - |\varphi|)} $$
- $\Rightarrow$ $X_{t}$ admits a **semi-strong** representation (à la Drost & Nijman, 1993)

$$\begin{aligned}
X_{t} & = \operatorname{sign}(\varphi)X_{t-1} + \tilde{\varepsilon}_{t} \text{ where } \tilde{\varepsilon}_{t} = \varsigma_{t}\tilde{\eta}_{t} \\
\varsigma_{t}^{2} & = \big(|\varphi|^{-1} - 1 \big)X_{t-1}^{2} + \frac{\sigma^{2}}{|\varphi|(1 - |\varphi|)}
\end{aligned}$$

where $\mathbb{E}(\tilde{\eta}_{t} | X_{t-1}) = 0$, $\mathbb{E}(\tilde{\eta}_{t}^{2} | X_{t-1}) = 1$ and $\tilde{\eta}_{t}$ is a Weak White Noise

- Remark $X_{t} =$ unit-root (if $\varphi > 0$) + ARCH (based on $X_{t-1}^{2}$ rather than $\tilde{\varepsilon}_{t-1}^{2}$)

- Fries & Zakoian (2019) extend these results to the Cauchy MAR$(p,q)$

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
Drost & Nijman, 1993 define 3 types of GARCH

- The strong GARCH where $\tilde{\eta}_{t}$ is a Strong White Noise

- The semi-strong GARCH where $\tilde{\eta}_{t}$ is a Weak White Noise

- The weak GARCH where only prejections of the conditional variance are considered

- Technically, the semi-strong representation does not exhibit an ARCH but a double-AR$(1)$ model à la Ling & Li, 2008 because the heteroscedastic component is based on $X_{t-1}^{2}$ rather than $\tilde{\varepsilon}_{t-1}^{2}$

- $\Rightarrow$ this model is new and should be termed « semi-strong double-AR$(1)$ »
slide_title: Cauchy Noncausal AR$(1)$ and forward conditional moments

text:
COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: $\alpha$-stable MAR
SLIDE: Strong causal representation for the Cauchy Noncausal AR$(1)$
CONTENU:
- As mentioned in , a **weak causal** representation exists...

- ... but, it is also possible to derive a **strong causal** representation

- Use some Gaussian innovations given by $\varepsilon_{t}^{*} = \Phi^{-1}\big(F(X_{t}|X_{t-1})\big)$ with

- ... $\Phi^{-1}(.)$ the Normal c.d.f. and $F(X_{t}|X_{t-1})$ the conditional c.d.f. of $X_{t}$ :

$$\begin{aligned}
F(X_{t}|X_{t-1}) & = \frac{\Lambda}{\pi}\log\Bigg( \frac{1 + (1 - |\varphi|)^{2}X_{t}^{2}}{1 + (X_{t-1} - \varphi X_{t})^{2}} \frac{\check{\varphi}^{2}}{(1 - |\varphi|)^{2}}\Bigg)\\
& + \frac{\Upsilon}{\pi}\Bigg( \frac{\pi}{2} - \operatorname{sign}(\varphi)\tan^{-1}(X_{t-1} - \varphi X_{t})\Bigg) + \frac{1 - \Upsilon}{\pi}\Bigg( \tan^{-1}((1 - |\varphi|)X_{t}) + \frac{\pi}{2} \Bigg) \\
\Lambda & = \frac{\varphi(1 - |\varphi|)^{2}X_{t-1}}{(1 - 2|\varphi|)^{2} + (1 - |\varphi|)^{2}X_{t-1}^{2}} \text{ and } \Upsilon = \frac{|\varphi|\big((1 - |\varphi|)^{2}X_{t-1}^{2} - (1 - 2|\varphi|)\big)}{(1 - 2|\varphi|)^{2} + (1 - |\varphi|)^{2}X_{t-1}^{2}}
\end{aligned}$$

- Inverting the relation $\varepsilon_{t}^{*} = \Phi^{-1}\big(F(X_{t}|X_{t-1})\big)$, one can derive

$$ X_{t} = G(X_{t-1},\varepsilon_{t}^{*}),\;\;\; G(X_{t-1},.) = F^{-1}\big(\Phi(.)|X_{t-1} \big),\;\;\; \varepsilon_{t}^{*} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1) $$
- $\Rightarrow$ the **strong causal** AR$(1)$ representation is highly **nonlinear**

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
Remind that if the c.d.f. of $X_{t}$ is $F(.)$, $F(X) \sim \mathcal{U}(0,1)$ and hence $\Phi^{-1}(F(X)) \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})$
slide_title: Strong causal representation for the Cauchy Noncausal AR$(1)$

text:
COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: $\alpha$-stable MAR
SLIDE: The Lévy Noncausal AR$(1)$
CONTENU:
- Let $X_{t}$ be a strong **Lévy** noncausal AR$(1)$

$$ X_{t} = \varphi X_{t+1} + \varepsilon_{t}, \;\;\; 0< \varphi < 1, \;\;\; \varepsilon_{t} \sim \mathcal{S}(1/2,1,\sigma,0), \;\;\; \alpha \in (0,2) $$
- As for the Cauchy case, Gouriéroux & Zakoian (2017) prove that

- $X_{t}$ has a causal predictive density given by

$$\begin{aligned}
f_{X}(X_{t}|X_{t-1}) & = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\Bigg( \frac{X_{t-1}}{X_{t}(X_{t-1} - \varphi X_{t} )} \Bigg)^{3/2} \\
& \times \exp\Bigg( \frac{-(X_{t-1} - \sqrt{\varphi} X_{t})}{2X_{t-1}X_{t}(1-\sqrt{\varphi})^{2}(X_{t-1} - \varphi X_{t})} \Bigg)\mathds{1}_{0< \varphi X_{t}< X_{t-1}}
\end{aligned}$$
- $\Rightarrow$ All the causal forward conditional moments exist whereas even the unconditional first moment does not

- $X_{t}$ admits an ARCH type (probably) **semi-strong** representation

$$ X_{t} = \varphi^{-1/2}X_{t-1} + \tilde{\varepsilon}_{t}, \;\;\; \mathbb{E}(\tilde{\varepsilon}_{t} | X_{t-1}) = 0 $$

albeit the form of $\tilde{\varepsilon}_{t}$ is tedious to derive

- The strong causal (non-linear) representation $X_{t}$ is untracktable

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
$\varphi > 0$ to ensure the positivity of the strictly stationary Lévy AR$(1)$ process $X_{t}$

CONTENU:

text:
COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: $\alpha$-stable MAR
SLIDE: Prediction of linear causal processes with infinite variance
CONTENU:
- The result in P can be generalized to the non-Gaussian $L^{2}$ framework

$$ \arg\min_{\mathcal{P}(X_{t+h})} \mathbb{E}\Big( (X_{t+h} - \mathcal{P}(X_{t+h}))^{2} \Big) = \mathbb{EL}(X_{t+h}|\mathscr{F}_{t-1}) $$

where $\mathcal{P}(X_{t+h})$ is a predictor of $X_{t+h}$ and $\mathscr{F}_{t} = X_{t},\ldots,X_{1}$

- Cline & Brockwell (1985) deal with the causal symmetric $\alpha$-stable case

- $\Rightarrow$ the best predictor cannot be defined in a mean square sense... however

$$ \arg\min_{\mathcal{P}(X_{t+h})} \mathbb{E}\Big( |X_{t+h} - \mathcal{P}(X_{t+h})|^{\alpha} \Big) =\mathbb{PL}(X_{t+h}|\mathscr{F}_{t-1}) $$

where $\mathbb{PL}(.)$ is a linear projection defined by the **minimum dispersion**

- If $\alpha \in (1,2]$, the $\mathbb{PL}(.)$ is unique and $\mathbb{EL}(X_{t+h}|\mathscr{F}_{t-1}) = \mathbb{PL}(X_{t+h}|\mathscr{F}_{t-1})$

- If $\alpha \in (0,1]$, the $\mathbb{PL}(.)$ is not unique
slide_title: Prediction of linear causal processes with infinite variance

text:
COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: $\alpha$-stable MAR
SLIDE: Prediction of linear stable non-causal processes
CONTENU:
- In the non-causal $L^{2}$ framework the optimal predictor is more tricky

- $\Rightarrow$ $\mathbb{E}(X_{n+h}|\mathscr{F}_{t-1})$ is generally a non-linear function of the observed values

- We know that $\mathbb{E}(|X_{t}|^{b}|X_{t+1}) < \infty$ only for $b<\alpha$

- $\Rightarrow$ fortunately, $\mathbb{E}(|X_{t+h}|^{c}|\mathscr{F}_{t-1}) < \infty$ for $c<2\alpha+1$ so that

$$ \mathbb{E}(X_{t+h}|\mathscr{F}_{t-1}) < \infty \;\;\; \forall \alpha \in (0,2) $$
- For some specific non-causal models we have a closed form expression :

- strong non-causal AR$(1)$ with stable errors for $\forall h \geq 0$:

$$ \mathbb{E}(X_{t+h}|X_{t-1}) = |\varphi|^{(h+1)(\alpha - 1)}X_{t-1} - \mathds{1}_{\alpha = 1} (h+1)\frac{2}{\pi}\beta\sigma\frac{\log \varphi}{1 - \varphi} $$
- strong S$\alpha$S mixed-causal MAR$(1,1)$ for $\forall h \geq 0$:

$$ \mathbb{E}(X_{t+h}|\mathscr{F}_{t-1}) = (\varphi^{\bullet})^{h+1}\Bigg( X_{t-1} + (X_{t-1} - \varphi^{\bullet}X_{t-2}) \sum_{j=1}^{h+1}(\varphi^{<\alpha-1>}\varphi^{\bullet})^{-j}\Bigg) $$

where $\varphi^{<x>} =\operatorname{sign}(\varphi^{\circ})|\varphi^{\circ}|^{x}$ (see Fries & Zakoian, 2019 for the MAR$(1,q)$)
slide_title: Prediction of linear stable non-causal processes

text:
COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: $\alpha$-stable MAR
SLIDE: Bubble prediction in stable non-causal processes
CONTENU:
- Consider $X_{t} = \varphi X_{t+1} + \varepsilon_{t}$, $\varepsilon_{t} \sim \mathcal{S}(\alpha,0,\sigma,0)$ and $\varphi \in (0,1)$

- $\Rightarrow$ multiple bubbles are likely to occur for large values of $\varepsilon_{t}$

- Remark $\mathbb{E}(X_{t+h}|X_{t-1}) = |\varphi|^{(h+1)(\alpha - 1)}X_{t-1}$ always predicts an exponential decay to the central values at rate $\varphi^{\alpha-1}$

- $\Rightarrow$ $\mathbb{E}(X_{t+h}|X_{t-1})$ describes paths that depart from the realized trajectory

- If the predictive density is known, once estimated, one can compute

$$ \mathbb{P}(X_{t+h} - \varphi X_{t+h+1} > c |X_{t}), $$

the probability of bubble collapse at $t+h$ for some critical level $c$

- $\Rightarrow$ As the predictive density is generally unknown Gouriéroux & Jasiak (2016) suggest a non-parametric approach

- $\Rightarrow$ Fries (2022) investigates higher moments through the joint density of $(X_{t+h},X_{t})$
slide_title: Bubble prediction in stable non-causal processes

text:
COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: $\alpha$-stable MAR
SLIDE: Fries (2022) : $\alpha$-stable random vectors and spectral measure
CONTENU:
- Samorodnitsky and Taqqu (1991) show that S$\alpha$S random vectors $\bm{X}$ are defined by a unique pair $(\bm{\Gamma},\bm{\mu})$ such that $\forall \bm{u} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$ and $s_{1},\ldots,s_{d} \in \bm{s}$

$$ \varphi_{\bm{X}}(\bm{u}) = \exp \Bigg(- \int_{S_{d}} |\langle \bm{u},\bm{s}\rangle|^{\alpha}\Big( 1 - i(\operatorname{sign} \langle \bm{u},\bm{s}\rangle) \omega(\alpha,\langle \bm{u},\bm{s}\rangle) \Big)\bm{\Gamma}(d\bm{s}) + i \langle \bm{s},\bm{\mu}\rangle \Bigg) $$

is the characteristic function of $\bm{X}$ with $\langle .,.\rangle$ the scalar product,

$$ \omega(\alpha,x) := \tan \bigg( \frac{\pi\alpha}{2} \bigg) \text{ if } \alpha \neq 1 \text{ and } \omega(1,x) := -\frac{2}{\pi}\log|x| $$

and $\bm{\Gamma}$ a spectral measure on the unit sphere $S_{d}$ and $\bm{\mu}^{0} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$

- $\bm{\Gamma} :=$ scale, asymmetry and dependence between $X_{(1)},\ldots,X_{(d)} \in \bm{X}$ and $\bm{\mu}$ is a non-random shift vector

- Results For some $\nu\geq 0$, $\mathbb{E}\Big(X_{(2)}^{\gamma}|X_{(1)}\Big) < \infty$ if

$$ \int_{S_{2}}|s_{1}|^{-\nu}\bm{\Gamma}(d\bm{s})<\infty \text{ and } \gamma < \min(\alpha+\nu,2\alpha+1) $$

so that if $\alpha > 3/2$ and $\nu \geq 4 - \alpha$, the fourth moment exists
slide_title: Fries (2022) : $\alpha$-stable random vectors and spectral measure

text:
COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: $\alpha$-stable MAR
SLIDE: Fries (2022) : non-causal $\alpha$-stable AR$(1)$ process and spectral measure
CONTENU:
- Fries (2022) shows that for $X_{t}$ a non-causal $\alpha$-stable AR$(1)$ process...

- ... $\bm{X}_{t} = (X_{t},X_{t+h})$ is $\alpha$-stable and has a spectral measure

$$\begin{aligned}
\bm{\Gamma}_{h} & = \frac{\bar{\sigma}^{\alpha}}{2}\sum_{\vartheta\in S_{1}}\Bigg(\Big( 1 - |\varphi|^{\alpha h} + 1 - (\varphi^{<\alpha>})^{h}\vartheta\bar{\beta}\Big)\delta(\vartheta,0)\Bigg.\\
& \Bigg. +\Big(1 + |\varphi|^{2h} \Big)^{\alpha/2} (1+\vartheta\bar{\beta})\delta(\vartheta_{\bm{s}_{h}})\Bigg)
\end{aligned}$$

with $\delta(x)$ the Dirac measure at $x \in \mathbb{R}$, $S_{1} = \{-1,+1\}$,

$$ \bar{\sigma}^{\alpha} = \frac{\sigma^{\alpha}}{1 - |\varphi|^{\alpha}} \text{ and } \bar{\beta} = \beta\frac{1 - |\varphi|^{\alpha}}{1 - |\varphi|^{<\alpha>}} $$

and finally $\bm{s}_{h} = (\varphi^{h},1)/\sqrt{1 + |\varphi|^{2h}} \in S_{2}$

- The analytical form of $\bm{\Gamma}_{h}$ allows to compute $\mathbb{E}\Big(X_{t+h}^{\gamma}|X_{h}\Big)$

- $\Rightarrow$ see Fries (2018) for the moments $\gamma = 1,\ldots,4$

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
$\bm{\Gamma}_{h}$ is discrete and concentrated on at most four points of the unit disk $(\pm 1,0)$ and $\pm(\varphi^{h},1)/\sqrt{1 + |\varphi|^{2h}}$. It collapses on exactly two points when $\varphi>0$ and $\beta = 1$ that is, when the marginal distribution of $X_t$ is totally skewed to the right. In particular, for any fixed $h\geq 1$, it is always charging zero mass to neighbourhoods close enough to the points $(0,\pm 1)$ which lead to the existence of the conditional moments and allows to compute them.

Ajouter exemple thèse de Sébastien p. 181-182. En fait Sébastien montre qu'on va vite être bloqué avec l'approche Taqqu car la mesure est implicitement définie sur une norme euclidienne (sphère unité) de $\bm{X}_{t}$. Plus précisément, la mesure spectrale décrit la distribution conditionnelle des trajectoires normalisées $\bm{X}_{t}/||\bm{X}_{t}||_{e}$. Le conditionnement comprend donc des valeurs inobservées $X_{t+h}$... Il propose donc de reconstruire une nouvelle mesure spectrale basée sur une semi-norme du type $||(X_{t},X_{t+h})|| = ||(X_{t},0)||$. Cette semi-norme déplace la mesure spectrale dans un cylindre unité pour lequel tous les processus n'admettent pas de représentation. Il est intéressant de voir que seuls les processus suffisamment anticipations (non-causaux admettent une représentation dans cette semi-norm). Dommage qu'on ait pas le temps de détailler ces résultats qui sont hélas très techniques... mais les doctorants intéressés peuvent voir le papier de Sébastien : Path prediction of aggregated $\alpha$-stable moving averagesusing semi-norm representations.
slide_title: Fries (2022) : non-causal $\alpha$-stable AR$(1)$ process and spectral measure

text:
COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: $\alpha$-stable MAR
SLIDE: Fries (2022) : non-causal $\alpha$-stable AR$(1)$ process and bubble behavior
CONTENU:
- Fries (2022) investigates how the standardized conditional moments

$$ m_{\gamma}(x) = \mathbb{E}\Big(X_{t+h}^{\gamma}|X_{t} = x \Big) $$

behave during a bubble driven by large values (i.e. as $x \to \infty$) for $\varphi > 0$

$$\begin{aligned}
m_{1}(x) & \sim (\varphi^{-h}x)\varphi^{\alpha h}, \;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\; \text{if } \alpha \in (0,2) \\
m_{2}(x) & \sim (\varphi^{-h}x)\varphi^{\alpha h}(1-\varphi^{\alpha h}), \;\;\; \text{if } \alpha \in (1/2,2) \\
m_{3}(x) & \to \frac{1 - 2\varphi^{\alpha h}}{\sqrt{\varphi^{\alpha h}(1 - \varphi^{\alpha h})}}, \;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\; \text{if } \alpha \in (1,2) \\
m_{4}(x) & \to \frac{1 - 6\varphi^{\alpha h}}{\varphi^{\alpha h}}, \;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\; \text{if } \alpha \in (3/2,2)
\end{aligned}$$
- These are the moments of a **weighted Bernoulli distribution** !

- charging probability $\varphi^{\alpha h}$ to the weight $\varphi^{-h}x$ ...

- ... and probability $1 - \varphi^{\alpha h}$ to the value 0

- $\Rightarrow$ $\varphi^{\alpha h} :=$ probability that the bubble survives at least $h$ more time periods

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
The unintuitive conditional expectation of the non-causal S$\alpha$S AR$(1)$

$$ \mathbb{E}\Big(X_{t+h}|X_{t} = x \Big) = \varphi^{h(\alpha - 1)}x $$

is barely yielding the probabilistic middle ground between two polarly-opposite paths: continued explosion or collapse.
slide_title: Fries (2022) : non-causal $\alpha$-stable AR$(1)$ process and bubble behavior

text:
COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: $\alpha$-stable MAR
SLIDE: Limitations of the Spherical Representation
CONTENU:
- de Truchis, Fries & Thomas (2025) suggest to extend this approach by considering

$$ \bm{X}_t = (X_{t-m}, \ldots, X_t, \ntxt{X_{t+1}, \ldots, X_{t+h}}) $$

where $X_{t}$ is defined as a general $\alpha$-stable infinite moving average

- Samorodnitsky & Taqqu (1991) defines the spectral measure $\bm{\Gamma}$ on the **unit sphere** $S_{m+1+h}$

- $\Rightarrow$ This representation is based on a **norm** (e.g., Euclidean) of the full trajectory vector $\bm{X}_t$

- Problem for prediction !

- $\Rightarrow$ the conditioning event, $||\bm{X}_t||_e > x$, **is not observable** at time $t$ as it contains $h$ future values

- de Truchis, Fries & Thomas (2025) propose a new representation theory to solve this

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: $\alpha$-stable MAR
SLIDE: de Truchis, Fries & Thomas (2025): Seminorm Representation
CONTENU:
- The key idea: replace the *norm* with a *seminorm* $||\cdot||$ that **only depends on the observed past**.

- The seminorm is defined to ignore all future components

$$ ||(x_{-m}, \ldots, x_0, \ntxt{x_1, \ldots, x_h})|| := ||(x_{-m}, \ldots, x_0, \ntxt{0, \ldots, 0})|| $$
- $\Rightarrow$ the **unit sphere** $S_{m+1+h}$ is forced to become a **unit cylinder** $C_{m+1+h}^{\|\cdot\|}$

- Fundamental result: not all processes admit such a representation as process is representable on this cylinder **if and only if** it is « anticipative enough »

- $\Rightarrow$ **Purely causal processes** are **non-representable** in this framework.

- $\Rightarrow$ This theory directly links **anticipativeness** to the **predictability** of extreme events.
slide_title: de Truchis, Fries & Thomas (2025): Seminorm Representation

text:
COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: $\alpha$-stable MAR
SLIDE: de Truchis, Fries & Thomas (2025): Prediction Framework
CONTENU:
- The prediction problem becomes

- finding the future, path defined by a Borel set $\ntxt{A}$ on the cylinder, that matches a known pattern
- given an extreme past trajectory, let say the Borel $\btxt{V}\subset S_{m+1}^{\|\cdot\|}$, that defines $\btxt{B(V)} = V \times \mathbb{R}^{h}$

- The limite behavior of $\boldsymbol{X}_{t} / \|\boldsymbol{X}_{t}\|$ reveals the discrete nature of the tail distribution

$$ \lim_{x \to \infty} \mathbb{P}\left(\frac{\boldsymbol{X}_{t}}{\|\boldsymbol{X}_{t}\|} \in \ntxt{A} \,\Bigg|\, \btxt{\|\boldsymbol{X}_{t}\| > x}, \, \frac{\boldsymbol{X}_{t}}{\|\boldsymbol{X}_{t}\|} \in \btxt{B(V)}\right) = \frac{\Gamma^{\|\cdot\|}(A \cap B(V))}{\Gamma^{\|\cdot\|}(B(V))} $$

where

- $\btxt{\|\boldsymbol{X}_{t}\| > x}$ $\Rightarrow$ The **observed past** is extreme.
- $\btxt{B(V)}$ $\Rightarrow$ The **shape** of the observed past matches pattern $V$.
- $\ntxt{A}$ $\Rightarrow$ The (unobserved) **future path** we are forecasting.

- $\Rightarrow$ For anticipative AR($p \geq 2$), the tail distribution degenerate to a single Dirac masses.

- $\Rightarrow$ If the past pattern is identified, the future path becomes **asymptotically deterministic**.
slide_title: de Truchis, Fries & Thomas (2025): Prediction Framework

text:
COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Simulation of MAR
SLIDE: Gouriéroux & Jasiak (2016) : partial fraction representation
CONTENU:
- Let $X_{t}$ be a strong MAR$(1,1)$ process

$$ (1 - \varphi^{\circ} F)( 1 - \varphi^{\bullet}B) X_{t} = \Phi^{\circ}(F)\Phi^{\bullet}(B)X_{t} = \varepsilon_{t}, \;\;\; |\varphi^{\circ}| < 1, \;\;\; |\varphi^{\bullet}| < 1 $$
- Gouriéroux and Jasiak (2016) suggest a partial decomposition of $\varepsilon_{t}$

$$ \varepsilon_{t} = \Phi^{\circ}(F)u_{t} = \Phi^{\bullet}(B)v_{t} $$

where $u_{t} = \Phi^{\bullet}(B)X_{t}$ and $v_{t} = \Phi^{\circ}(F)X_{t}$ hence leading to

$$\begin{aligned}
X_{t} & = \frac{1}{1 - \varphi^{\bullet}\varphi^{\circ}}\Bigg( \frac{1}{1 - \varphi^{\circ}F} + \frac{\varphi^{\bullet}L}{1 - \varphi^{\bullet}L}\Bigg)\varepsilon_{t} \\
& = \frac{1}{1 - \varphi^{\bullet}\varphi^{\circ}}\Big( \varphi^{\circ}u_{t+1} + v_{t} \Big) \\
& = \frac{1}{1 - \varphi^{\bullet}\varphi^{\circ}}\Big( u_{t} + \varphi^{\bullet}v_{t-1} \Big)
\end{aligned}$$

where $v_{t}$ and $u_{t}$ are the causal and noncausal components of $\varepsilon_{t}$

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Simulation of MAR
SLIDE: Beyond partial fraction decomposition
CONTENU:
- The approach of Gouriéroux & Jasiak (2016) is general...

- $\Rightarrow$ ...but analytical solutions are complex and essentially known only for the MAR(1,1) case

- For higher orders $(p,q)$, usual methods rely on **recursive** algorithms

- Problem: these methods introduce a systematic **truncation bias** by approximating the infinite sum

- de Truchis & Thomas (2025) propose an **exact** analytical solution for MAR$(p,q)$

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Simulation of MAR
SLIDE: **Exact** analytical solution
CONTENU:
- We use the MA($\infty$) representation under the strict stationarity assumption:

$$ X_t = [\varphi^{\circ}(F)\varphi^{\bullet}(B)]^{-1}\varepsilon_t = \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} \delta_k \varepsilon_{t+k} $$
- By the fundamental theorem of algebra, we have $\varphi^{\bullet}(B) = \prod_{i=1}^q (1 - \lambda_i B)$ and $\varphi^{\circ}(F) = \prod_{j=1}^p (1 - \zeta_j F)$.

- de Truchis & Thomas (2025) obtain via the contour integral method:

- Future coefficients (non-causal, $k > 0$):

$$ \delta_k = \sum_{j=1}^p \frac{\zeta_j^{(p-1)+k}}{\prod_{m \neq j}^p (\zeta_j - \zeta_m) \cdot \prod_{i=1}^q (\lambda_i \zeta_j - 1)} \cdot (-1)^{q} $$
- Past coefficients (causal, $k \leq 0$):

$$ \delta_k = \sum_{i=1}^q \frac{\lambda_i^{(q-1) + |k|}}{\prod_{l \neq i}^q (\lambda_i - \lambda_l) \cdot \prod_{j=1}^p (\lambda_i \zeta_j - 1)} \cdot (-1)^{p} $$

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Simulation of MAR
SLIDE: Simulation (exact)
CONTENU:
- **Step 1: Coefficient computation**

- Use the exact formulas to compute the $\delta_k$ for $k \in [-m, m]$.

- $m$ is chosen large enough so that $\delta_k \approx 0$ if $|k| > m$.

- **Step 2: Innovation generation**

- Simulate a long path of i.i.d.
innovations $\varepsilon_t$ (e.g., $\alpha$-stable $S(\alpha, \beta, \sigma, 0)$ or Student's $t$).

- **Step 3: Simulation (Convolution)**

- Compute $x_t$ by direct convolution (a simple finite MA filter):

$$ x_t = \sum_{k=-m}^{m} \delta_k \varepsilon_{t+k} $$
- Remarks:

- $\Rightarrow$ Avoids the recursive approximation of the $u_t$ and $v_t$ components.

- $\Rightarrow$ Eliminates the systematic truncation bias of recursive methods.

- $\Rightarrow$ The $\delta_k$ coefficients are also the basis for new **forecasting** methods ("pattern-based forecasting").

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Simulation of MAR
SLIDE: Simulation of noncausal AR$(1)$ processes
CONTENU:
- In all cases, $\varphi = 0.8$ / the bottom-right case is $\varepsilon_{t} \sim \mathcal{S}(1.8,0,0.01,0)$

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Estimation of MAR
SLIDE: Incomplete literature review
CONTENU:
- **Ordinary Least Squares** : Davis and Resnick (1986)

- Distribution assumptions : very general and mild

- Limit theory : depends on distribution parameters ($\alpha$ if $\varepsilon_{t}$ is $\alpha$-stable)

- Other : simple but cannot identify the causal and noncausal components

- Stable Maximum Likelihood : Andrews et al. (2009)

- Limit theory : converges $n^{1/\alpha}$ if $\varepsilon_{t}$ is $\alpha$-stable

- Other : computationally cumbersome

- **Least Absolute Deviation** : Davis and Wu (2010)

- Limit theory : locally Gaussian and converges $n^{1/2}$ if $\varepsilon_{t}$ is Laplacian

- Other : simple but sensitive to causal and noncausal misspecification

- Semi-parametric log-concave projected MLE : Davis and Zhang (2017)

- Powerful and very general albeit tedious to implement

- Frequency domain Minimum Distance : Lobato and Velasco (2018), Velasco (2022)

- Powerful and general albeit requiring higher moments to exist

- **Generalized Covariance (GCov)** : Gourieroux and Jasiak (2023)

- Powerful and general albeit requiring higher moments to exist

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Estimation of MAR
SLIDE: Autocorrelation of strong noncausal AR$(p)$
CONTENU:
- Assumed that $\varepsilon_{t}$ in $X_{t} = \sum^{\infty}_{j = -\infty} \psi_{j} \varepsilon_{t - j}$ has Pareto-like tail

$$ \mathbb{P}(|\varepsilon_{t}| > x) = x^{-\alpha}L(x) \text{ and } \sum |\psi_{j}|^{s} < \infty, \text{ for } s \in (0,\alpha) \cap [0,1] $$
- $\Rightarrow$ $X_{t}$ is stationary and $\varepsilon_{t}$ enters the domain of attraction of $\alpha$-stable laws

- Davis and Resnick (1986) investigates the limit theory for sample autocorrelation of strong non-Gaussian linear processes

$$ \hat{\rho}_{n}(h) = \Bigg(\sum_{t =h+1}^{n} X_{t}X_{t-h}\Bigg)\Bigg(\sum_{t =1}^{n}X_{t}^{2}\Bigg)^{-1} $$

and prove that $n^{1/\alpha}\Big(\hat{\rho}_{n}(h) - \rho(h)\Big)\,{\buildrel p \over \longrightarrow}\, 0$ where

$$ \rho(h) = \Bigg(\sum_{j = -\infty}^{\infty}\psi_{j}\psi_{j+h}\Bigg)\Bigg(\sum_{j = -\infty}^{\infty}\psi_{j}^{2}\Bigg)^{-1} $$
- Note that for $h = 1$, $\hat{\rho}_{n}(1)$ is the **OLS estimator** of $\rho(1) = \varphi$

- Remark $\rho(h) \neq$ theoretical autocorrelations of $X_{t}$ as **the latter do not exist**

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
Notice that the quantity
$$ \rho(h) = \Bigg(\sum_{j = -\infty}^{\infty}\psi_{j}\psi_{j+h}\Bigg)\Bigg(\sum_{j = -\infty}^{\infty}\psi_{j}^{2}\Bigg)^{-1} $$
is finite although neither the autocovariance function nor the variance exist. Accordingly, $\rho(h)$ is not the autocorrelation function although it is a real finite quantity

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Estimation of MAR
SLIDE: Limit theory of OLS estimator of strong noncausal AR$(p)$
CONTENU:
- Then, Davis and Resnick (1986) prove that for $h\geq 1$,

$$ \hat{\bm{\rho}}_{n} = \big(\hat{\rho}_{n}(1),\ldots,\hat{\rho}_{n}(h)\big)' \text{ and } \bm{\rho} = \big(\rho(1),\ldots,\rho(h)\big)' $$

the limit distribution of $\hat{\bm{\rho}}_{n}$ is a function of stable variables

$$ \frac{a_{n}^{2}}{b_{n}}(\hat{\bm{\rho}}_{n} - \bm{\rho}) \,{\buildrel d \over \longrightarrow}\, (\zeta_{1},\ldots,\zeta_{h}) $$

with $a_{n} = \inf\{x : \mathbb{P}(|\varepsilon_{1}| > x) \leq n^{-1}\}$, $b_{n} = \inf\{x : \mathbb{P}(|\varepsilon_{1}\varepsilon_{2}| > x) \leq n^{-1}\}$ and

$$ \zeta_{l} = \sum_{j = 1}^{\infty}\big(\rho(j+l) + \rho(l - j) - 2\rho(j)\rho(l)\big) \frac{S_{j}}{S_{0}}, $$

where $S_{j}$ are i.i.d. $\alpha$-stable and $S_{0}$ is positive $\alpha/2$-stable

- If the law of $|\varepsilon_{t}|$ is asymptotically equivalent to a Pareto distribution

$$ \frac{a_{n}^{2}}{b_{n}} \equiv \Bigg(\frac{n}{\log(n)}\Bigg)^{\alpha} $$
- $\Rightarrow$ the limit theory of the OLS estimator $\hat{\varphi}_{n} = \hat{\bm{\rho}}_{n}$ depends on $\alpha$
slide_title: Limit theory of OLS estimator of strong noncausal AR$(p)$

text:
COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Estimation of MAR
SLIDE: Limit theory of OLS estimator of noncausal Cauchy AR$(1)$
CONTENU:
- Let $X_{t}$ be a strong Cauchy AR$(1)$ process

- $\Rightarrow$ Then, the OLS estimator $\hat{\varphi}$ satisfies

$$ \frac{n}{\log(n)}(\hat{\varphi}_{n} - \varphi) \,{\buildrel d \over \longrightarrow}\, (1 + \varphi)S_{1}/S_{0} $$

where $S_{1} \sim \mathcal{C}(0,1)$ and $S_{0} \sim \mathcal{L}(0,1)$ and hence $1/S_{0} \sim \chi^{2}(1)$

- $\Rightarrow$ the Cauchy case is very surprising because

- limit distribution: ratio of standard Cauchy and Chi-squared variables

- $\hat{\varphi}_{n}$ converges faster than $\sqrt{n}$ even if $\mathbb{E}(S_{1}/S_{0}) = \infty$

- Remark As $\mathbb{E}(X_{t}|X_{t-1}) = |\varphi|^{(\alpha - 1)}X_{t-1} = \operatorname{sign}(\varphi)X_{t-1}$ in the Cauchy case, we show that even if $\mathbb{E}(X_{t}|X_{t-1}) \neq \varphi X_{t-1}$, $\hat{\varphi}_{n}$ converges to $\varphi$ !

- $\Rightarrow$ the empirical auto-correlation function reveals serial dependence in reverse time, not in direct time
slide_title: Limit theory of OLS estimator of noncausal Cauchy AR$(1)$

text:
COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Estimation of MAR
SLIDE: Limit theory of OLS estimator of noncausal MAR$(p,q)$
CONTENU:
- Let $X_{t}$ be a strong MAR$(p,q)$ process

$$ \Phi(L)X_{t} = \varphi^{\circ}(F)\varphi^{\bullet}(B) X_{t} = \varepsilon_{t} \text{ with } \mathbb{P}(|\varepsilon_{0}| > x) = x^{-\alpha}L(x) $$

and denote by $\hat{\Phi}_{n}$ the OLS estimator of $\Phi$, the parameters of $\Phi(L)$

- Fries & Zakoian (2018) show that

$$ \frac{a_{n}^{2}}{b_{n}}(\hat{\Phi}_{n} - \Phi) \,{\buildrel d \over \longrightarrow}\, R^{-1}(\bm{\zeta} - \bm{Z} \Phi) $$

with $R = \rho(|i - j|)_{i,j= 1,\ldots,p+q}$, $\bm{\zeta} = (\zeta_{1},\ldots,\zeta_{p+q})$, $\bm{Z} = (\zeta_{i-j})_{i,j= 1,\ldots,p+q}$

$$ \zeta_{l} = \sum_{j = 1}^{\infty}\big(\rho(j+|l|) + \rho(|l| - j) - 2\rho(j)\rho(|l|)\big) \frac{S_{j}}{S_{0}}, $$

and $\zeta_{0} = 0$ where $S_{j}$ are i.i.d. $\alpha$-stable and $S_{0}$ is positive $\alpha/2$-stable

- Remark causal and noncausal parameters are not identifiable in the MAR$(p,q)$
slide_title: Limit theory of OLS estimator of noncausal MAR$(p,q)$

text:
COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Estimation of MAR
SLIDE: Least Absolute Deviation (LAD)
CONTENU:
- The LAD criterion is derived via a likelihood approximation assuming that the underlying noise $\varepsilon_{t}$ is **Laplacian**

$$ f_{\varepsilon} = (2\sigma)^{-1}\exp\big(-|\varepsilon_{t}|\sigma^{-1}\big), \;\;\; \sigma > 0 $$
- $\Rightarrow$ the approximate log-likelihood is

$$ L_{n}(\bm{\theta}|\varepsilon_{t}) = -(n-r)\log(2\sigma)-\frac{1}{\sigma}\sum_{t=1}^{n}|\varepsilon_{t}| $$

and can be maximized with respect to the scale parameter to obtain

$$ \hat{\sigma} = (n - r)^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{n}|\varepsilon_{t}| $$

and derive the following concentrated likelihood objective function

$$ Q_{n}(\bm{\theta}|\varepsilon_{t}) = -(n-r)(1+\log(2)) - (n - r)^{-1}\log\big(2(n-r)^{-1}\big) -\log\Bigg(\btxt{\sum_{t=1}^{n}|\varepsilon_{t}|}\Bigg) $$

where $\bm{\theta}$ is a $r$ vector of parameters

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Estimation of MAR
SLIDE: Least Absolute Deviation for generalized Mixed Phase ARMA
CONTENU:
- As the **Laplace** distribution has fat tails, it is attractive here
- Let $X_{t}$ be a generalized Mixed Phase ARMA

$$ \varphi^{\circ}(F)\varphi^{\bullet}(B) X_{t} = \theta^{\circ}(F)\theta^{\bullet}(B)\varepsilon_{t} $$

with $\varepsilon_{t}$ a SWN in the domain of attraction of $\alpha$-stable distributions

- Wu (2011) shows that the LAD objective function

$$ Q_{n}(\bm{\theta}|\varepsilon_{t}) \equiv \btxt{\sum_{t=1}^{n+p-q}|\frac{\theta^{\circ}_{q^{\circ}}}{\varphi^{\circ}_{p^{\circ}}}\varepsilon_{t}(\bm{\theta})|} $$

with $p = p^{\circ} + p^{\bullet}$, $q = q^{\circ} + q^{\bullet}$ and $\bm{\theta}$ a vector of $p+q$ parameters

- In practice, to build $\varepsilon_{t}(\bm{\theta})$, Wu and Davis (2010) suggest

- 1 to compute forwards $v_{t}^{\circ}(\bm{\theta}) = \Phi(L)X_{t} - \theta^{\bullet}_{1}v_{t-1}^{\circ}(\bm{\theta}) - \ldots - \theta^{\bullet}_{q^{\bullet}}v_{t-q^{\bullet}}^{\circ}(\bm{\theta})$ recursively for $t = 1,\ldots,n+p$ and $v_{t}^{\circ}(\bm{\theta}) = 0$ for $t \leq 0$

- 2 to compute backwards $\varepsilon_{t}(\bm{\theta})$ given that $v_{t}^{\circ}(\bm{\theta}) = \theta^{\circ}(F)\varepsilon_{t}$ and hence

$$ \varepsilon_{t}(\bm{\theta}) = \frac{1}{\theta^{\circ}_{q^{\circ}}}\Big( v_{t+q^{\circ}}^{\circ}(\bm{\theta}) - \varepsilon_{t+q^{\circ}}(\bm{\theta}) - \theta^{\circ}_{1}\varepsilon_{t+q^{\circ}-1}(\bm{\theta}) - \ldots - \theta^{\circ}_{q^{\circ}-1}\varepsilon_{t+1}(\bm{\theta})\Big) $$

for $t = n+p-q^{\circ},\ldots,-q^{\circ}+1$ and $\varepsilon_{t}(\bm{\theta}) = 0$ for $t > n + p - q^{\circ}$.
slide_title: Least Absolute Deviation for generalized Mixed Phase ARMA

text:
COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Estimation of MAR
SLIDE: Limit theory of the LAD for generalized Mixed Phase ARMA
CONTENU:
- Wu (2011) shows that the LAD estimator $\hat{\bm{\theta}} = \arg\min\limits_{\bm{\theta} \in \Theta} Q_{n}(\bm{\theta}|\varepsilon_{t})$

$$ a_{n}(\hat{\bm{\theta}} - \bm{\theta}) \,{\buildrel d \over \longrightarrow}\, \bm{\nu}_{\min}, \;\;\; a_{n} = \inf\{x : \mathbb{P}(|\varepsilon_{1}| > x) \leq n^{-1}\} $$

with $\bm{\nu}_{\min}$ a random variable with no closed form expression

- $\Rightarrow$ the LAD estimator is $n^{1/\alpha}$-consistent $> n^{1/2}$ when $\alpha \in (0,2)$

- As $\bm{\nu}_{\min}$ is untracktable $\Rightarrow$ bootstrap : Davis and Wu (1997) & Cavaliere et al. (2018)

- Davis and Wu (2010) discuss the finite variance case

- $\Rightarrow$ for instance, if $X_{t}$ is a strong MAR$(p,q)$ with Laplacian errors

$$ \sqrt{n}(\hat{\bm{\varphi}}^{\bullet} - \bm{\varphi}^{\bullet}) \,{\buildrel d \over \longrightarrow}\, \mathcal{N}\Bigg(0,\frac{1}{4 f_{\varepsilon}^{2}(0)\mathbb{E}\big(v_{t}^{2}\big)}\Bigg), \;\;\; \sqrt{n}(\hat{\bm{\varphi}}^{\circ} - \bm{\varphi}^{\circ}) \,{\buildrel d \over \longrightarrow}\, \mathcal{N}\Bigg(0,\frac{1}{4 f_{\varepsilon}^{2}(0)\mathbb{E}\big(u_{t}^{2}\big)}\Bigg) $$

with $v_{t} = \varphi^{\circ}(F)X_{t}$, $u_{t} = \varphi^{\bullet}(L)X_{t}$ and $\bm{\varphi}^{\circ} = \varphi^{\circ}_{1},\ldots,\varphi^{\circ}_{p}$ ($\bm{\varphi}^{\bullet}$ resp.)

- To evaluate $f_{\varepsilon}^{2}(0)$ a logistic kernel can be used (see Hecq et al. 2017)

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
- Davis and Wu (1997) explored the bootstrap procedure for causal autoregressive processes with infinite variance, and showed its asymptotic validity. It should be possible to adapt this approach to the noncausal case in the spirit of Cavaliere et al. (2018) who suggest a non-causal bootstrap for other purpose.
- $\alpha$ can be estimated in a 2nd step using for instance the Hill's tail-index estimator on $\hat{\varepsilon}_{t}$
slide_title: Limit theory of the LAD for generalized Mixed Phase ARMA

text:
COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Estimation of MAR
SLIDE: Generalized Covariance (GCov) Estimator
CONTENU:
- **Motivation:** estimate semi-parametric dynamic models with **i.i.d. errors**.

- Applicable to models like non-linear mixed causal-noncausal VAR, Stochastic Volatility...

- Let the model be: $g(\tilde{Y}_{t};\theta)=u_{t}$, where $u_t$ is i.i.d. ($\tilde{Y}_t$ contains current/lagged $Y_{t}$).

- Core Idea: Minimize a residual-based multivariate **portmanteau statistic**.

- Define residuals $\hat{u}_t(\theta) = g(\tilde{Y}_{t};\theta)$.

- Let $\hat{\Gamma}(h;\theta)$ be the sample autocovariance of $\hat{u}_t(\theta)$ at lag $h$.

- Define $\hat{R}^{2}(h,\theta)=\hat{\Gamma}(h;\theta)\hat{\Gamma}(0,\theta)^{-1}\hat{\Gamma}(h;\theta)^{\prime}\hat{\Gamma}(0;\theta)^{-1}$.

- GCov Estimator of Gourieroux & Jasiak (2023)

$$ \hat{\theta}_{T}(H)= \arg \min_{\theta}\sum_{h=1}^{H}Tr[\hat{R}^{2}(h,\theta)] $$

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Estimation of MAR
SLIDE: Properties of the GCov Estimator
CONTENU:
- **Asymptotic Properties:** Under regularity conditions:

- Consistent: $\hat{\theta}_{T}(H) \,{\buildrel p \over \longrightarrow}\, \theta_0$
- Asymptotically Normal: $\sqrt{T}(\hat{\theta}_{T}-\theta_{0})\sim N[0,\Omega(\theta_{0})^{-1}]$
- Semi-parametrically efficient

- **Identification:**

- Identifies parameters characterizing **serial dependence**
- Does **not** identify drift or scale parameters affecting only the marginal distribution of $u_t$

- **Drawbacks:** relies on higher moment conditions (although simulations support good performance in absence of finite variance)

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Applications
SLIDE: Empirical papers
CONTENU:
1. Forecasting extreme trajectories using seminorm representations by G. de Truchis, S. Fries, A. Thomas, 2025

2. Autoregression-based estimation of the new Keynesian Phillips curve by M. Lanne and J. Luoto, 2013

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Applications
SLIDE: Empirical Application: Forecasting El Niño/La Niña
CONTENU:
- **Context:** El Niño and La Niña are major climate anomalies with significant societal and economic impacts (extreme weather, agriculture, commodity prices, macroeconomic fluctuations)

- They are often measured by the Southern Oscillation Index (SOI), derived from air pressure differences

- The SOI exhibits patterns resembling explosive bubbles followed by crashes, making it suitable for non-causal modeling

- **Goal:** Apply the seminorm representation theory to forecast:

- The probability of returning to normal conditions (reversal probabilities)

- The exact timing of the peak and end of El Niño/La Niña episodes (reversal dates)

- Uses the results from de Truchis, Fries & Thomas (2025)

- **Sample Period:** 01/1951 to 01/2024, split into:

- In-sample: 01/1951 - 12/1991 (for estimation)

- **SOI Time Series Plot:**

- **Model Selection:**

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Applications
SLIDE: Forecasting Reversal Probabilities
CONTENU:
- **Goal:** Estimate the probability of El Niño and La Niña reversal

- **Methodology:** Approximate $\mathbb{P}(\text{Crash at } t+h | \text{Extreme at } t, \text{Pattern matched})$

- Condition 1: extreme magnitude $\|\boldsymbol{X}_{t}\| > x$, approximated by $X_t \ge q_{\tau}$ (e.g., 90th or 95th quantile)

- Condition 2: observed pattern
$$ (X_{t-m}, \ldots, X_t)/\|\boldsymbol{X}_{t}\| $$
falls in a small neighborhood $B(V_0)$ around a theoretical pattern $\vartheta_0 \boldsymbol{d}_{k_0}/\|\boldsymbol{d}_{k_0}\|$

- Target Event: future path returns to central values

- **Results (Selected):** Probabilities (in %) of returning to central values ($\delta=0.5$)

[Tableau]

| In-Sample | Out-of-Sample
Horizon ($h$) | $p_{0.95}$ | $\hat{p}_{0.95}$ | $p_{0.95}$ | $\hat{p}_{0.95}$
$h=3$ | 54.17 | 75.00 | 63.46 | 67.31
$h=5$ | 83.33 | 87.50 | 92.31 | 84.62

Notes: $p_q$ = theoretical prob., $\hat{p}_q$ = empirical freq. for quantile $q=0.95$. $m=2$.
- High probability of reversal within 5 months: unlikely persistence of very extreme La Niña events

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Applications
SLIDE: Forecasting Reversal Dates: Methodology
CONTENU:
- **Goal:** Predict the exact peak and end date of an El Niño/La Niña episode

- Leverage the **deterministic** nature of asymptotic forecasts for MAR(0,2) when $m \ge 1$

- If $\|\boldsymbol{X}_{t}\|$ is large and $(X_{t-m}, \ldots, X_t)$ matches a specific MA($\infty$) segment, the future path is determined

- **4-Step Procedure**:

- 1. Compute the observed normalized pattern $(X_{t-m}, \ldots, X_t) / \|\boldsymbol{X}_{t}\|$ for a chosen $m \ge 1$
- 2. Compute theoretical patterns $\vartheta \boldsymbol{d}_k / \|\boldsymbol{d}_k\|$ for a range of $k$ (using the exact $\delta_k$ coefficients)
$$ \boldsymbol{d}_k = (\delta_{k+m}, \ldots, \delta_k, \ldots, \delta_{k-h}) $$
- 3. Find the unique $k_0$ such that $\vartheta_0 \boldsymbol{d}_{k_0} / \|\boldsymbol{d}_{k_0}\|$ is closest to the observed pattern with $\vartheta_0$ the sign of the event
- 4. The future path is predicted to follow the shape of $\vartheta_0 \boldsymbol{d}_{k_0}$

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Applications
SLIDE: Forecasting Reversal Dates: El Niño 1991/1992 Example
CONTENU:
- **Scenario:** forecast the El Niño event starting at the end of the in-sample period (Dec 1991) with $X_t$ large and negative ($\vartheta_0 = -1$)

- **Pattern Matching:**

- Try different past window lengths $m \in [1, 10]$

- For $m=1, 2$ and $m \in [5, 10]$, the procedure robustly identifies $k_0 = 1$

- Retain $k_0 = 1$ with $m=10$. This means the observed pattern matches the segment $(\delta_{11}, \ldots, \delta_1)$

- **Prediction:**

- Since $k_0 = 1$, the process is predicted to follow the shape $-\boldsymbol{d}_1 / \|\boldsymbol{d}_1\|$

- The coefficients $\delta_k$ for $k \le 0$ are zero for MAR(0,2). The peak occurs at $t+k_0 = t+1$. The reversal (return to zero) occurs shortly after, at $t+k_0+1 = t+2$

- Predicted peak date: Jan 1992. Predicted reversal date: Feb 1992

CONTENU:
- New Keynesian Phillips curve (NKPC) :

$$ \pi_t=\gamma_f \mathbb{E}_t \pi_{t+1} + \lambda x_t $$

inflation rate $\pi_t$ depends linearly on

$\bullet$ the expected inflation rate next period, $E_t\pi_{t+1}$ , and

$\bullet$ a measure of marginal costs, $x_t$.

- Hybrid NKPC (Gali and Gertler, 1999) : also include lagged inflation

$$ \pi_t=\gamma_f \mathbb{E}_t \pi_{t+1} +\gamma_b\pi_{t-1}+ \lambda x_t $$

- Inflation is highly persistent $\rightarrow$ debate on the source :

$\bullet$ dependence on past inflation in forming expectations ?

$\bullet$ agents’ forward-looking behavior ?

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Applications
SLIDE: Empirical paper 2 : stylized facts
CONTENU:
- Main issue: the marginal cost variable $x_t$ is not directly observable

$\bullet$ use real unit labor cost

$\bullet$ use the output gap
- Following the rational expectations literature

$$ \pi_t=\gamma_f \pi_{t+1} +\gamma_b\pi_{t-1}+ \eta_{t+1}, $$

where $\eta_{t+1} = \xi_{t+1}+\lambda x_t$, with $\xi_{t+1}=\gamma_f \mathbb{E}_t\pi_{t+1}-\gamma_f\pi_{t+1}$

- If $\eta_t$ were i.i.d., this would be the MAR(1, 1) model of Lanne and Saikkonen (2011a)

- In practice, need to allow $\eta_t$ to be autocorrelated, hence assume the autocorrelation in the error term $\eta_t$ to be adequately captured by a (potentially noncausal) MAR$(p-1, q-1)$ process

$$ \varphi^{\circ}(F)\varphi^{\bullet} (B) y_t=\varepsilon_t $$

NOTES DE L'ENSEIGNANT:
- AR(r, s) model of Lanne and Saikkonen (2011a)

- the polynomials $\varphi^{\circ}$ and $\varphi^{\bullet}$ have their zeros outside the unit circle

-Lanne and Saikkonen (2011a) showed how model (1) can be consistently estimated by the method of maximum likelihood (ML).

- (local) ML estimator is asymptotically normally distributed, and a consistent estimator of the limiting covariance matrix is obtained in the usual way from the standardized Hessian of the log- likelihood function.

- need to impose estimation constrants on the two gamma param such that phi-roots are outside the unit cercle and psi-roots are greater than unity

-similar write-up for the purely forward-looking NKPC model

SLIDE: Empirical paper 2 : further results
CONTENU:
- Finding the correct variable driving the process of inflation is crucial for identification in conventional GMM and ML estimation approaches put forth in the previous literature

- Because here we have no estimate of $\lambda$, the deep parameters cannot be uniquely solved, but $\lambda x_t$ can be solved as
$$ \lambda x_t=\pi_t-\hat\gamma_f \mathbb{E}_t \pi_{t+1}-\hat\gamma_b \pi_{t-1} $$

once the NKPC is estimated and the obtained time series is informative about the properties of the implied drivers of the inflation series.

- The authors find that the driving processes of the two inflation series exhibit relatively low persistence

- This indicates that persistence is mostly intrinsic instead of being inherited from a persistent driving process

CONTENU:
- The results lend support to both forward-looking and backward-looking dynamics, with the former clearly dominating

- Consequently, inflation persistence appears to be intrinsic as opposed to being inherited from a persistent driving process

COURS: Research_Econometrics (M2)
CHAPITRE: Résumé
CONTENU:
Ces dernières années l'économétrie des séries temporelles a connu un changement de paradigme important avec l'avènement des processus anticipatifs ou non-causaux, jusque là confinés aux sciences physiques. La force de cette approche réside dans la capacité des modèles à capturer des dynamiques non-linéaires, complexes et d'apparence non-stationnaire, au travers d'équations linéaires et parcimonieuses mais orientées vers le futur. De plus, ces dynamiques anticipatives trouvent des fondements profonds dans la théorie macro-économique et la finance car les agents économiques sont par essence « foward looking » et susceptible de générer des trajectoires auto-réalisatrices ou spéculatives. Mais pour être en mesure d'identifier ces dynamiques, il faut accepter de s'affranchir de l'hypothèse canonique de normalité des erreurs. Dès lors, surviennent de nouveaux enjeux de modélisation, d'estimation et de prédiction, notamment parce que les comportements des séries économiques présentant des trajectoires non-causales appellent à considérer des lois à queues Paretiennes pour les innovations. Cette thèse d'HDR s'inscrit principalement dans l'exploration de ces défis relevant de la théorie économétrique, passe en revue mes travaux en cours et s'essaye à construire un agenda de recherche ambitieux pour les années à venir. Des contributions plus spécifiques en économétrie financière sont également discutées, en cohérence avec l'évolution de ma recherche en économétrie des séries temporelles durant ces 10 dernières années.

Mon parcours académique débute en 2010 à l'Université d'Aix-Marseille (AMU) au sein d'Aix-Marseille School of Economics (AMSE) où j'ai effectué une thèse en **économétrie des séries temporelles** sous la supervision de Gilles Dufrénot et Marcel Aloy. Ma première année a été marqué par un changement radical de thématique recherche car mon financement de thèse a été obtenu intialement pour un sujet sur le marché du travail. Conscient dès mon mémoire de master que mon réel intérêt était orienté sur les aspects méthodologiques et l'économétrie, j'ai demandé à mes directeurs une réorientation qu'ils ont acceptée. Mes travaux se sont alors focalisés sur la modélisation des séries financières et macro-financières avec une attention particulière sur les phénomènes de co-mouvement et de dépendance à longue portée.
